Raw-JSON import of tables/columns/checks, either preserving external primary keys or letting the system generate new ones.

Item Content URL POST /api/model/table/import/preserveId Params bodyJson: body, string (raw JSON text), required, the import JSON must contain a table (object) and a columns (array) node, with checks (array) optional; every record in all three parts must carry an id. ddl: query, boolean, optional, default true, whether to create/update the database table structure right after a successful import. Returns ApiResult<Map<String,Object>>: import counts tables/columns/checks; all records are saved as-is under their external IDs (forceId preserves the primary key), audit fields are overwritten with the current user/tenant/time, and the entity metadata cache is refreshed afterwards.

Item Content URL POST /api/model/table/import/create Params bodyJson: body, string (raw JSON text), required, the import JSON must contain a table (object) and a columns (array) node, with checks (array) optional; every record in all three parts must NOT carry an id. ddl: query, boolean, optional, default true, whether to create/update the database table structure right after a successful import. Returns ApiResult<Map<String,Object>>: import counts tables/columns/checks; all records are saved with new system-generated IDs, audit fields are overwritten with the current user/tenant/time, and the entity metadata cache is refreshed afterwards.
Design-time CRUD and name-uniqueness validation of views (TableView).
Item Content URL POST /api/model/view/pageQuery Params Pagination and filter params: see Conventions Returns ApiPagedResult<TableView>: paged list of views.
Item Content URL GET /api/model/view/query Params Pagination and filter params: see Conventions Returns ApiResult<List<TableView>>: list of views (method signature declares a raw ApiResult).

Item Content URL GET /api/model/view/get/{id} Params id: path, string, required, view ID. Returns ApiResult<TableView>: view detail; the view column configuration viewColumn is converted into column metadata structures.

Item Content URL POST /api/model/view/createOrUpdate Params form: body, TableView object, required. Common fields: view name viewName, view type viewType, construct SQL viewConstruct, view columns viewColumn, connection connectId, etc. Returns ApiResult<TableView>: before saving, the view columns are mapped into database object structures; after saving, the metadata cache is refreshed by view name (method signature declares a raw ApiResult).

Item Content URL DELETE /api/model/view/isDelete/{id} Params id: path, string, required, view ID. Returns ApiResult<NullResult>: marks disabled and soft-deletes (the database view is renamed for archival, except materialized views) and removes the view metadata cache; data is empty.

Item Content URL POST /api/model/view/validate Params form: body, TableView object, required; uses viewName, connectId, appId, tenantCode. Returns ApiResult<Boolean>: checks whether the view name is duplicated within the same connection (queries platform_dev_view); true when available.

1 controller with 13 endpoints in total. All endpoints in this domain are design-time APIs (@DesignTimeApiRestController): engine-neutral materialized view acceleration management. Dual-record architecture — enabling adds a same-named materialized replica row in the platform (metadata loading prefers the materialized row and queries route to the engine), disabling soft-deletes the replica row and falls back to the original view, and dropping removes it entirely; the engine (e.g. RisingWave) is chosen by the connection's db_type and dispatched via adapters.

Full lifecycle management of materialized views: precheck, CDC source creation, preview/validate/step-by-step execution of the 3-step DDL, view initialization, enable/disable, metadata refresh, data comparison and drop. All endpoints are POST with a JSON object body.

Item Content URL POST /api/model/mv/precheck Params engineConnectId: body, string, required, engine connection ID. originConnectId: body, string, required, source database connection ID. viewName: body, string, optional, view name (used in the precheck report). tables: body, string array or comma-separated string, optional, source table list. database: body, string, optional, source database name (falls back to the name registered on the source connection). snapshot: body, boolean, optional, default true, whether to run the initial snapshot backfill. Returns ApiResult<Map<String,Object>>: passed indicates whether all checks passed; items is the per-item check result (engine adapter, non-empty table list, source object resolution/expansion, engine-side checks, etc.). No DDL is executed.

Item Content URL POST /api/model/mv/source/create Params engineConnectId: body, string, required. originConnectId: body, string, required. viewName: body, string, required (normalized to lowercase automatically). tables: body, string array or comma-separated string, required, source table list (MySQL views are expanded to physical tables automatically; an error is raised when no physical table resolves). database: body, string, optional, source database name. snapshot: body, boolean, optional, default true. Returns ApiResult<Map<String,Object>>: engineType, sourceName, physicalTables, tableMapping (source table → engine ingest table) and the 3-step DDL payload ddl; executes the DDL to set up the ingest channel and persists the DDL JSON to the replica row.

Item Content URL POST /api/model/mv/ddl/preview Params engineConnectId: body, string, required. originConnectId: body, string, required. viewName: body, string, required. originSql: body, string, optional, the view's defining SELECT (falls back to the defining SQL of the same-named original view row when absent). tables: body, string array or comma-separated string, optional, source table list. database: body, string, optional, source database name. snapshot: body, boolean, optional, default true. Returns ApiResult<Map<String,Object>>: sourceName, expandedSql, engineSql, physicalTables, expandedViews, passed and steps (per-step DDL text and per-item check results); no DDL is executed against the engine, and the DDL JSON is persisted to the replica row only on first preview.

Item Content URL POST /api/model/mv/ddl/validate Params Same params as previewDdl, plus ddl: body, object, optional, the (possibly edited) 3-segment DDL payload sent back by the front end (sourceDdl, a cdcTables array with originTable/engineTable/ddl, mvDdl; CDC ingest table identifiers cannot be modified). Returns ApiResult<Map<String,Object>>: validation result shaped like the preview (passed and per-step steps conclusions); no DDL is executed.

Item Content URL POST /api/model/mv/ddl/step/execute Params stepKey: body, string, required, step identifier (source / cdc:<originTable> / mv). Other params are the same as previewDdl (including the optional edited ddl payload). Returns ApiResult<Map<String,Object>>: executed/reused/message/passed/items/detail; steps failing validation are blocked from execution; when stepKey=mv executes successfully, materialized, mode, columns and ddlJson are included (platform replica row and metadata are synced).

Item Content URL POST /api/model/mv/view/create Params engineConnectId: body, string, required. originConnectId: body, string, required. viewName: body, string, required. originSql: body, string, optional, defining SELECT (falls back to the original view row when absent). tables: body, string array or comma-separated string, optional, source table list. database: body, string, optional, source database name. snapshot: body, boolean, optional, default true. recreate: body, boolean, optional, default false, set true when legacy channel naming conflicts or a rebuild is needed. ddl: body, object, optional, edited 3-segment DDL payload (validated per step first; no DDL runs when validation fails). Returns ApiResult<Map<String,Object>>: after all prechecks pass (view expansion, SQL rewrite, SELECT syntax, CDC column types, platform default columns), the 3-step DDL is executed; returns mode, reused, sourceName, expandedSql/engineSql, physicalTables, ddlJson, columns, engine status and message; before backfill completes (status=BACKFILLING) query results are incomplete — confirm READY via view/status before serving queries.

Item Content URL POST /api/model/mv/view/status Params engineConnectId: body, string, required. viewName: body, string, required. Returns ApiResult<Map<String,Object>>: engineType, viewName, enabled (whether an enabled materialized replica row exists in the platform) and the engine-reported status (used to confirm backfill READY).

Item Content URL POST /api/model/mv/view/enable Params engineConnectId: body, string, required, engine connection ID. viewName: body, string, required, original view name (a materialized view is an acceleration replica of an existing view). originSql: body, string, optional, defining SELECT (falls back to the original view row when absent). Returns ApiResult<Map<String,Object>>: only creates/restores the materialized replica row (the engine is not initialized); returns mode (created/updated), enabled=true and a note (view columns pending backfill; run view/create before serving queries).

Item Content URL POST /api/model/mv/view/disable Params viewName: body, string, required. Returns ApiResult<Map<String,Object>>: soft-deletes the materialized replica row and refreshes metadata (queries fall back to the source database view; the engine-side materialized view is kept and can be reused without backfill on re-enable); returns enabled=false and a note.

Item Content URL POST /api/model/mv/view/refreshMeta Params viewName: body, string, required. Returns ApiResult<Map<String,Object>>: reloads entity metadata and clears the data source routing cache; when the replica row's column metadata is missing and the view exists in the engine, columns are re-synced, returned as syncedColumns (-1 when no re-sync was triggered).

Item Content URL POST /api/model/mv/view/compareData Params engineConnectId: body, string, required. originConnectId: body, string, required. viewName: body, string, required. originSql: body, string, optional, defining SELECT. tables: body, string array or comma-separated string, optional, source table list. database: body, string, optional, source database name. Returns ApiResult<Map<String,Object>>: allMatch and per-table results in tables (source row count vs engine ingest table row count with countMatch, latest-row column diffs by update_at in latestMismatches), plus a row-count comparison between the materialized view and the original view's query; large-table COUNTs are slow, avoid frequent calls.

Item Content URL POST /api/model/mv/view/checkQuery Params engineConnectId: body, string, required. viewName: body, string, required. Returns ApiResult<Map<String,Object>>: runs SELECT * ... LIMIT 1 and COUNT(*), returning queryOk, totalRows, columns, sampleRow (one sample row) and the engine status.

Item Content URL POST /api/model/mv/view/drop Params viewName: body, string, required. dropSource: body, boolean, optional, default false, whether to also drop the CDC source and ingest tables. originConnectId: body, string, required when dropSource=true. database: body, string, required when dropSource=true (unless the source connection has a registered database name). Returns ApiResult<Map<String,Object>>: drops the engine-side materialized view and soft-deletes the replica row; with dropSource=true ingest tables are cleaned according to shared-channel references (a shared source still referenced by other views is kept), returning droppedCdcTables and sharedSourceKept.
1 controller with 9 endpoints in total. Controllers marked with ⚙ are design-time APIs.

Platform notification center: inbox paging for the current user, unread-count badge, read/star/archive/delete, proactive sending and recall. Importance has four levels: 0 normal, 1 reminder, 2 important, 3 urgent.

Item Content URL POST /api/notification/pageQuery Params readStatus: body, int, optional, read-status filter (0 unread, 1 read). archived: body, int, optional, archive filter (0/1). bizType: body, string, optional, business-type filter (e.g. order/contract/task). keyword: body, string, optional, fuzzy search over title or content (OR semantics). title: body, string, optional, fuzzy search over the title only; when passed together with keyword the semantics are an intersection. priorityGe: body, int, optional, importance lower bound (0-3, >= the given level). orderByPriority: body, boolean, optional, when true sorts by importance from high to low (time descending within the same level); time descending by default. Pagination and filter params: see Conventions (page size is clamped to [1,100]). Returns ApiPagedResult: data is a flat row set of your inbox (recipient status joined with the notification subject, including title, content, action URL actionUrl, etc.).

Item Content URL GET /api/notification/unread-count Params priorityGe: query, int, optional, importance lower bound (0-3); e.g. priorityGe=2 counts unread items that are "important and above". Returns ApiResult<Long>: unread notification count of the current user (bell badge).

Item Content URL POST /api/notification/read/{id} Params id: path, string, inbox record ID. Returns ApiResult<Boolean>: data indicates whether the marking succeeded; validated against inbox ownership.
Item Content URL POST /api/notification/read-all Params None Returns ApiResult<Integer>: data is the number of records marked as read.

Item Content URL POST /api/notification/star/{id} Params id: path, string, inbox record ID. value: body, int, optional, 1 to star, 0 to unstar; default 1. Returns ApiResult<Boolean>: data indicates whether the update succeeded.

Item Content URL POST /api/notification/archive/{id} Params id: path, string, inbox record ID. value: body, int, optional, 1 to archive, 0 to unarchive; default 1. Returns ApiResult<Boolean>: data indicates whether the update succeeded.

Item Content URL DELETE /api/notification/delete/{id} Params id: path, string, inbox record ID. Returns ApiResult<Boolean>: data indicates whether the deletion succeeded; only removes your own inbox record and does not affect other recipients.

Item Content URL POST /api/notification/send Params recipients: body, List<String>, required, list of recipient userIds. channels: body, List<String>, optional, delivery channels; defaults to in-app only [inapp] when empty. title: body, string, title. content: body, string, content. senderId: body, string, optional, sender userId; falls back to the current logged-in user, or system when there is no login context. senderName: body, string, optional, sender name. senderType: body, string, optional, sender type; defaults to USER, set it to SYSTEM explicitly for system triggers. bizType: body, string, optional, business type for business idempotency and classification. bizId: body, string, optional, business key; combined with bizType it forms the idempotency key. actionUrl: body, string, optional, click-through URL. priority: body, int, optional, importance: 0 normal (default)/1 reminder/2 important/3 urgent; invalid values are rejected. Returns ApiResult<String>: data is the created notification subject ID. Dispatch orchestration: writes the subject and the outbox per channel. Callable by external systems (Authorization: SystemToken <fixed key>).

Item Content URL POST /api/notification/recall/{id} Params id: path, string, notification subject ID. Returns ApiResult<Boolean>: data indicates whether the recall succeeded; logically deletes the notification subject (del_status), which invalidates every user's inbox association, so inbox queries no longer show it. Fails when the notification does not exist.
6 controllers, 24 endpoints in total. Endpoints marked with ⚙ are design-time APIs.
Template supporting APIs for PDF recognition: parse PDF annotation meta, resolve or clear PDF content by template, rule testing, and time format validation.

Item Content URL GET /api/ocr/pdf/meta/{fileId} Params fileId: path, string, attachment ID of the PDF file. Returns ApiResult<List<PDFAnnotationMeta>>: data is the annotation meta list resolved from the PDF (via the OCR plugin).

Item Content URL GET /api/ocr/pdf/resolve0 Params fileId: query, string, attachment ID of the PDF file. templateId: query, string, OCR PDF template ID. wholeContent: query, boolean, optional, default false, whether to return the whole resolved PDF content. Returns With wholeContent=true, data is a PDFResolveData (whole PDF content resolved by the template meta); otherwise a List<PDFAnnotationPickContent> (contents picked at annotation positions). Fails when the file does not exist or the template/template meta is empty.

Item Content URL POST /api/ocr/pdf/content/clear Params fileId: query, string, attachment ID of the PDF file. annotationPositionMetaList: body, List<AnnotationPositionMeta>, annotation position regions whose content should be cleared. Returns ApiResult<String>: data is the new attachment ID of the saved PDF with cleared content (genre clearPdf).

Item Content URL GET /api/ocr/pdf/resolve Params fileId: query, string, attachment ID of the PDF file. templateId: query, string, OCR PDF template ID; supports multiple comma-separated IDs, tried one by one. wholeContent: query, boolean, optional, default false, whether to return the whole resolved PDF content. Returns On a template match, with wholeContent=true returns ApiResult<OcrPdfWhole> (with formatted contents), otherwise ApiResult<List<OcrPdfContent>> (formatted field contents); fails with Template matching failure when no template matches. Candidate templates must first pass the whole-content regexp validation.

Item Content URL POST /api/ocr/pdf/meta/test Params data: body, Map<String,Object>, keys: content (content string to process), rule (rule JSON array string, parsed into List<OcrPdfMetaRule>), metas (meta JSON array string, parsed into List<OcrPdfContent>). ORM entity hooks are a purely additive feature: after the transaction of any entity insert/update/delete in the platform commits, the full payload JSON is POSTed to the hook URL and the downstream system dispatches by entityName/eventType; triggering and execution are fully asynchronous, retried/dead-lettered through the outbox (platform_orm_hook_log), and failures never propagate to the business path. This domain covers hook configuration CRUD, execution outbox monitoring and dead-letter replay.

Runtime data (audit logs, number-issuing records, notifications, mail bodies, page version history, low-code business tables) keeps growing and drags down query performance, backup size and packaging size. The data-archive feature provides a policy-driven, observable, recoverable general archive engine: it moves expired data from source tables to an archive target (MySQL archive database/table in phase 1), and two-phase reconciliation guarantees that a crash at any moment leaves at most extra data in the source table — data is never lost.

Module Responsibility geelato-archive-policy Policy management: policy entity (platform_archive_policy), enable-gate validation (hard failure), preset templates, entity-management "enable archive" entry, policy REST API geelato-archive-engine Archive engine: target table structure check, two-phase reconciled migration (SERVER/LOCAL_FILE/JDBC), daily scheduling, run records (platform_archive_run), manual trigger/cancel/restore, run REST API Both modules are fully self-contained (no changes to geelato-web-platform) and are customization modules (not in the scaffold or the standard-part version catalog; no host includes them yet). A single dependency on geelato-archive-engine activates everything: auto-configuration, idempotent table creation, preset loading, controllers registered via the host's @ComponentScan("cn.geelato").

Policies are table-based (decoupled from entities): table_name + condition. Usually created from entity management "enable archive" (POST /api/archive/entity/enable {entityName} → resolve physical table name → insert a disabled policy), or manually via POST /api/archive/policy/createOrUpdate. DEFAULT policy: condition fixed to create_at < now - retention_days; the watermark is locked once at run start (no boundary drift during long runs). CUSTOM policy: where_condition is an arbitrary WHERE fragment (e.g. batch < 'B2024-001'). Safety model: the condition only participates in "selecting ids"; migration and deletion always execute precisely by id IN (...) — a wrong condition can only move fewer rows, never lose them. Enabling runs a static safety validation (no semicolons/comments/DML/DDL/file-keywords) + a trial run (syntax errors hard-fail 70001). Target: target_type (MYSQL in phase 1; MONGODB/ELASTICSEARCH in phase 2) + connect_id (dev_db_connect system; empty = archive within the primary database) + target_table_name (derived if empty: same name cross-database; {source}_archive in the same database). Execution parameters: execution_mode (AUTO/SERVER/LOCAL_FILE/JDBC), batch_size (default 200), batch_interval_ms (default 200 throttle), max_rows_per_run (default 1,000,000 — progressive archiving: large tables complete over multiple days), include_deleted (default true). Lifecycle: policies are disabled by default — with no enabled policy, no data is ever touched; enabling passes the gate (below); parameters are snapshotted at run start; one run per policy at a time.

Mode Data path Fit & performance SERVER INSERT INTO target SELECT … WHERE id IN + DELETE, all server-side Same DB/instance; zero data out of the database, fastest LOCAL_FILE Stream export to temp file → LOAD DATA LOCAL INFILE into the archive DB Recommended cross-instance; near-native LOAD DATA (an order faster than INSERT); auto-degrades to JDBC if localInfile is disabled or binary columns exist JDBC Streaming read + batch insert (rewriteBatchedStatements) General fallback AUTO (default) Runtime probe: same instance → SERVER; otherwise LOCAL_FILE (falls back to JDBC) Always the fastest path for the current topology

Per batch (id cursor ascending, LIMIT batch_size): Phase 1 write archive: clear leftovers DELETE → write (by mode) → reconcile (loaded rows == expected AND target count == expected) mismatch → 70003 abort (source untouched, zero loss) Phase 2 delete source (transaction): DELETE WHERE id IN → reconcile (deleted == expected) mismatch → 70004 abort and roll back the whole batch (archive complete; rerun safe) Update run progress (rows/batches/cursor) → check cancel flag → sleep(batch_interval_ms) Crash safety: at any crash point the source table has at most extra data, never missing data; reruns clear leftovers first (no INSERT IGNORE, so errors are not masked). Directional principle: prefer duplicates (data in both sides) over loss (deleted from source, absent in archive). Run records: platform_archive_run records status/rows/batches/cursor/watermark/actual mode/duration; failures carry error_json with table, batch index, cursor, expected vs actual counts and the stack trace.

Source table name is valid (injection-safe) and not in the protected list (archive's own tables, user/role/org/tenant, dev_db_connect, etc.); Policy type valid: DEFAULT requires retention_days ≥ platform minimum (default 30); CUSTOM requires a condition that passes safety validation; Source table physically exists; DEFAULT requires a date-typed create_at column; Archive connection (connect_id) reachable; In-database archive target must differ from the source table name; One enabled policy per table; CUSTOM condition trial run (syntax interception); Target structure check: create from SHOW CREATE TABLE if absent; if present, compare columns — a missing column → 70002 abort (never silently skipped).

note All endpoints are declared via @ApiRestController/@ApiRuntimeRestController; in hosts with the /api prefix (quickstart, scaffold) the real path carries /api. Authentication goes through the platform interceptor. Endpoint Description POST /api/archive/policy/pageQuery Policy page query GET /api/archive/policy/get/{id} Policy detail POST /api/archive/policy/createOrUpdate Create/update (new policies always disabled) DELETE /api/archive/policy/isDelete/{id} Soft delete (rejected while running) POST /api/archive/policy/validate/{id} Pre-enable validation POST /api/archive/policy/enable/{id} · /disable/{id} Enable (gate-checked) / disable POST /api/archive/entity/enable Entity-management "enable archive" (input: entityName) POST /api/archive/run/pageQuery · GET /api/archive/run/get/{id} Run history POST /api/archive/run/trigger/{policyId} Trigger one policy (synchronous) POST /api/archive/run/triggerAll Run all enabled policies once (silent afterwards) POST /api/archive/run/cancel/{policyId} Graceful cancel (finishes current batch) POST /api/archive/scheduler/start · /stop · GET /api/archive/scheduler/status Runtime scheduler start/stop/status (in-memory; resets on restart) POST /api/archive/run/archivedData Online read-only paging over archived data POST /api/archive/run/restore Restore (body: policyId + ids; reverse two-phase reconciliation) Error codes 70xxx are listed in the Error Code Reference (70xxx data-archive section).

Besides /api/archive/run/archivedData (per-policy single-table query), the platform provides a request-level switch: with the header X-Gl-Archive-Query: true, all ORM reads within that request route to the archive database — a business page can toggle between "online data / archived data" views without any API change. This is a platform standard part (neutral request-level datasource override in geelato-orm + archive semantics and request filter in geelato-web-platform); it does not depend on the archive customization modules.
documents.s: Online Query of Archived Data (request-level datasource switch)

documents.t: spring.datasource.archive.jdbc-url=jdbc:mysql://localhost:3306/geelato_archive?useUnicode=true&characterEncoding=utf-8&useSSL=false&serverTimezone=GMT%2B8 spring.datasource.archive.username=geelato_user spring.datasource.archive.password=****** spring.datasource.archive.driver-class-name=com.mysql.cj.jdbc.Driver Configuring jdbc-url enables it (nothing is wired otherwise); the archive schema must match the primary database (guaranteed by the engine's table cloning) and dbType must match.

Only entities without explicit ownership switch: entities without connectId and without an effective catalog route to the archive DB; catalog=platform entities (users/dictionaries/menus/metadata) keep their routing — page framework, dictionary translation and permissions keep working. Explicit routing is never hijacked: explicit entity connectId, DSL useDataSource, programmatic withDataSource all take precedence over the request-level override. Read-only; writes hard-fail: insert/update/delete on unowned entities throws a clear exception in archive mode — archive consistency is guaranteed by two-phase reconciliation; online writes would bypass it. Generic entity template endpoints hard-fail: BaseService.pageQueryModel/queryModel/getModel uses primaryDao and does not participate; in archive mode they hard-fail and direct you to /meta/list (the MQL generic query path routes correctly). Request context is cleaned up automatically; schedulers/engines/async threads without request context are unaffected.

"archive" is a reserved datasource key — never use it as a platform_dev_db_connect row id; Dynamic switching inside transactions has known limits — archive mode is read-only browsing; avoid write transactions in archive-mode requests; Template queries joining platform tables (e.g. tree queries joining platform_tree_node) hard-fail in archive mode (the archive DB lacks platform tables) — use dedicated endpoints; SQL logging (p6spy) and pool monitoring apply to the archive datasource as well.

In "view archived data" browse mode the HTTP interceptor injects X-Gl-Archive-Query: true on all requests (accepted values true/1/on, case-insensitive); leaving browse mode stops the injection. If the archive datasource is not configured, the backend hard-fails such requests (pointing out the missing spring.datasource.archive.jdbc-url), never silently degrading.

The engine does not run by default — no scheduler thread, no automatic archiving (geelato.archive.scheduler-enabled defaults to false). Three ways to run: Method Endpoint/config Description Trigger one policy POST /api/archive/run/trigger/{policyId} Synchronous single run Trigger all once POST /api/archive/run/triggerAll Serial run of all enabled policies, silent afterwards Temporary daily schedule POST /api/archive/scheduler/start Daily at schedule-time (default 02:00); /stop anytime; in-memory, resets on restart For a permanent schedule set geelato.archive.scheduler-enabled=true. Policies run serially by seq_no; one failure does not block the rest. The scheduler is a self-managed daemon thread (per the NotificationOutboxScheduler convention, no @EnableScheduling).

Key Default Description scheduler-enabled false Start the scheduler with the application schedule-time 02:00 Daily execution time min-retention-days 30 Minimum retention gate protected-tables core tables Protected list default-batch-size / default-batch-interval-ms 200 / 200 Defaults for new policies default-max-rows-per-run 1000000 Per-run row cap default temp-dir ${java.io.tmpdir}/geelato-archive LOCAL_FILE temp directory auto-init-tables true Idempotent table creation at startup auto-load-presets true Load preset templates at startup (idempotent)

Data archive is a customization module: not in geelato-app-scaffold-starter, not in geelato-framework-starter / geelato-framework-bom, not registered in the root aggregate pom (same precedent as geelato-mail's commented entry). Build standalone (policy first, then engine): mvn clean install -f geelato-archive-policy/pom.xml -DskipTests mvn clean install -f geelato-archive-engine/pom.xml -DskipTests Then declare the dependency explicitly (with version): <dependency> <groupId>cn.geelato</groupId> <artifactId>geelato-archive-engine</artifactId> <version>1.0.0-SNAPSHOT</version> </dependency> (geelato-archive-policy comes in transitively.) A logback routing rule for cn.geelato.archive is recommended. On startup: idempotent table creation → preset loading (disabled) → daily scheduler. Review and enable policies from policy management.

The front-end entry lives in the geelato-front repo: model management (GlModelList) → entity detail tabs → the "Data Archive" tab (next to "Entity Hooks"). Location: packages/gl-ide-arco/src/views/sidebar/model/archive/; API wrappers in packages/gl-runtime-core/src/m/datasource/ModelApi.ts. Shape: one policy per entity, a configuration panel — empty state with "Enable Archive" (idempotent policy creation); once enabled, a policy form (type/retention/condition/target DB/target table/execution params) + enable/disable switch (gate failures show the 70001 reason) + save/delete + run records (paged dialog with status/rows/batches/duration/error detail, manual run and cancel). Note: the IDE hardcodes Chinese by convention (no i18n); the online-query and restore UIs are not in the phase-1 tab (APIs are ready).

MongoDB / Elasticsearch archive channels (Channel SPI: bulkWrite / _bulk; target_type reserved; the request-level switch is dbType-agnostic); SeaTunnel external executor (data plane delegated to a dedicated sync engine; executor field reserved); Front-end management pages; Separate soft-deleted window (by delete_at), tenant-differentiated retention.

This page explains how to extend the platform runtime authentication chain with a new authentication scheme (authenticator). The runtime authentication entry point of the platform is DefaultSecurityInterceptor, which itself knows nothing about concrete authentication schemes. All schemes — JWTBearer, Anonymous, WeixinUnionId, WeixinWorkUserId, SystemToken, Bearer (OAuth2), WeixinCode — are plugged in through the same SPI interface TokenAuthenticator. Adding a new authentication method requires no changes to the interceptor: just implement the interface and register it as a Spring Bean.

Read this page if: You want the platform to recognize a new Authorization header prefix (e.g. DingtalkCode <code>, ApiKey <key>) You want to integrate a new external identity source (DingTalk scan, third-party OAuth, device fingerprint) while reusing the platform user system and session chain You want an external system credential to be exchanged directly for a runtime user context This page is not the right place if: You only want to change where user data is loaded from → see Provider Contracts You only want to adjust how organizations or roles are loaded → see Provider Contracts You need a brand-new Shiro credential type that no existing Realm can express → framework-level evolution, see LoginCredential semantic boundary

The responsibilities of the authentication chain are split in two halves. Make this split clear before extending: Request (Authorization: <scheme> <credential>) │ ▼ TokenAuthenticatorRegistry Routes by prefix to the single authenticator │ ▼ TokenAuthenticator (yours) Does exactly two things: credential check + user resolution │ — must not import any Shiro type ▼ DefaultSecurityInterceptor Uniformly responsible for: │ SecurityContext population │ Shiro session establishment (routes to existing Realms by credential type) │ Context cache / delegation / traffic tagging / online tracking ▼ Business request proceeds This boundary is a hard constraint: Authenticator implementations must not import any org.apache.shiro type. Shiro's Subject.login(...) and all AuthenticationToken types are handled uniformly by the interceptor Authenticators should not perform context operations other than returning the result — the interceptor completes the remaining steps in a fixed order All schemes share the same "uniform session establishment" tail logic, so a new scheme inherits cache restoration, delegation, online tracking and other capabilities for free
The interface and data carriers live in the cn.geelato.web.common.security.spi package.

Method Contract Collection<String> schemePrefixes() The Authorization header prefixes this authenticator owns, with a trailing space (e.g. "DingtalkCode "). Prefixes must be mutually exclusive across authenticators default boolean supports(String rawToken) Whether the header value starts with one of this authenticator's prefixes (default: prefix list check) default void preAuthCheck(TokenAuthenticationContext ctx) Method-level access gate, executed before cache restoration so cached credentials cannot bypass it. Default: no gate TokenAuthentication authenticate(ctx) Credential check + user resolution. Return the result on success; throw UnauthorizedException (with root cause) on failure — never swallow exceptions or return null

The result carrier on success: public record TokenAuthentication(User user, String password, LoginCredential login, boolean trackOnline) { public TokenAuthentication(User user, String password, LoginCredential login) { this(user, password, login, true); // trackOnline defaults to true } } Field Meaning user Session user (already cloned per token; used directly by the interceptor, no further cloning needed) password Credential written into SecurityContext; Shiro session establishment depends on it login Credential descriptor required for session establishment, see below trackOnline Whether to count into online users. Virtual principals (e.g. system tokens) pass false

public record LoginCredential(String type, String principal, String credential) The interceptor routes the authentication result to an existing Shiro Realm by type: Constant Realm Check semantics TYPE_USERNAME_PASSWORD DbRealm / AnonymousRealm Login name + password (salted hash or fixed anonymous password) TYPE_WEIXIN_UNION_ID WeixinUnionIdRealm Reverse lookup on User.weixinUnionId column TYPE_WEIXIN_WORK_USER_ID WeixinWorkUserIdRealm Reverse lookup on WeCom userId TYPE_OAUTH2 OAuth2Realm Reverse lookup by accessToken TYPE_SYSTEM_TOKEN SystemTokenRealm Constant-time fixed secret comparison principal / credential values vary by type (login name and password for the password scheme, the extend key itself for extend-key schemes) — refer to the existing authenticator implementations.

Input of a single authentication: Field Meaning rawToken Raw Authorization header value (with prefix) request Current request handlerMethod Target handler method (for gates reading annotations; guaranteed non-null by the interceptor) stripped(prefix) Convenience: credential body with the scheme prefix removed

The following semantics are enforced by the framework and must be respected: Mutually exclusive prefixes, fail fast at startup. If two authenticators register the same prefix, application startup throws IllegalStateException. Confirm no conflict with existing prefixes (JWTBearer , Anonymous , WeixinUnionId , WeixinWorkUserId , SystemToken , Bearer , WeixinCode ). Unrecognized prefixes are rejected with 401. Requests carrying an unregistered prefix throw UnauthorizedException with no fallback. Only registered prefixes enter authentication. Failures must throw with root cause. Do not catch (Exception) { return false; } and do not return null. The legacy implementation swallowed exceptions, making troubleshooting hard; the current contract is to throw UnauthorizedException("...: " + cause). The HTTP outcome is still 401, but logs pinpoint the failing step. preAuthCheck runs before cache restoration. A cache hit short-circuits authentication, so a method-level gate placed inside authenticate would be bypassed by cached credentials — that is exactly why the @AllowSystemAccess gate of SystemToken lives in preAuthCheck. If your scheme has similar per-method restrictions, the gate must be overridden in preAuthCheck.
Pick a prefix that does not conflict with existing schemes. The trailing space is mandatory (matching is startsWith; the space separates scheme from credential).

package com.example.auth; import cn.geelato.core.GlobalContext; import cn.geelato.security.OrgProvider; import cn.geelato.security.User; import cn.geelato.security.UserProvider; import cn.geelato.web.common.interceptor.UnauthorizedException; import cn.geelato.web.common.security.auth.AbstractTokenAuthenticator; import cn.geelato.web.common.security.spi.LoginCredential; import cn.geelato.web.common.security.spi.TokenAuthentication; import cn.geelato.web.common.security.spi.TokenAuthenticationContext; import cn.geelato.web.common.security.spi.TokenAuthenticator; import org.springframework.stereotype.Component; import java.util.Collection; import java.util.List; @Component public class DingtalkCodeTokenAuthenticator extends AbstractTokenAuthenticator { public static final String PREFIX = "DingtalkCode "; private final DingtalkClient dingtalkClient; private final UserProvider userProvider; public DingtalkCodeTokenAuthenticator(OrgProvider orgProvider, UserProvider userProvider, DingtalkClient dingtalkClient) { super(orgProvider); this.userProvider = userProvider; this.dingtalkClient = dingtalkClient; } @Override public Collection<String> schemePrefixes() { return List.of(PREFIX); } @Override public TokenAuthentication authenticate(TokenAuthenticationContext ctx) { String code = ctx.stripped(PREFIX); try { // 1. Credential check: call the external system to exchange for an identity String unionId = dingtalkClient.exchange(code); // 2. User resolution: map to a platform user User user = userProvider.getUserByExtendKey(unionId, "weixinUnionId"); if (user == null) { throw new UnauthorizedException("DingTalk identity not bound to any platform account"); } // 3. Load the full session user (with org info), return the result — the rest is up to the interceptor User currentUser = loadUser(user.getLoginName(), user.getTenantCode()); return new TokenAuthentication(currentUser, GlobalContext.getAnonymousPwd(), new LoginCredential(LoginCredential.TYPE_USERNAME_PASSWORD, currentUser.getLoginName(), GlobalContext.getAnonymousPwd())); } catch (UnauthorizedException e) { throw e; } catch (Exception e) { throw new UnauthorizedException("DingTalk credential check failed: " + e.getMessage()); } } } Three key points: Extend cn.geelato.web.common.security.auth.AbstractTokenAuthenticator to reuse loadUser(loginName, tenantCode) (load user + org info + the clone protecting the shared snapshot), setupOrgInfo(user, orgId) and copyOf(user) A plain @Component is enough. BootApplication scans the whole cn.geelato package and host projects usually scan their own packages; TokenAuthenticatorRegistry collects all TokenAuthenticator beans automatically OrgProvider and UserProvider required by the constructor are existing container beans — inject them directly
documents.s: Step 2: Implement the authenticator and register it as a Spring Bean

documents.t: Only needed when your scheme restricts which endpoints may be called with this credential — see how SystemTokenAuthenticator handles @AllowSystemAccess.

Do not stop at a successful Spring startup. Call a protected endpoint with the new prefix and confirm business data is returned and SecurityContext holds the current user; then call once with a wrong credential and once with an unbound identity, confirming 401 with the root cause in logs.
documents.s: Step 4: Verify with a real request

documents.t: The SPI extension covers "credential check + user resolution": a new credential source mapped onto one of the existing Realm semantics. The existing 5 type values (table above) cover most scenarios: password-based, WeChat-based, OAuth2-based, system-token-based If an external identity system fits none of them (e.g. challenge-response credentials), a new Realm must be added at framework level and the routing switch of DefaultSecurityInterceptor#createShiroToken extended — that is framework-level evolution with the same cost as before, not part of the host-side SPI extension

A real two-layer extension case: the platform provides a generic authenticator, the host implements only a smaller SPI. In WeChat mini-program scenarios, business requests may carry Authorization: WeixinCode <js_code> (the one-time credential of wx.login()) for authentication. Since each host integrates its own mini-program appid/secret, the platform-side WeixinCodeTokenAuthenticator only handles generic orchestration: code → unionid result cache (5 minutes, aligned with the code validity, covering frontend retries that reuse the same code and avoiding WeChat error 40163) unionid → platform user: reuses the existing UserProvider.getUserByExtendKey(unionid, "weixinUnionId") chain Session establishment: LoginCredential(TYPE_WEIXIN_UNION_ID, ...) → WeixinUnionIdRealm How the code is exchanged for a unionid (calling WeChat jscode2session, which requires appid/secret configuration) is implemented by the host through a smaller SPI exposed by the platform: package cn.geelato.web.common.security.spi; public interface WeixinCodeResolver { /** js_code → unionid. Throw UnauthorizedException (with root cause) on failure. */ String resolveUnionId(String jsCode); } Host-side implementation (excerpt from customer-client): @Component @ConditionalOnProperty(prefix = "customer-client.wx.miniapp", name = "enabled", havingValue = "true", matchIfMissing = true) public class WxMiniAppCodeResolver implements WeixinCodeResolver { // GET https://api.weixin.qq.com/sns/jscode2session?appid=..&secret=..&js_code=.. // errcode 40029/40163/45011 mapped to UnauthorizedException with readable messages // missing unionid (mini-program not bound to WeChat Open Platform) → UnauthorizedException } WeixinCodeTokenAuthenticator wires the resolver via ObjectProvider: when the host provides no implementation, the WeixinCode channel uniformly returns 401 (channel disabled) and all other schemes are unaffected. Combined with a @ConditionalOnProperty switch, the channel can be turned off in one place. The pattern behind this example is reusable: when the orchestration logic of a scheme family is generic but the credential exchange depends on host-specific external configuration, put a generic authenticator plus a host-implemented exchange SPI on the platform side.
documents.s: Worked Example: the WeixinCode Mini-Program Fallback Channel

documents.t: Three root causes of 401: missing Authorization header / unregistered prefix (including a channel switched off) / gate or credential check failure. The first two show up in interceptor and registry warn logs; the third carries the root cause in the authenticator's UnauthorizedException message Authenticated but still 401: check that authenticate returned a proper user (with loginName/tenantCode); loadUser throws "user not found" when the user cannot be loaded Caching and validity: after a successful authentication the interceptor writes tokenContextCache (30 minutes); subsequent requests with the same credential are restored from cache. Scheme-specific external credential caches (like WeixinCode's code→unionid) are maintained by each authenticator Log hygiene: never print credential raw values (tokens, codes, secrets) inside authenticators — record only scheme and prefix, as OAuth2TokenAuthenticator does

Authentication and Authorization — full runtime authentication chain Provider Contracts — replacing user / organization / role sources Security Context — SecurityContext lifecycle and usage constraints

The unified authentication center is the authoritative data source for organizations, users, and roles (the identity directory). Data integration answers: how do integrated business systems sync this master data and its relationships (user↔org, user↔role, org↔role) to their own side, or how do they provision their user data into the auth center. Login integration (Lite Login Integration / OAuth2 Protocol Integration) answers "where the identity comes from"; this chapter answers "where the data comes from and how to manage it".

Users and orgs: tenant-level shared. All integrated systems under the same tenant share one set of users (auth_user) and orgs (auth_org) — accounts work across systems, which is the prerequisite of unified login (SSO). Roles: bound to appCode. Each business system only sees and manages "its own" roles, plus read-only references to __global__ roles (e.g. the four built-in data scopes). User directory mode: geelato.auth.user-directory.mode=central|primary. The standalone auth center and the Open Management API always operate on the central directory tables (auth_user / auth_org); primary mode is for embedded hosting that keeps its own user tables.

Relationship Table Notes User ↔ Org auth_user_r_org A user belongs to an org (direct department); membership itself does not inherit that org's roles User ↔ Role auth_user_r_role Granted per appCode; only affects this system, never the user's roles in other systems Org ↔ Role auth_org_r_role Dept role: a role granted to an organization User ↔ Dept role auth_user_r_org_role The dept role effective for a user in a given org — the only way a dept role takes effect User ↔ Permission auth_user_r_permission Permissions granted directly to a user Effective permissions = user roles ∪ effective dept roles ∪ direct grants; see Permission Integration for details.

Channel Direction Best for Notes ① Open Management API (CRUD) Write / query the auth center Initializing master data, day-to-day self-management Machine token; endpoint reference in Open Management API ② geelato-auth-client SDK Query / read Java backends querying users / orgs / roles (picker components, auth context) Machine token managed automatically ③ Account Provision API Write to the auth center Approval flows / process platforms auto-provisioning accounts per business request Idempotent, one-time password, forced first-login password change ④ SQL scripts Cross-database sync Platform-side historical data migration, read-table sync for process platforms Ops scenario, not API-based

With a machine token (how to obtain), call /api/open/v1/** to create, read, update, and delete orgs, users, roles, and their relationships: Orgs: POST /api/open/v1/orgs create, GET /tree fetch the org tree, GET /{orgId}/users-tree fetch an org with its users, GET /{orgId}/ancestors|descendants ancestor / descendant chains; Users: POST /api/open/v1/users create (pass orgId in the body to attach to an org), PUT /{userId}/roles overwrite-style role assignment; Roles: POST /api/open/v1/roles create (auto-bound to the caller's appCode), PUT /{roleId}/permissions assign permissions, PUT /{roleId}/users overwrite-style user assignment; Dept roles: GET /api/open/v1/orgs/{orgId}/roles, GET /{orgId}/roles/{roleId}/users inspect dept roles and their effective users. Full endpoint reference: Open Management API. New-system initialization example (create org → create user → create role → grant): BASE=https://<auth-center> # 1) Exchange machine token TOKEN=$(curl -s -X POST "$BASE/oauth2/client_token" \ -d "grant_type=client_credentials&client_id=<client_id>&client_secret=<client_secret>" \ | sed -E 's/.*"access_token":"([^"]+)".*/\1/') # 2) Create an org curl -s -X POST "$BASE/api/open/v1/orgs" -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \ -H "Content-Type: application/json" -d '{"code":"dev-dept","name":"R&D","type":"dept"}' # 3) Create a user attached to the org curl -s -X POST "$BASE/api/open/v1/users" -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \ -H "Content-Type: application/json" \ -d '{"loginName":"zhangsan","name":"Zhang San","password":"Init@123","orgId":"<orgId>"}' # 4) Create a role, assign permissions, grant the role to the user (overwrite-style) curl -s -X POST "$BASE/api/open/v1/roles" -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \ -H "Content-Type: application/json" -d '{"code":"demo-admin","name":"Demo Admin"}' curl -s -X PUT "$BASE/api/open/v1/roles/<roleId>/permissions" -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \ -H "Content-Type: application/json" -d '{"ids":["<permissionId1>","<permissionId2>"]}' curl -s -X PUT "$BASE/api/open/v1/users/<userId>/roles" -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \ -H "Content-Type: application/json" -d '{"ids":["<roleId>"]}'

Java backends should prefer the SDK over hand-written HTTP and token handling: <dependency> <groupId>cn.geelato</groupId> <artifactId>geelato-auth-client</artifactId> </dependency> Configuration (prefix geelato.auth.client.*): Property Description Default enabled Enable auto-configuration true base-url Auth center base URL; the SDK is only wired when set — client-id / client-secret OAuth client credentials (machine token) — connect-timeout-millis / read-timeout-millis Timeouts 5000 / 15000 token-refresh-seconds Machine token proactive refresh window 3600 provisioning-cache-ttl-seconds Provisioning cache TTL (0 = disabled) 0 Capability 1: AuthCenterSecurityProvider implements the geelato-security SecurityProvider contract for querying users / orgs / roles: getUserById / getUserByLoginName / getOrgByCode / getRoleByCode / getUserRoles / queryUsersByIds / queryUsersOfOrg / queryUsersOfOrgRole / queryOrgRoles / querySubOrgs / queryAncestorOrgs / queryPermissionsOfRole / queryPermissionsOfUser, etc. — all mapped to /api/open/v1/**. Machine tokens are obtained and cached automatically by AuthCenterTokenManager. Ideal for user-picker components and org / person lookups on business forms. Capability 2: AuthCenterProvisioningClient pulls effective permissions and visible menus (getPermissions / getMenus, mode=simple|full); this belongs to the permission distribution channel — see Permission Integration.

Endpoint prefix: /api/open/v1/account-provisions. Designed for process / approval platforms: once an approval is passed, provision the account automatically per request. Method Path Description POST / Provision an account; body: {requestId, loginName, name, mobilePrefix?, mobilePhone?, email?, roleCodes or roleIds, orgId?, tenantCode?} GET /{requestId} Query the provisioning result by request id POST /{requestId}/regenerate-password Regenerate the initial password for a provisioned account Key semantics: Idempotent resume: requestId is the caller's idempotency key (backed by the auth_account_request table). Calling a COMPLETED request again returns repeated=true and never returns the password again; PENDING / FAILED requests resume automatically. One-time password delivery: the initial password is 12 strong-random characters, returned once in the success response only, never stored server-side; if lost, regenerate via regenerate-password. Forced first-login password change: provisioned users get must_change_password=1; the login response carries user.mustChangePassword=true so the frontend guides the change (the Lite Login response already includes it together with mobilePrefix / mobilePhone for the change-password verification code). Roles fail-closed: pass exactly one of roleCodes / roleIds (both → 400); if any role cannot be resolved / belongs to another system / is disabled, the whole request fails with FAILED — no partially-authorized accounts.

For bulk sync between platform tables and auth center tables (database level, not API integration). The auth center repo provides under docs/sql/: Script Purpose migrate-platform-user-to-auth-user.sql One-shot idempotent migration platform_org/user/... → auth_org/user/... (when switching to the central directory mode) sync-auth-to-platform.sql Reverse add-only backfill auth_* → platform_* (re-populating platform tables after switching modes) sync-auth-core-tables-to-wf.sql Full idempotent upsert auth_* → wf_* (read-side tables for the process platform) create-auth-core-tables.sql Manually create the 7 core tables (identical to the Flyway final state) tip Scripts only fit ops scenarios where both databases are reachable on the same instance; regular integrations should always use channels 1–3.

appCode binding: roles, menus, permissions, and grants are isolated by app_code (= the caller's oauth_client.system_code); requests must not specify another appCode (mismatch → 403, omitted → auto-assigned); tenantCode binding: users and orgs are tenant-level data; the tenant comes from the client record and cannot be specified; __global__ is read-only: global roles / menus / permissions are visible and referencable to every integrator (e.g. assignable to your own roles), but cannot be modified or deleted via the Open API; Audit and notifications: every write is recorded in the audit hash chain as CLIENT:clientId; permission-related changes automatically trigger the Redis notification (geelato:permission:change) and version bumps — downstream mirror systems need no extra handling.

Use channel 1: follow the example above to create orgs, users (attached to orgs), roles with permission assignments, then grant roles to users; afterwards wire up Permission Integration to pull effective permissions.

documents.t: Use channel 3: approval passed → POST /api/open/v1/account-provisions (requestId = the approval id) → deliver initialPassword once via SMS / ticket → the user changes the password on first login.
documents.s: Scenario B: auto-provision accounts from an approval flow

documents.t: Use channel 2: add geelato-auth-client and call queryUsersOfOrg / querySubOrgs / getUserByLoginName etc. through the SecurityProvider contract for picker components and form displays.
documents.s: Scenario C: query org / person data from a business backend

documents.t: Note: this chapter introduces the feature menus that ship with the Auth Center admin console, following the actual structure of the admin sidebar and explaining what each feature is for. Integrators can use this chapter to understand what capabilities the Auth Center offers out of the box and the problems each one solves; administrators can use it as a menu-by-menu orientation. For how these features are consumed via the Open API, refer to the integration chapters.

The Auth Center admin console has six menu groups: Menu Group Features Purpose in One Sentence Client Management Clients Register and maintain OAuth2 client applications (client_id / secret / redirect URIs) Identity Management Organizations, Users, Roles Maintain the org structure, accounts and roles — the source of identity and authorization data Permission Management Menus, Permissions Register downstream menus and the five types of permission points for role binding and distribution Authentication Social Login, Token Query Configure third-party login channels; inspect token details during integration Business Audit Audit Records, Session Control Search audit events with tamper-evident verification; manage online sessions and force logout System Management Dictionaries, App Config Routine maintenance of system-level dictionaries and runtime parameters

Manages the clients (applications) registered with the Auth Center — a prerequisite for OAuth2 integration: Register a new client and get a client_id / client_secret pair Configure redirect URIs, grant types, token validity and other integration parameters Reset the client secret when needed Any business system adopting OAuth2 Protocol Integration (authorization code or machine-to-machine) must be registered here first; Lite lightweight integration relies on client configuration as well.

Maintains the org structure of the Auth Center: a company / department hierarchy, with users assigned to departments. Org data forms the backbone of user master data and underpins department-level authorization (departments bound to roles). To sync org data into business systems, see Data Integration.

Manages the full lifecycle of user accounts: create / edit accounts, enable or disable them, reset passwords, and assign each user a department and roles. Which permissions a user ends up with after login is determined by the roles and departments assigned here.

Maintains roles and their authorization bindings: a role can bind users, menus and permission points at the same time. Roles are the bridge between "people" and "permissions" — permission distribution is computed from a user's effective permissions, which are aggregated from roles. For how permissions are distributed to business systems, see Permission Integration.

Registers menu trees for downstream applications: menus come in three types — catalog, menu and button — and can carry a permission code. Menu data serves two purposes: it is the object of role authorization (which menus a role can bind), and it is distributed together with the user's effective permissions so business systems can render dynamic menus. Under the Management Integration mode, integrators can also read menu data via the Open API — see Management Integration.

Registers and manages permission points. Permission points come in five types, corresponding one-to-one with the five groups of a user's effective permissions: Type Meaning dp Data Permission mp Model Permission cp Column Permission ep Element Permission (element-level control such as page buttons) fp Function Permission (API / operation level) The set of valid permission types is enforced by a system whitelist; the dictionary only maintains their display metadata. Business systems consume the distributed result in a fail-closed manner via Permission Integration.

Configures the application credentials and callback parameters of third-party login channels (WeChat, WeCom, Feishu, DingTalk) per tenant. Once configured, the unified login page and Lite login can present the corresponding third-party login options. See Lite lightweight integration.

Paste an access_token to inspect its details: token storage mode (memory / redis), owning client, the logged-in user behind it, validity, and more. Primarily for integration debugging — for example, confirming whether a token was issued successfully and which application and user it belongs to.

Searches the security audit events of the Auth Center: filter by category, result (success / failure / denied / error), actor and keyword, and inspect event details. Audit events are recorded as a hash chain with an integrity verification entry point, so any tampering with records can be detected — meeting security audit requirements.

Views and manages online sessions: list all current sessions, or query all sessions of a user by login name; kick out all sessions of a login name, or kick out a specific device by device type. Used for emergency logout and session governance when an account is compromised.

Maintains the dictionaries and dictionary items of the Auth Center: three built-in dictionaries — permission type (permission_type), org type (org_type) and menu type (menu_type) — plus custom dictionaries for business extensions. Built-in dictionaries are protected (cannot be deleted, codes cannot be modified, controlled dictionaries reject new items); dropdowns across the admin console are driven by them.

Maintains the runtime parameters of the Auth Center (key-value configuration in app_config). Changes take effect online via hot refresh — no restart required — making it easy to toggle runtime switches of the Auth Center modules.

The admin console maintains the "source data"; business systems consume it through the integration blocks: Admin Feature Data Produced How Integrators Consume It Client Management OAuth2 client credentials OAuth2 Protocol Integration, Lite lightweight integration Orgs / Users / Roles Identity master data Data Integration (Open API / SDK / SQL scripts) Menus / Permission points + Role binding User effective permissions Permission Integration (five-type distribution) Social Login Third-party login channels Third-party login entries of both login integration methods Audit Records / Session Control Auditing and session governance Built-in console capabilities for operational security Dictionaries / App Config System-level configuration Management Integration (Open API reads dictionaries, etc.)
documents.s: How Admin Features Map to the Integration Blocks

documents.t: Service and blocks overview: Independent Service — Unified Authentication Center Login integration: Lite lightweight integration, OAuth2 Protocol Integration Data integration: Data Integration Permission integration: Permission Integration Open API reference: Management Integration

This page explains how any third-party application can integrate with the lite-login lightweight login facade provided by the unified authentication center, focusing on two things: how the frontend obtains the token issued by auth-server how the third-party backend uses that token to call OAuth endpoints and confirm user identity This guide does not assume that the third-party application already has fixed endpoints such as /api/user/info, /session/me, or /auth/profile. Those endpoints are application-specific. Sample projects: Repository: geelato-hello-example lite-login integration sample: sample-lite-login

The minimal acceptable result is: the third-party frontend can open or embed lite-login the frontend receives LOGIN_SUCCESS after login succeeds the frontend can extract and store the token the third-party backend can call /oauth2/userinfo with a Bearer token the third-party backend can build its own local identity mapping from the returned user

auth-server is the only token issuer lite-login is the lightweight login facade lite-login handles login and returns the token auth-server confirms the identity behind that token through OAuth endpoints
opens or embeds lite-login listens to postMessage extracts accessToken/token stores the token temporarily passes the token to its own backend in later requests

reads the Bearer token from the request header calls /oauth2/userinfo extracts user identity from the response establishes session state, account mapping, or permission context according to its own domain model

Use the explicit lightweight login entry: https://<auth-host>/lite-login Do not reuse: /login?display=embedded Each third-party application should keep its own: /login That page is only the third-party handoff page and should not implement username-password authentication itself.

The lite-login page ships with the following login methods — business systems need no extra development: Username-password login: with graphic / slider / rotate captchas (as configured in the auth center). SMS verification-code login: mobile phone + code; the code channel is isolated from the forgot-password channel. Third-party login: the page automatically renders the third-party providers enabled for the current tenant (WeChat, WeCom, Feishu, DingTalk); clicking redirects to the corresponding platform for authorization; unbound users go through an "verify account-password then bind" flow. Forgot / reset password: built into the login page. First-login forced password change: users created through account provisioning (see Data Integration) carry a forced-change flag in the login result; the frontend guides them through the change accordingly. Underlying Lite authentication APIs (provided by the auth center's geelato-auth-login; you can also call them directly to build your own login UI): Method Path Description POST /api/auth/login Password or SMS login; body: {username, password?, captchaToken?, scene?, loginType?, authCode?}; loginType=sms switches to SMS verification POST /api/auth/login/sms/send Send the login SMS code (unregistered numbers are rejected) POST /api/auth/refresh Refresh the token; body: {refreshToken} POST /api/auth/logout Log out the current session GET /api/auth/captcha, /slider, /rotate, etc. Captcha image and verification endpoints GET /api/oauth2/providers Third-party providers enabled for the current tenant GET /api/oauth2/authorize/{provider} Start third-party authorization (302 to the platform) POST /api/oauth2/callback Third-party callback (unbound users get 2001 needBind plus a bindToken valid for 5 minutes) POST /api/oauth2/bind Complete binding with bindToken + account-password, then log in Login is risk-controlled: repeated failures trigger account locking (423) and rate limiting (429); surface these response codes as hints.
The complete interaction sequence for integrating a business system with lite-login is as follows:

The user visits the third-party application's own /login The application loads /lite-login?display=embedded&redirect=... lite-login sends LOGIN_INIT The user completes login inside lite-login lite-login sends LOGIN_SUCCESS The frontend extracts the token The frontend stores the token temporarily The frontend includes the token when calling its own backend The backend calls /oauth2/userinfo The backend continues business processing with the resolved user identity
At minimum prepare: liteSsoBaseUrl the base address of the lightweight login facade for example: http://app.localgl.cn liteSsoOrigin the allowed postMessage origin for example: http://app.localgl.cn

Each application should provide its own /login page as the handoff page for unified authentication. Recommended options: iframe embedded login popup or new-window fallback The iframe URL should be built as: /lite-login?display=embedded&redirect=<business-target-url>

The frontend should at least handle: LOGIN_INIT the login page is initialized LOGIN_SUCCESS login succeeds the token payload exists in data LOGIN_CLOSE the user closes or cancels login SET_LOCALE the parent page controls the display language of the embedded lite-login mainly for host pages that manage multi-language state centrally

The frontend should at least be compatible with this structure: { "type": "LOGIN_SUCCESS", "data": { "accessToken": "xxx", "token": "xxx", "refreshToken": null, "expireInSeconds": 7199, "tokenType": "Bearer", "issuer": "auth-server", "user": { "id": "123", "username": "zhangsan", "nickname": "Zhang San", "email": "zhangsan@example.com", "mustChangePassword": false, "mobilePrefix": "+86", "mobilePhone": "13800000000", "phone": "+8613800000000" } } } Use this priority when extracting the token: accessToken token First-login forced password change: when user.mustChangePassword === true, the account was created by the account-provision flow and its initial password must be changed on first login. After receiving LOGIN_SUCCESS, guide the user to the change-password flow (the auth center ships a reset page at /oauth2/lite-reset, or build a custom one); the verification-code parameters can be taken directly from mobilePrefix / mobilePhone in the contract. Do not let the user into the business system before the change completes.

When lite-login is embedded in a third-party application via iframe with display=embedded, the language switcher is no longer exposed by the embedded page itself — the parent page controls it centrally. This design has two purposes: the host page maintains its own language state without a second switch inside the iframe embedded login is usually just part of the host's login flow, so following the host's language feels natural Current constraints: applies only to /oauth2/lite-login?display=embedded supported locale values are zh-CN and en-US invalid values fall back to the default locale via the system's existing logic

Depending on whether the parent page and the auth center share the same origin, use one of two approaches: Approach 1: same-origin iframe direct call​ If the parent page and lite-login are same-origin, call the global method exposed by the child page directly: iframe.contentWindow?.setLiteLoginLocale?.('en-US') This fits: host page and lite-login sharing the same domain or both being unified under one origin via a reverse proxy Approach 2: cross-origin iframe via postMessage​ If the parent page and lite-login have different origins, the parent cannot access contentWindow.setLiteLoginLocale; send a language-switch message via postMessage instead: iframe.contentWindow?.postMessage( { type: 'SET_LOCALE', data: {locale: 'en-US'} }, targetOrigin ) Recommendations: write targetOrigin explicitly as the auth center domain — never * after the parent completes its own language switch, notify the embedded page to follow
documents.s: How the Parent Page Switches the Embedded Page's Language

documents.t: In cross-origin scenarios, the message the parent page sends to lite-login looks like: { "type": "SET_LOCALE", "data": { "locale": "en-US" } } Field notes: type fixed value SET_LOCALE data.locale target locale recommended values: zh-CN, en-US Security requirements: lite-login still validates the message origin the parent page must not rely on "any origin may send messages" for cross-origin deployments, make sure the auth center side has configured trusted origins

After receiving LOGIN_SUCCESS, the standard frontend actions are only: extract and store the token pass that token to the application's own backend in later requests Do not hard-code a rule that login success must always be followed by a call to a fixed user-info endpoint, because different third-party applications may not expose the same endpoint shape.
At minimum store: geelato_sso_token geelato_sso_user geelato_sso_expires Whether the application also stores additional local session data is application-specific.
The application's shared request layer should automatically read the token and append: Authorization: Bearer <token> This avoids repeating manual header wiring in every business request.
A lightweight startup recovery flow can be: read geelato_sso_token if the token exists and is not expired, continue using it if the backend later confirms the token is invalid, clear the local token

The third-party backend does not need to expose a fixed user-info confirmation endpoint of its own. The minimal viable approach is: any business endpoint reads Authorization extract the Bearer token call /oauth2/userinfo extract the user from the response build the application's own identity mapping continue the current business request

The current /oauth2/userinfo response is no longer a direct User, but a session wrapper: { "code": 200, "msg": "ok", "data": { "accessToken": "...", "token": "...", "tokenType": "Bearer", "issuer": "auth-server", "loginId": "demo", "user": { "...": "..." } } } So the backend must: parse data then extract data.user Do not parse the entire data block directly as a User.
Recommended shared helper logic: if data.user exists, parse data.user otherwise fall back to the older data -> User structure This keeps backward compatibility with historical versions.

After resolving the central-authentication user, the application decides its own follow-up logic, for example: use the central user directly as the current user map the system account from loginId bind accounts by email, phone number, or employee number create or update a local user mirror enrich the user with local tenant, role, or organization context No unified LoginResult response shape is required here.
The frontend must validate: event.origin === liteSsoOrigin Never trust arbitrary page origins by default.
The user returned in LOGIN_SUCCESS is only auxiliary display information. The final trusted identity must be confirmed by the backend through the authentication center.
documents.s: Do Not Trust Frontend user Alone

documents.t: When the frontend or backend detects token expiration, it should: clear the local token clear local application session state redirect back to the application's own /login Do not jump directly to the authentication center page.

const handleSsoMessage = (event: MessageEvent) => { if (event.origin !== liteSsoOrigin) return if (event.data?.type !== 'LOGIN_SUCCESS') return const token = event.data?.data?.accessToken || event.data?.data?.token if (!token) return localStorage.setItem('geelato_sso_token', token) localStorage.setItem('geelato_sso_expires', String(Date.now() + 7200 * 1000)) navigateTo('/dashboard') } If the application wants the backend to confirm identity immediately, it may call any of its own backend endpoints right after login success, but that is not a mandatory platform rule.

If the host page supports switching between Chinese and English, fold the iframe language sync into the same switch action: const syncLiteLoginLocale = (iframe: HTMLIFrameElement, locale: 'zh-CN' | 'en-US') => { const childWindow = iframe.contentWindow if (!childWindow) return try { childWindow.setLiteLoginLocale?.(locale) return } catch (error) { // cross-origin falls into message mode } childWindow.postMessage( { type: 'SET_LOCALE', data: {locale} }, liteSsoOrigin ) } Recommended wiring: the host page updates its own i18n state first then calls syncLiteLoginLocale(iframe, locale) if the iframe has not finished loading, re-send the current locale after its load event

public CurrentUser resolveCurrentUser(HttpServletRequest request) { String authorization = request.getHeader("Authorization"); String accessToken = extractBearerToken(authorization); OAuth2ServerResult result = oauth2Service.getUserInfo(authServerUrl, accessToken); JSONObject session = JSON.parseObject(result.getData()); User user = JSON.parseObject(JSON.toJSONString(session.get("user")), User.class); return CurrentUser.from(user); } If old-structure compatibility is required, keep the parsing logic inside a shared helper.

does the application have its own /login does it use /lite-login as the real authentication facade does it validate event.origin does it handle LOGIN_INIT / LOGIN_SUCCESS / LOGIN_CLOSE can it extract accessToken/token correctly can it attach Authorization automatically in later requests can it clear local state when the token expires does it handle the first-login forced password change when user.mustChangePassword=true

can it extract the Bearer token from headers correctly does it trust and verify the auth-server token does it parse the user through data.user is it compatible with the legacy userinfo structure has it implemented its own account-mapping logic

The user was created by the account-provision flow (approval platform) and must change the initial password on first login. Standard handling: read user.mustChangePassword from LOGIN_SUCCESS when it is true, redirect to the change-password page (the auth center ships /oauth2/lite-reset, or build a custom one) and complete the change using mobilePrefix / mobilePhone from the contract to send the verification code only let the user into the business system after the change succeeds For the full account-provision semantics, see Data Integration.
documents.s: What should I do when mustChangePassword=true

documents.t: Check these first: whether the request sent to the third-party backend actually includes the Bearer token whether /oauth2/userinfo is still parsed as the old structure whether the unauthenticated frontend fallback mistakenly treats lite-login as a normal business page
documents.s: Why does the app return to the login page right after successful login

documents.t: This is expected behavior. In display=embedded mode, language switching is controlled by the parent page; the embedded page no longer exposes its own switcher to avoid a language-state mismatch between host and embedded page.
documents.s: Why is there no language switcher in embedded mode

documents.t: Because the browser's same-origin policy blocks the parent from accessing runtime objects of a cross-origin iframe. In that case use: iframe.contentWindow?.postMessage( { type: 'SET_LOCALE', data: {locale: 'en-US'} }, liteSsoOrigin )
documents.s: Why can't the parent call contentWindow.setLiteLoginLocale directly across origins

documents.t: Because it is still a cross-window control message. Without origin validation, any page could forge language-switch messages, making integration behavior uncontrollable. Even though such messages carry no sensitive credentials, they should satisfy the same security requirements as the login messages.
documents.s: Why must SET_LOCALE also validate its origin

documents.t: Because: lite-login only handles unified authentication the third-party application still decides how that user maps into its own system that decision must be made by the third-party backend
documents.s: Why can't we trust the token and user returned directly to the frontend

documents.t: Because: the application needs its own return path the application needs its own wording and handoff page the authentication center only provides the authentication facade, not the entry experience of each application

Use this pattern consistently: the authentication center provides a unified lite-login each third-party application keeps its own /login each third-party frontend follows embedded login, postMessage, parent-controlled embedded language, token storage, and automatic Bearer propagation each third-party backend follows Bearer extraction, /oauth2/userinfo, data.user, and application-specific identity mapping With this pattern, onboarding a new third-party application only requires changing: the application's own /login UI the application's own user-mapping logic The rest of the integration skeleton stays reusable.

The unified authentication center implements standard OAuth2/OIDC protocol endpoints. Whether it is the user-facing authorization code flow (browser login for business systems) or the user-less machine-to-machine flow (client_credentials), both are part of the standard OAuth2 protocol and are documented together in this chapter. If your scenario only needs "a ready-made login page + frontend integration", start with Lite Login Integration; if you need to sync organization / user / role data into your own system, see Data Integration.
