Knowing which beans appear under which conditions helps diagnose "why didn't it switch": Starter side (when spring.datasource.primary.jdbc-url is present): primaryDataSource → primaryJdbcTemplate → primaryDao; with spring.datasource.secondary.* configured, secondaryDataSource and friends appear too. primaryDao connects straight to the physical primary and bypasses routing Dynamic datasource stack (auto-configured when primaryJdbcTemplate exists in the container): dynamicDataSource (routing) → dynamicJdbcTemplate → dynamicDao, plus the definition loader, registry and aspects applications not using the Starter can trigger the dynamic datasource stack by providing a bean named primaryJdbcTemplate themselves The bean topology and "only dynamicDao can switch" are covered fully in Switching.

No restart is needed after connection definitions change. The framework provides two refresh entries, and both steps are required (full code in the extension page, "Runtime Hot Refresh"): DynamicDataSourceRegistry.refreshDataSource(key) / refreshAllDataSources() — update the definitions and instances in the registry (rebuilding the pool when necessary); deleted or disabled connections are removed from registration DynamicRoutingDataSource.refreshDataSource(key) / refreshAllDataSources() — reassemble the routing table Under lazy loading, connections that never built a pool only get their definition updated and still build lazily on first route. :::note Entity mapping cache and connection config snapshot EntityDataSourceResolver keeps an in-memory cache of "entity → datasource" resolutions, but every hit re-checks that the target datasource is still registered; the cache invalidates itself when a datasource is removed. No extra cleanup of entity mappings is needed after refreshing connection definitions. On the core side, DataSourceManager also holds a snapshot of connection definitions (used by readers such as dbType resolution); on a snapshot miss it loads the row on demand via the definition loader's loadOne — connections created at runtime (e.g. a materialized-view engine connection) become visible to dbType resolution immediately, with no extra refresh. :::

Binding & Priority — the four binding styles and the full priority chain Switching — automatic switching, manual APIs and transaction limits Host Mapping — mapping intranet addresses locally for development ORM / Datasource Extension — the definition-source SPI, the field contract and hot refresh

This page answers one question: which datasource does an entity finally land on. In day-to-day use of the dynamic datasource capability, most scenarios need no manual switching — as long as the relationship between an entity and its datasource is declared clearly, the ORM routes automatically at execution time. That declaration is the "entity binding". This page covers all four binding styles, their priorities, and the complete decision chain from an entity to a physical datasource for a single SQL statement.

Binding style Declared in Typical use Takes effect @Entity(connectId) Java entity annotation The entity inherently belongs to one database, fixed in code Backfilled at scan time @Entity(catalog) + catalog-mapping Entity annotation + YAML/properties A group of entities belongs to one logical database group Resolved at query time Runtime registration Runtime governance channel (the platform provides the online registration entry) Online entities registered at runtime Merged when registered addEntityMapping(...) EntityDataSourceResolver API In-memory correction or override at runtime Immediate (lost on restart) The first three are adjudicated uniformly by MetaManager.resolveConnectId; the fourth writes directly into the resolver cache.

Declare the datasource directly on the entity class: @Entity(name = "demo_order", table = "t_demo_order", connectId = "order_db") public class DemoOrder { // ... } the value of connectId is the dynamic datasource routing key, i.e. the id of the definition Map in the datasource-definition SPI contract at startup scan time, MetaReflex.getTableMeta backfills the annotation value into TableMeta.connectId on the entity metadata this is the most direct declaration of entity ownership; it wins over catalog mapping within the same slot (see Style 3 below) Once declared, every ORM query and write against this entity is routed to order_db automatically — nothing to do at the call site.

If a batch of entities belongs to the same database, tagging each with connectId is tedious. Tag them with the same catalog (a logical group) instead, then map the group to a datasource via configuration: @Entity(name = "demo_order", catalog = "business") public class DemoOrder { } @Entity(name = "demo_order_item", catalog = "business") public class DemoOrderItem { } geelato: datasource: dynamic: catalog-mapping: platform: primary business: order_db to switch databases, change configuration only — all entities in the business group switch together catalog mapping is not resolved at scan time; MetaManager.resolveConnectId resolves it on demand at query time, so it does not matter when the configuration is injected if an entity declares both connectId and catalog, connectId wins (see priority below)

The runtime governance channel (the platform provides the online registration entry) can register a datasource owner for an entity after it has gone live; the registered value is merged into entity metadata at runtime. There is a key mechanism you must understand here: :::note The annotation value and the registered value share one slot The @Entity(connectId) annotation value and the runtime-registered value both end up in the same field of the entity metadata: TableMeta.connectId. They are not two priority levels — they are two write paths into the same slot: at startup, the explicit annotation value is backfilled into TableMeta.connectId first when a registration happens at runtime, the registration source's (DB-sourced) TableMeta (including the registered connection id) is merged into the existing entity metadata — for non-platform entities, the registered value overwrites the previous annotation value entities with catalog = "platform" are protected: the Java class definition always wins, registration never overwrites, and runtime refresh is forbidden So for ordinary (non-platform) entities: whichever declaration arrives later owns TableMeta.connectId. In practice, pick a single declaration channel per entity to avoid confusion between annotations and online registration. ::: This style suits runtime governance scenarios where "the entity goes live first, its ownership is adjusted later", operated through the platform's online governance UI.

EntityDataSourceResolver exposes in-memory mapping APIs: // add or override the mapping for one entity (target datasource must be registered, otherwise rejected with a warning) entityDataSourceResolver.addEntityMapping("demo_order", "order_db"); // remove the mapping (next resolution falls back to the metadata chain) entityDataSourceResolver.removeEntityMapping("demo_order"); // clear the whole mapping cache entityDataSourceResolver.clearCache(); writes directly into the resolver cache, taking precedence over metadata resolution memory-only, lost on application restart — suitable for runtime correction, not for permanent declarations before adding, it verifies the target key is registered in DynamicDataSourceRegistry

The first three styles are adjudicated by MetaManager.resolveConnectId with the following rules (high → low): TableMeta.connectId is non-blank — the annotation value or the platform-table registered value (same slot, see above) the mapping of catalog in catalog-mapping — routes by logical group when no connectId is declared neither → return null and hand over to the fallback chain at Dao-call time (next section) The resolution result also passes an existence check: EntityDataSourceResolver confirms the resolved key is actually registered in DynamicDataSourceRegistry (an enabled connection provided by the definition source, or another registration channel). If the resolved key's datasource is not registered, resolution fails hard — an IllegalStateException is thrown ("entity xxx explicitly owns datasource yyy which is not registered; refusing to silently fall back to the primary") — it never routes to a nonexistent database, nor quietly lands on a different one. When you hit this exception, check whether the key has been provided by the definition source (or registered through another channel).

Entity-level resolution only answers "does this entity have an explicit owner". A complete Dao call is adjudicated by the DataSourceInterceptor aspect, whose full priority (high → low) is: 1. Entity mapping the entity declares connectId / hits a catalog mapping, and that datasource exists (hard-fails when unregistered) 2. Annotation default the call is inside a class/method-level @UseDynamicDataSource scope, use value() 3. Outer explicit key the thread already has a key set by an outer DynamicDataSourceScope.switchTo / withDataSource 4. Request-level override applies only to entities without an explicit owner (DataSourceOverrideContext, e.g. the archive-query header) 5. Platform default the default datasource key written into DataSourceManager at startup 6. primary the final hard fallback when everything else is absent Details of each level: Level 1: entity mapping. The aspect first resolves the entity name from the Dao method arguments (recognition rules in Switching); if it resolves and yields a valid key, that key is used. This is the path most business calls take. When the resolved key is not registered, EntityDataSourceResolver fails hard (see the existence check above). Level 2: annotation-scoped default. When a service class or method carries a class/method-level @UseDynamicDataSource("xxx"), the annotation value is written into the thread context as the scoped default before the method runs. Note: a field-level @UseDynamicDataSource is only an injection marker for dynamicDao and produces no scoped default. Level 3: outer explicit key. If outer code set a key in the thread context via DynamicDataSourceScope.switchTo(...) (the platform BaseController / BaseService switchDbByConnectId(...) is a thin delegate of it), a DynamicDataSourceScope.withDataSource(...) block, etc., and no annotation scope is active, that key is reused. This level protects nested switching semantics — an inner operation without an explicit declaration continues on the database the outer scope selected. Level 4: request-level override. When the current thread carries a request-level datasource override context (DataSourceOverrideContext) and the entity has no explicit owner (no connectId and no mapped catalog), the call routes to the overridden datasource. The typical driver is online archive querying: with the request header X-Gl-Archive-Query: true, read operations on owner-less entities within that request automatically go to the archive database. No explicit designation (entity ownership / annotation / DSL / scoped block) is ever hijacked by the request-level override. See Online Archive Querying for the full semantics. Level 5: platform default key. Resolved automatically by the ORM at startup and written into DataSourceManager: if geelato.orm.default-data-source-key is configured, that value is used; otherwise "primary" when any of primaryDataSource / primaryJdbcTemplate / primaryDao beans exists. Level 6: primary hard fallback. When all of the above are empty, the constant "primary" is used. primary is forcibly registered by the routing datasource and can never be null, so this chain always resolves to a concrete datasource key and never ends with null. The above is the Dao aspect chain. The MQL / Fluent DSL executor follows a different consumption chain (AbstractExecutionStrategySupport) with a slightly different order: explicit DSL useDataSource(...) > explicit entity ownership > request-level override > platform default key > primary — an explicit DSL designation ranks before entity ownership, so a single call can override the entity's declaration; the remaining levels match the aspect chain.
documents.s: The Full Priority Chain at Dao-Call Time

documents.t: Misconception 1: the annotation value and the DB registered value are two priority levels. They are not. Both write into the same slot TableMeta.connectId; runtime registration (for non-platform entities) overwrites the backfilled annotation value. Priority exists only between "the connectId slot" and "catalog mapping". Misconception 2: an unconfigured catalog mapping means it never works. Catalog mapping is resolved on demand at query time; configuring it after startup takes effect immediately, regardless of entity scan order. Misconception 3: a bound connectId always routes. Two preconditions also apply: the execution entry must be dynamicDao, the only Dao that consumes routing keys (primaryDao connects straight to the physical primary and never routes — see Switching); and the key must correspond to an existing, enabled datasource — when unregistered, the first resolution fails hard (an IllegalStateException is thrown, refusing silent fallback to primary); check whether the key has been provided by the definition source and is enabled. Misconception 4: platform entities can be registered to another database. Entities with catalog = "platform" are protected: the Java class definition wins, runtime refresh and DB override are forbidden. Mapping platform to primary in catalog-mapping is recommended to stay consistent with the system database.

The db_hostname_ip / db_port in the dynamic datasource connection definitions might store intranet addresses (depending on the definition provider). When developers connect directly to the production main database locally (to access table data), they often don't have the same network segment environment, causing the dynamic datasource to fail to connect upon first use. This feature is used to: Under the premise of not modifying database table data, do a "local mapping rewrite" for the intranet host/port through an independent text file, allowing the dynamic datasource to connect in the local environment (e.g., via public network, VPN, or SSH Tunnel).

Only affects the host/port used during the creation of the JDBC URL by the dynamic datasource. Does not affect fields like database name, username, password, etc. When the mapping file is not enabled/configured, the behavior remains the same as before (still connecting directly according to the host/port in the connection definition).
Default path: conf/db-host-map.txt under the application running directory. You can also specify an absolute path via an environment variable: GEELATO_DS_HOST_MAP_FILE=D:\path\to\db-host-map.txt

Blank lines are ignored Lines starting with # or // are ignored (comments) Supports the following three formats: sourceHost=targetHost sourceHost:sourcePort=targetHost:targetPort sourceHost=targetHost:targetPort Explanation: sourceHost supports IP or domain name When both sourceHost:sourcePort and sourceHost mappings exist, sourceHost:sourcePort takes priority.

SSH Tunnel (Recommended for local troubleshooting)​ The table has 172.20.10.8:3306, locally forwarded via SSH to 127.0.0.1:13306: 172.20.10.8:3306=127.0.0.1:13306 Direct Public Network Connection​ The table has 172.20.10.8:3306, the actual reachable public network is 47.xx.xx.xx:3306: 172.20.10.8:3306=47.xx.xx.xx:3306 Change Host Only (Don't change port)​ 172.20.10.8=47.xx.xx.xx

The mapping file is read and cached by the dynamic datasource component, and automatically refreshes based on the "file last modified time". Before creating the HikariDataSource and assembling the JDBC URL, the mapping result is used to rewrite the host/port.

It is recommended to use this mapping only in local/troubleshooting scenarios; production environments should generally not rely on such rewrites. It is recommended not to commit the mapping file to the version repository to avoid leaking public network addresses, jump host strategies, or port planning. The mapping only solves "unreachable addresses" and does not solve account permissions, whitelists, SSL, network jitter, etc.

This page explains the dynamic datasource capability provided by geelato-orm (the cn.geelato.datasource package), including how the runtime handles: datasource definition loading datasource instance construction datasource routing entity-to-datasource resolution reserved transaction-related capabilities If your goal is not just to understand the built-in behavior but to replace the default definition source or deeply customize the strategy, continue with: ORM / Datasource Extension This page is the overview; the other pages expand by topic: Binding & Priority — how entities bind to datasources and the full priority chain Configuration — the connection-definition contract, configuration properties and the default datasource Switching — automatic/manual switching, the request-level override, nested semantics and transaction limits Host Mapping — local mapping of intranet addresses during development

The dynamic datasource capability is not just a standalone connection-pool helper. It is the component inside geelato-orm that provides dynamic routing around the ORM and Dao execution chain. Its responsibility can be summarized as: letting dynamicDao and dynamicJdbcTemplate switch connections by entity or context converting platform-managed datasource definitions into real DataSource instances allowing host applications to adopt multiple datasources without changing the Dao calling style So business code focuses more on "which datasource should this entity use" than on manually managing pool instances.

The configuration entry is: DynamicDataSourceConfiguration It currently creates: dynamicDataSource dynamicJdbcTemplate DynamicDataSourceDefinitionLoader Where: dynamicDataSource is the real routing datasource dynamicJdbcTemplate is a JdbcTemplate built on top of it DynamicDataSourceDefinitionLoader is the definition source abstraction If the host application does not provide its own DynamicDataSourceDefinitionLoader, the default bean is: PlatformDynamicDataSourceDefinitionLoader

The runtime flow can be understood as: DynamicDataSourceRegistry loads datasource definitions at startup the registry keeps datasource configs and builds DataSource instances on demand DataSourceInterceptor resolves the entity owner before Dao execution; DynamicDataSourceScope (the single switching entry point) writes the datasource key into the thread context DynamicRoutingDataSource selects the real datasource by the current thread key at the end of the request, DataSourceContextCleanupFilter clears the thread context (the request-level override context is reclaimed as well) So the core chain is a combination of: metadata resolution ThreadLocal-based selection (single entry point DynamicDataSourceScope) routing-datasource execution

The framework abstracts "where datasource definitions come from" into one SPI: DynamicDataSourceDefinitionLoader (loadAll() / loadOne(key)) The rules: when the host or the platform provides an implementation, all connection definitions are loaded from it; each definition Map's id is the routing key with no implementation at all, the framework only uses primary / secondary and still runs standalone The platform layer provides the default implementation (PlatformDynamicDataSourceDefinitionLoader, in the business layer geelato-web-platform), which loads from the connection definitions maintained platform-side. If you want to switch the source of truth to a configuration center, YAML, an external service, or a registry, do not modify the built-in implementation directly. Read: ORM / Datasource Extension

The class that turns a datasource definition into a real DataSource is: DataSourceFactory It currently supports: MySQL PostgreSQL and uses: HikariDataSource as the default pool implementation. It also handles: password decryption host remapping through DbHostMapFileLoader unified pool settings optional Seata proxy wrapping So this is not only JDBC URL assembly. It centralizes: address resolution driver selection pool tuning secure password handling host mapping in one factory.

The routing core is: DynamicRoutingDataSource which extends: AbstractRoutingDataSource The current lookup key comes from: DynamicDataSourceHolder (essentially a ThreadLocal<String>) and every write to it converges on the single entry point: DynamicDataSourceScope — withDataSource(...) block scope / switchTo(...) request-scoped default So the current routing model is: write a datasource key into the current thread let the routing datasource read that key at execution time resolve the real DataSource If the key exists but the datasource has not been physically created yet, DynamicRoutingDataSource will: create it lazily add it into the internal routing map refresh target datasource mappings This is the foundation of the current lazy-loading behavior.

When the routing map is refreshed, DynamicRoutingDataSource requires: primaryDataSource must not be null and uses it as: the default datasource If secondaryDataSource exists, it is also added into the routing map. So the current design is: primary is the mandatory fallback datasource secondary is an optional fixed datasource other dynamic datasources extend on top of those two

The component that resolves datasource by entity is: EntityDataSourceResolver Its current logic is: check the local entity-to-datasource cache if needed, resolve from entity metadata read connectId from table metadata verify the key is registered in DynamicDataSourceRegistry — an unregistered key fails hard, refusing silent fallback to primary So the key mapping is: EntityMeta.tableMeta.connectId -> dynamic datasource key This means once an entity is bound with connectId, ORM execution can route to the matching datasource automatically. Besides reading connectId from database metadata, an entity can also declare its datasource via the @Entity annotation, adjudicated uniformly by MetaManager.resolveConnectId. The resolution rules (high → low) are: TableMeta.connectId is non-blank — note that an explicit @Entity(connectId) and a runtime-registered value (the registration entry is provided by the platform) write into the same slot (runtime registration merges later and can overwrite the annotation value for non-platform entities); they are not two priority levels the mapping of @Entity(catalog) in catalog-mapping neither → null, handed over to the fallback chain at Dao-call time In other words, even without a registered connectId in the platform table, routing works through @Entity(connectId=...) alone or @Entity(catalog=...) plus catalog-mapping. See Binding & Priority for the dedicated coverage of binding styles and the full priority chain. It also provides manual operations such as: addEntityMapping(...) removeEntityMapping(...) clearCache() which are useful for runtime cache correction or local overrides.
documents.s: How an Entity Maps to a Datasource

documents.t: The aspect responsible for setting the current datasource key is: DataSourceInterceptor It handles two main things.
documents.s: How Dao Calls Automatically Switch Datasource

documents.t: If a class or method is annotated with: @UseDynamicDataSource the annotation value() becomes the current default datasource. This is suitable when: a whole service class should default to one datasource one method explicitly wants a default routing target

The aspect wraps: cn.geelato.core.orm.Dao.*(..) and tries to extract entity information from the arguments in order (unrecognized arguments are skipped): BoundPageSql / BoundSql (the entityName carried by the command) entity classes annotated with @Entity non-empty List (batchSave / multiSave / multiDelete — the first element is recognized with the same rules) entity instances annotated with @Entity (insert / save / update) Once the entity name is resolved, it calls: EntityDataSourceResolver.resolveDataSource(entityName) If resolution succeeds, it switches to the entity datasource; if no ownership is resolved, the fallback chain applies, and the outer key is restored after the call (protecting nested switching semantics). So the current priority is (high → low): entity mapping (TableMeta.connectId, annotation and DB registration share one slot → @Entity(catalog) mapping) the class/method-level @UseDynamicDataSource default the outer explicit key (thread-context value set by DynamicDataSourceScope.switchTo / withDataSource) the request-level override (only for entities without an explicit owner, driven e.g. by the archive-query header) the platform default key (written into DataSourceManager at startup by OrmAutoConfiguration) the primary hard fallback See Switching for the dedicated coverage of switching styles and transaction limits.

The registry is: DynamicDataSourceRegistry It maintains: datasource instance cache dataSourceMap datasource config cache dataSourceConfigMap It supports: full refresh at startup refresh of one datasource by key datasource removal direct registration of an already-built datasource If: geelato.datasource.dynamic.delay-load-data-source=true is enabled, startup loads only definitions and not every physical pool instance. The real DataSource is created only when the route first needs that key. This is more suitable when there are many configured datasources but only a small subset is active at the same time.

The unified configuration prefix is: geelato.datasource.dynamic.* Key properties include: delay-load-data-source enable-jta-transaction enable-seata-proxy minimum-idle maximum-pool-size idle-timeout-ms max-lifetime-ms connection-timeout-ms validation-timeout-ms keepalive-time-ms initialization-fail-timeout-ms connection-test-query The default direction is: keep ordinary business applications lightweight keep heavy transaction frameworks disabled by default centralize pool settings in one place

The implementation reserves extension points for: JTA Seata and related configuration and transaction classes already exist, but the default strategy is still: do not enable them automatically Important details: TransactionalAspect is currently not actively intercepting method calls Seata proxy support is reserved as a compatibility entry JTA and distributed transactions are optional enhancements, not part of the minimum default path So for ordinary business applications, it is better to understand the current state as: extension points exist wiring positions exist but the default path still focuses on lightweight local routing

The recommended mental model is: treat the primary datasource as the stable fallback leave the source of truth for connection definitions to the definition-source SPI (the platform provides the default implementation) treat connectId in entity metadata as the core entity-to-datasource binding treat dynamicDao as the preferred ORM execution entry for routed access do all manual switching through DynamicDataSourceScope: withDataSource(...) for block scope, switchTo(...) for a request-scoped default (the platform switchDbByConnectId(...) is a thin delegate) enable JTA or Seata only when there is a clear need

If you only want to: understand how the current dynamic datasource works use the routing capability as provided switch datasource automatically by entity this page is enough. If you want to do things such as: replacing DynamicDataSourceDefinitionLoader loading datasource definitions from a config center or files overriding the default ORM Dao binding customizing a multi-Dao strategy enabling JTA or Seata and integrating further then continue with: ORM / Datasource Extension

This page covers every way to switch datasources: which execution entries can switch at all, how Dao calls select a datasource automatically, the manual switching APIs, and the limits of switching inside a transaction — the boundary you should understand before using dynamic datasources. Switching falls into two categories: Automatic: the entity has a declared owner (see Entity Binding) and the aspect routes automatically, invisibly to business code Manual: the caller explicitly specifies a datasource, overriding the entity declaration Both rely on the same underlying mechanism: at execution time the routing datasource DynamicRoutingDataSource reads the datasource key from the thread context (DynamicDataSourceHolder, a ThreadLocal<String>) and picks the corresponding physical datasource. When the key's datasource has not been created yet, lazy pool creation is triggered.

Switching capability depends on which datasource the Dao is bound to — this is the most common cause of "why didn't it switch": Dao bean Datasource Can switch? primaryDao direct physical primary never routes — no key has any effect on it dynamicDao DynamicRoutingDataSource the only Dao that consumes routing keys The ORM runtime's Dao binding rules (OrmDaoResolver, high → low): explicit geelato.orm.dao-bean-name configuration dynamicDao (bound preferentially whenever present — otherwise switching would silently not work) primaryDao the single Dao bean (multiple beans without standard names raise an error asking for explicit configuration) In a typical project (using the Starter with spring.datasource.primary.jdbc-url configured) dynamicDao always exists and the ORM binds it automatically. But if your code bypasses the ORM and injects primaryDao directly, switching never applies to those calls — inject dynamicDao instead. For field injection, pair it with the @UseDynamicDataSource annotation: public class OrderService { @UseDynamicDataSource private Dao dynamicDao; // resolved by "dynamic" + simple field type name }
documents.s: Precondition: the Entry Must Be dynamicDao

documents.t: The DataSourceInterceptor aspect intercepts all Dao methods (cn.geelato.core.orm.Dao.*(..)) and selects before execution: recognize the entity: inspect arguments in order to resolve an entity name resolve the datasource key: adjudicate per the priority chain (see Entity Binding) set the thread-context key, then run the method restore the outer key in finally — protecting nested calls Entity recognition in step 1 (in argument order; unrecognized arguments are skipped): Argument shape Recognition Typical methods BoundPageSql / BoundSql the entityName carried by the command paged queries, MQL execution a Class annotated @Entity the annotation name (or the simple class name when blank) querys(clazz, ...) etc. a non-empty List recurse on the first element with the same rules batchSave / multiSave / multiDelete an instance annotated @Entity same as above insert / save / update When nothing is recognized, the entity name is empty and the fallback chain applies directly (annotation-scoped default > outer explicit key > request-level override > platform default > primary). With an entity name resolved, the key is resolved per the priority chain in Entity Binding; if the resolved key's datasource is not registered, resolution fails hard (an IllegalStateException is thrown, refusing silent fallback to primary) — it never routes to a nonexistent datasource, nor quietly lands on a different one.
documents.s: Automatic Switching: How a Dao Call Selects

documents.t: Business code writes the thread-context key exclusively through cn.geelato.datasource.DynamicDataSourceScope (provided by geelato-orm) — the single entry point for datasource switching. DynamicDataSourceHolder (a ThreadLocal<String>) is only its underlying carrier; business code should not read or write it directly.

Effective inside the block, restored on exit — ideal for temporary, code-level switching: List<Map<String, Object>> rows = DynamicDataSourceScope.withDataSource("biz_db", () -> dao.querys(SomeEntity.class)); the pre-call value is restored whether the block ends normally or exceptionally (finally semantics built in), no manual cleanup framework paths — the MQL executor, the DataSourceInterceptor aspect, async tasks — all follow this semantic a blank connectId leaves the current key untouched and simply executes

Stays in effect until the next switch or the end of the request — ideal for switching an entire request at its entry point: // inside a Controller / Service method: subsequent calls on this request thread that do not hit an entity mapping go to biz_db DynamicDataSourceScope.switchTo("biz_db"); a blank argument throws IllegalArgumentException immediately — never silently ignored it sets a thread-level key that applies to all subsequent calls that do not hit an entity mapping; calls that do hit an entity mapping still follow the entity's declared datasource (entity mapping has higher priority, see Entity Binding) at the end of the request, the web-layer cleanup safety net reclaims it: DataSourceContextCleanupFilter (order=-100, outermost in the filter chain) clears both the thread key and the request-level override context in a finally block, so thread-pool reuse never carries the key into the next request the switchDbByConnectId("biz_db") retained on the platform BaseController / BaseService is a thin delegate of this method with identical semantics

Specify the datasource on the ORM fluent API — effective for this call only, restored automatically afterwards, no manual cleanup: // query List<Map<String, Object>> orders = MetaFactory.query("demo_order") .useDataSource("biz_db") .list(); // insert (entity-instance entry works the same: MetaFactory.insert(entity).useDataSource("biz").save()) MetaFactory.insert(DemoOrder.class) .useDataSource("biz_db") .save(order); Override relationship at the DSL level: explicit useDataSource(...) > the entity's connectId declaration > request-level override > platform default. Even when the entity is bound to a database, a single call can temporarily point elsewhere with useDataSource.

Four layers of protection keep nested switching from polluting each other: interceptor finally-restore: after an inner Dao call finishes, the thread-context key is restored to its pre-call value; keys set by the outer scope are unaffected block scope: DynamicDataSourceScope.withDataSource is effective inside the block and restores the previous value whether the block ends normally or exceptionally — the executor-side DSL useDataSource is implemented through it too (set → execute → restore in finally) annotation defaults cleared eagerly: the scoped default of a class/method-level @UseDynamicDataSource is cleared when the method ends and never leaks into the next request on a reused thread cleanup safety net: the request-scoped key set by switchTo and the request-level override context are reclaimed at the end of the request by DataSourceContextCleanupFilter (order=-100) — no reliance on caller discipline So the semantics of a typical nested scenario are: DynamicDataSourceScope.switchTo("biz_db"); // outer scope switches to biz_db (equivalent to switchDbByConnectId) dao.querys(SomeEntity.class, ...); // SomeEntity has no declared owner → stays on biz_db (fallback level 3) dao.querys(OtherEntity.class, ...); // OtherEntity declares connectId="order_db" → routed to order_db (entity mapping wins) dao.querys(ThirdEntity.class, ...); // ThirdEntity has no declared owner → back to biz_db (inner call restored the outer key)

Besides the code-level switching above, there is a request-level default-source override channel: with the request header X-Gl-Archive-Query: true, all read operations on entities without an explicit owner within that request automatically route to the archive database. Underneath, geelato-orm provides the neutral request-level datasource override capability (DataSourceOverrideContext), and geelato-web-platform carries the archive semantics and the request filter. Key points: only owner-less entities are switched: entities with neither a connectId nor a mapped catalog; explicitly owned entities (users / dictionaries / metadata, etc.) keep their routing so the page framework works as usual no explicit designation is ever hijacked: entity ownership, annotations, the DSL useDataSource, and withDataSource blocks all take precedence over the request-level override read-only: write operations on owner-less entities in archive mode fail hard hard failure: when the archive datasource is not configured, requests carrying the header fail with an explicit error instead of silently degrading See Online Archive Querying for the full configuration, constraints and frontend contract.

Once a transaction begins, the datasource binding is fixed; changing the key inside the transaction has no effect. The reason: DataSourceTransactionManager borrows the first physical connection from the routing datasource when the transaction begins (doBegin) and binds it to the transaction. Afterwards, changing the thread-context key still leaves in-transaction operations on that already-bound connection. Concrete symptoms: inside a Spring @Transactional method, operating on database A then switching to B: the B operations actually still land on A's connection the ORM's batchSave(transaction = true): the first command's connectId decides the transaction's database for the whole batch; other commands' connectIds do not change the transaction's ownership Practical advice: do not wrap cross-database operations in one transaction — split transaction boundaries by database, or accept an eventual-consistency approach within one transaction, keep all operations' entity ownership (or explicitly specified connectId) consistent when cross-database strong consistency is truly required, evaluate the reserved JTA / Seata capabilities (disabled by default, see the overview)

Switching itself goes through the mechanisms above (entity binding / manual switching) and is tenant-agnostic. A common tenant isolation approach — "after switching to a tenant datasource, automatically append tenant filters" — is implemented via the Fluent DSL's filter-injection SPI and is not part of datasource routing.

This page covers 8 entities across application definition, version management, page collaboration, multi-language, and menu navigation. The application (App) is the aggregate root of the low-code platform; the page (AppPage) is the core artifact produced by the designer; pages support multi-user collaboration through a check-in/check-out mechanism; the multi-language entities carry i18n text for applications and pages; TreeNode and MenuItem carry navigation.

Application definition — the aggregate root of the low-code platform: the runtime loads pages, menus and themes per application. Extends BaseSortableEntity; common fields are listed in Overview. This page covers 7 entities across three mechanisms: in-app messages, notices and the notification pipeline. The core is the notification trio: Notification (the subject, one notification per row) + NotificationUser (recipient status, one row per recipient) + NotificationOutbox (delivery outbox, one row per channel); their separated responsibilities support independent read states for multiple recipients and reliable per-channel delivery. Message/Notice are the earlier single-table message and notice; UserEmailAccount is the user's external mailbox configuration.

Platform in-app message (earlier single-table form): one message with sender, receiver and send status. Extends BaseEntity; common fields are listed in Overview; no catalog specified. Property Column Type Description appId app_id String Application id title title String Message title content content String Message content receiver receiver String Receiver sender sender String Sender sendTime send_time Date Send time sendMethod send_method String Send method sendType send_type String Send category sendStatus send_status int Send status: 0 not sent, 1 sent, 2 failed, 3 read

Platform notice (earlier single-table form): one notice with receiver and business reference. Extends BaseEntity; no catalog specified. Note: this entity declares its own deptId/buId/tenantCode fields whose column names collide with the BaseEntity base-class fields (same-column shadowing). Property Column Type Description receiver receiver String Receiver noticeTitle notice_title String Title noticeContent notice_content String Content sender sender String Sender bizRef biz_ref String Business reference status status String Status deptId dept_id String Department info buId bu_id String Enterprise info tenantCode tenant_code String Tenant code

The notification subject, one notification per row. Separated from NotificationUser (recipient status): one notification can be sent to many people, each with an independent read state; separated from NotificationOutbox (delivery outbox): asynchronous, reliable delivery per channel. Extends BaseEntity. Property Column Type Description title title String Title, non-null, length 128 content content String Content senderId sender_id String Sender id (userId); system when sent by the system, length 64 senderName sender_name String Sender name, length 64 senderType sender_type String Sender type: system or user, length 16 bizType biz_type String Business type, a business identifier such as order/contract/task, length 32 bizId biz_id String Business key, length 64 actionUrl action_url String Action URL, opened when the notification is clicked (frontend router.push or window.open), length 512 channels channels String Delivery channel snapshot JSON, e.g. ["inapp","email"], length 256 priority priority int Importance level: 0 normal, 1 reminder, 2 important, 3 urgent

Recipient status of a notification, one row per recipient; separated from the notification subject so each recipient has independent read/starred/archived states and per-user inbox queries are supported. Extends BaseEntity. Property Column Type Description notificationId notification_id String Notification id, non-null, length 32 userId user_id String Recipient id, non-null, length 64 readStatus read_status int Read status: 0 unread, 1 read readAt read_at Date Read time starred starred int Starred: 0 no, 1 yes archived archived int Archived: 0 no, 1 yes (archived by the user; hidden from the default inbox)

The notification delivery outbox, one row per delivery channel. Transactional outbox: written inside the business transaction (ready), then asynchronously scanned, claimed (CAS → processing) and delivered by the scheduler through the corresponding DeliveryChannel; success → success, failure → exponential-backoff retry → dead letter (dead). A single channel's failure does not affect other channels. Extends BaseEntity. Property Column Type Description notificationId notification_id String Notification id, non-null, length 32 channel channel String Delivery channel: inapp / email / sms / wecom etc., non-null, length 32 recipientJson recipient_json String Recipient userId list JSON, e.g. ["u1","u2"], non-null, length 2048 status status String Delivery status: ready / processing / success / fail / dead, length 16 retryCount retry_count int Retry count nextRetryAt next_retry_at Date Next retry time errorMsg error_msg String Error message, length 512

geelato-meta is the module where the platform's business entities are centrally defined: the entities the platform itself needs to run — applications, organizations, users, roles and permissions, dictionaries, message notifications, file attachments, scheduling and integration — are all declared with the @Entity annotation in the module's cn.geelato.meta package, 54 in total. This chapter provides a field-level catalog, entity by entity, grouped by business domain; entities of other feature modules (business alerting, business exceptions, mail, etc.) are listed in the Platform Entity Index.

Item Description Module coordinates geelato-meta (cn.geelato.meta package) Upstream dependencies geelato-utils, geelato-lang (annotations), geelato-core (entity base classes and meta model) Downstream consumers geelato-web-common, geelato-web-platform, geelato-mcp-fms, geelato-mcp-platform Registration Zero manual registration: at startup MetaConfiguration scans @Entity classes under geelato.meta.scan-package-names (default cn.geelato) and registers them into MetaManager automatically How entity metadata is parsed, cached and consumed (ORM SQL generation, MQL validation, datasource routing, etc.) belongs to the framework metadata mechanism; see Metadata Overview. For how to write entities with @Entity/@Col/@Title annotations, see ORM Annotations.

The "Column" in each field table comes from @Col(name); fields without @Col derive their column name from the property name via camelCase-to-snake_case conversion. Field meanings follow the field-level @Title (title + description) in the source code. A few class-level titles are distorted (e.g. Schedule's class title mislabeled as "应用" while it is actually a scheduled task; Tenant mislabeled as "租户站点"; UserStockMap contains "stock" in its name but actually means frequent contacts). This chapter documents actual semantics and notes the distortion in place. Entities suffixed with *Map are relation tables (mappings between two tables) and usually carry few fields.

This page covers Role, Permission and 9 permission-related relation tables — 11 entities in total. All relation tables extend BaseEntity; common fields are listed in Overview. Attachment semantics (aligned with the security contract cn.geelato.security, see Security Contract Overview): Direct user-role attachment: RoleUserMap; role attachment to organizations: OrgRoleMap (effective only for the direct department, no recursion up the organization tree). The only way a department role takes effect for a user is a direct UserOrgRoleMap attachment (userId × orgId × roleId); attaching a role to an organization does not automatically grant the role to its members; membership (OrgUserMap) and direct role attachment are independent. Permissions come in two levels: role-permission (RolePermissionMap) and direct user permission (UserPermissionMap).

Role definition, application-level or platform-level. Extends BaseSortableEntity, implements EntityEnableAble. Property Column Type Description appId app_id String Application name name String Name code code String Code type type String Type: app (application-level role) or platform (platform-level role) enableStatus enable_status int Enable status: 1 enabled, 0 disabled; tinyint, non-null description description String Description weight weight Integer Weight usedApp used_app int Whether used by applications appName — String @Transient, not persisted appIds — String @Transient, not persisted usedApp (boolean view) — boolean @Transient method-level derived property, usedApp > 0

Permission point definition. This entity has no class-level @Title; documented here as a permission point by field semantics. Extends BaseSortableEntity. Property Column Type Description appId app_id String Application id name name String Name code code String Code type type String Type object object String Object, the target the permission acts on parentObject parent_object String Parent object, forming the permission object hierarchy rule rule String Rule, length 1024; auto-decoded on save when it is a base64 data URI (afterSet) description description String Description perDefault — boolean @Transient, not persisted

Direct role-user attachment relation. Extends BaseEntity. Property Column Type Description roleId role_id String Role id, @ForeignKey to Role roleName role_name String Role name, reference column (isRefColumn; same below, fetched from the main table's name column) userId user_id String User id, @ForeignKey to User userName user_name String User name, reference column

Role attachment to an organization. Semantics: the role is attached to the direct department and is effective only there, without recursion up the organization tree; attaching a role to an organization does not automatically grant it to department members — members obtain the department role only through a direct UserOrgRoleMap attachment. Extends BaseEntity. Property Column Type Description orgId org_id String Organization id, @ForeignKey to Org orgName org_name String Organization name, reference column roleId role_id String Role id, @ForeignKey to Role roleName role_name String Role name, reference column

Membership relation between users and organizations (belonging / part-time). Extends BaseEntity. Property Column Type Description orgId org_id String Organization id, @ForeignKey to Org orgName org_name String Organization name userId user_id String User id, @ForeignKey to User userName user_name String User name defaultOrg default_org int 1 default organization, 0 part-time post post String Position

Direct attachment of a role to a user within an organization: the only way a department role takes effect for a user. Semantics: the userId × orgId × roleId combination; orgId records the department the role comes from; the user need not be a member of that department (membership is in OrgUserMap, independent of this table, with no role inheritance). Extends BaseEntity. Property Column Type Description userId user_id String User id, @ForeignKey to User userName user_name String User name, reference column orgId org_id String Source organization id (the department the role is attached to), @ForeignKey to Org orgName org_name String Source organization name, reference column roleId role_id String Role id, @ForeignKey to Role roleName role_name String Role name, reference column

Role-permission relation. Extends BaseEntity. Property Column Type Description appId app_id String Application id roleId role_id String Role id, @ForeignKey to Role permissionId permission_id String Permission id, @ForeignKey to Permission permissionIds — String @Transient, not persisted; the set of permission ids of the role roleName role_name String Role name, reference column permissionName permission_name String Permission name

Permissions granted directly to a user (bypassing roles). Extends BaseEntity. Note: field-level @Title in the source is misaligned by copy-paste (userId's title says "role id", roleName's title says "role name"); the table below documents actual semantics. Property Column Type Description appId app_id String Application id userId user_id String User id, @ForeignKey to User permissionId permission_id String Permission id, @ForeignKey to Permission permissionIds — String @Transient, not persisted; set of permission ids roleName user_name String User name, reference column (the property keeps the name roleName, the column is user_name) permissionName permission_name String Permission name

Role-application (accessible applications) relation. Extends BaseEntity. Property Column Type Description roleId role_id String Role id, @ForeignKey to Role roleName role_name String Role name, reference column appId app_id String Application id, @ForeignKey to App appName app_name String Application name, reference column

Role-menu tree node relation. Menu nodes live in platform_tree_node (flag = menuItem). Extends BaseEntity. Property Column Type Description appId app_id String Application id treeId tree_id String Tree id, non-null roleId role_id String Role id, @ForeignKey to Role treeNodeId tree_node_id String Menu id, @ForeignKey to TreeNode treeNodeText tree_node_text String Menu name, reference column (fetched from platform_tree_node.text) roleName role_name String Role name, reference column title title String Name

Delegation/assistant relation between users: a delegating user (user) can configure a delegate (delegate_user) to handle affairs on their behalf. One delegator may configure multiple delegates; multiple business scopes for the same pair are stored as multiple rows (one scope value per row). Business uniqueness: the combination of delegator (user_id) + delegate (delegate_user_id) + scope must not repeat. Other modules can query valid delegates by user_id + scope + enable_status=1. Extends BaseEntity, implements EntityEnableAble. Property Column Type Description userId user_id String Delegator id, the user initiating the delegation, @ForeignKey to User userName user_name String Delegator name, reference column delegateUserId delegate_user_id String Delegate id, the user handling affairs on behalf, @ForeignKey to User delegateUserName delegate_user_name String Delegate name, reference column delegateUserEnName delegate_user_en_name String Delegate English name, reference column (fetched from platform_user.en_name) relationType relation_type String Relation type, defaults to delegate, reserved for extension, length 32 scope scope String Business scope, a single business identifier (e.g. periodic_report); one scope per row, length 64 enableStatus enable_status int Enable status: 1 enabled, 0 disabled

This page covers 7 entities across scheduled tasks, ORM hooks and various logs. OrmHook + OrmHookLog form the "configuration + outbox" mechanism for pushing entity events outward; Schedule + ScheduleLog form the scheduled-tasking pair; EncodingLog records document number/serial generation; AppPageLog and PlatformExceptionLog are the page operation log and the platform error log.

Scheduled task definition: driven by a cron expression, supporting java-type tasks with parameters, retries and a persisted context. Its class title is mislabeled as "应用" (application); documented here by actual semantics. Extends BaseEntity; common fields are listed in Overview. See the Scheduler module for the scheduling engine view. Property Column Type Description appId app_id String Owning application name name String Name code code String Code classInfo class_info String When type=java: "class name, method name" expression expression String Cron expression type type String Type params params String Parameters status status Integer Status: 0 stopped, 1 started; defaults to 0 description description String Description retryTimes retry_times Integer Retry count extra extra String Redundant field lastStartTime last_start_time Date Last task start time lastFinishTime last_finish_time Date Last task finish time context context String Persisted task context

ORM entity hook configuration: one Hook = name + URL + on/off. After the transaction of any entity's insert/update/delete commits, the platform POSTs the full payload JSON (entityName/eventType/values) to the URL and the downstream dispatches by itself. Purely additive: zero extra work inside the business transaction; trigger and execution are fully asynchronous, retried/dead-lettered through the outbox platform_orm_hook_log, with failures never thrown upward; the hook mechanism's own two tables do not trigger hooks (recursion guard). Extends BaseEntity. Property Column Type Description title title String Hook name, non-null, length 128 httpUrl http_url String URL, the downstream address that receives the POST after entity events commit, non-null, length 512 enableStatus enable_status int Whether enabled: 0 disabled, 1 enabled; defaults to 1

Page (designer) operation log, saving a snapshot of the page source content. Extends BaseEntity. Property Column Type Description appId app_id String Application id, owning application pageId page_id String Page id, the related page code code String Code label label String Title type type String Type, e.g. api/form/table version version int Version extendId extend_id String Extension info, extension id (e.g. the corresponding leaf node id) description description String Description sourceContent source_content String Source content, longText, non-null

Scheduled task execution log, one row per execution. Extends BaseEntity. Property Column Type Description appId app_id String Owning application scheduleId schedule_id String Owning schedule id scheduleCode schedule_code String Schedule code scheduleName schedule_name String Owning schedule name scheduleInfo schedule_info String Schedule info: expression, parameters, retry count type type String Type: start, running, finish startAt start_at Date Execution start time finishAt finish_at Date Execution finish time status status String Status: success, failure result result String Execution result

The ORM hook execution outbox, one row per trigger. Written asynchronously after transaction commit (afterCommit callback) with status ready and executed once immediately; on failure the scheduler asynchronously scans, claims (CAS → processing) and executes: success → success, failure → exponential-backoff retry → dead letter (dead, manually replayable). At execution time the hook configuration is re-read current by hook_id (a deleted/disabled configuration dead-letters); this table stores only the trigger context snapshot and does not copy action configuration, so configuration changes take effect immediately for pending retries. Reads and writes on this table all go through direct JdbcTemplate SQL (not through ORM save), eliminating event recursion at the root. Extends BaseEntity. Property Column Type Description hookId hook_id String Hook configuration id, non-null, length 32 eventId event_id String Trigger event id (the ORM event's eventId), length 36 entityName entity_name String Entity name, non-null, length 64 eventType event_type String Event type: insert / update / delete, non-null, length 16 opType op_type String Operation type: Insert / Update / Delete, length 16 actionType action_type String Action type, an informational snapshot at trigger time: script / http; actual execution follows the current configuration, non-null, length 16 payloadJson payload_json String Trigger payload JSON: new-value snapshot values, session info, eventId, etc. status status String Execution status: ready / processing / success / dead, length 16 retryCount retry_count int Retry count nextRetryAt next_retry_at Date Next retry time errorMsg error_msg String Error message, length 512

Document number/serial generation record: records each generated instance and serial by template. Extends BaseEntity. Note: this entity's catalog is email — stored in the mail database (historical attribution); one of only two non-platform catalogs in this module. Property Column Type Description encodingId encoding_id String Encoding template id template template String Template example example String Instance (the generated number) exampleDate example_date String Time exampleSerial example_serial String Serial enableStatus enable_status int Status. Carries an enable_status field without implementing EntityEnableAble description description String Remark

Platform exception/error log. Extends BaseEntity, catalog platform-log (separate log database). Error codes are centralized per module in XxxErrorCodes enums; see the Chinese page 错误码参考 (reference/error-codes.md) for the catalog. Property Column Type Description happenedTime happened_time Date Occurrence time exceptionClass exception_class String Exception class, length 255 exceptionStacktrace exception_stacktrace String Exception stacktrace appId app_id String Owning application, length 255 exceptionCode exception_code String Error code, length 255 tenantCode tenant_code String Tenant code. Overrides the base-class field to align the column with varchar(64)

The business exception center is a rule-based judging → one-instance-per-person → resolution-loop engine: business semantics like "booking acceptance stuck" or "billed beyond credit" become configurable exception rules; judging pipelines built on the framework's script engine (geelato-script) detect hits in batch or on change, and a unique exception instance is maintained per "rule × business object × participant" until resolved. Module: cn.geelato:geelato-exception. The engine is off by default (geelato.exception.engine.enabled, default false); rule-management REST works regardless of the switch — engine beans (scan/event/submit chain) are wired only when enabled.

Concept Description Exception rule Table platform_exception_rule: rule_code (EXC-{domain}-{seq}), domain_code, level (P0~P3), rule_kind (ALERT / ESCALATE with escalation_of_rule_code) Trigger trigger_type: CHANGE (entity event re-evaluation) / SCAN (scheduled full scan) / BOTH; SCAN uses cron_expression Judging pipeline pipeline_json.steps[{name, lang, content}] — geelato-script scripts (js/python) run step by step; each step's output feeds the next step's $input; the final step returns a hits contract array Hits contract Typed Hit: bizId is the only required field; optional bizType/bizLabel/title/anchorTime/snapshot; anything else goes to extras; validated at three points (save-time static check / enable-gate dry-run / runtime fallback) Participant selectors owner_selector, six kinds: USER, ROLE, DEPT, DEPT_ROLE (optionally the business org of the hit), BIZ_FIELD (default ownerId), ORG_TREE_UP (escalation up the org tree) One-instance-per-person Table platform_exception: fingerprint active_fingerprint = {rule_code}|{biz_type}|{biz_id}|{participant_id} is permanently unique; statuses OPEN/PROCESSING/RESOLVED/IGNORED/ESCALATED; renewal while active, reopen after closure, group-level AUTO_RECOVER

Scan leg (ExceptionScanScheduler, self-managed daemon, 30s tick) → CAS claim on the rule row (scan_status/scan_runner, stale recovery, cluster-safe) → rebuild tenant context → pipeline SCAN judging → hit submission Event leg (EntityEventReactor) → listen_entities [{entity, operations, role, refField, fields}] matches ORM change events → PRIMARY/RELATED normalization (child id → parent id) → RECHECK single-object re-evaluation (same pipeline as scan) → events affect freshness only: duplicate/out-of-order/ghost signals are harmless; judging re-queries the database Hit submission chain (HitSubmitService) inhibition (storm_json.inhibitedBy) → circuit break (hitLimit, overflowPolicy) → cooldown (cooldownMinutes) → participant solving → one-instance-per-person upsert → notification touch (handlers and cc each become instances) The scan scheduler does not depend on the host's @EnableScheduling (self-managed-thread convention); the due baseline is the last scan log start_at, missed fires replay once. Escalation chains: ESCALATE rules use $gl.target.targetInstance(bizId) to read the parent rule's active instances. Alert integration: platform_exception lifecycle events are the alert center's only built-in event source — see Business Alert.

geelato.exception.engine.enabled=true Key (geelato.exception.engine.*) Default Description scan.tick-seconds / thread-pool-size / lock-stale-minutes 30 / 2 / 30 Scan cadence / pool / CAS stale recovery pipeline.step-timeout-ms / pipeline-timeout-ms 30000 / 120000 Step / whole-pipeline timeout pipeline.trial-timeout-ms 30000 Trial-run timeout pipeline.step-output-max-bytes 2MB Step output size circuit breaker sql.connect-id primary Default pipeline datasource http.enabled / allowlist / timeout-ms false / empty / 5000 Pipeline outbound whitelist (second-level gate above geelato.script.engine.http.enabled) trigger.queue-capacity 1000 Bounded change-event queue (drops with a log when full) The script base (geelato-script, prefix geelato.script.engine) has three channels on by default: python-enabled=true, http.enabled=true (empty allowlist still rejects), dao.write-enabled=true (dao.dry-run=true still rolls back by default).

Judging scripts run under the exception-judge profile: all namespaces and variables are open — built-in kits and consumer-registered kits are all visible; only timeouts are tightened. Common entries: $gl.sql / $gl.dao for data access, $gl.target.targetInstance(bizId) for escalation chains, and the federated ConnectPoolProvider for cross-datasource queries. See Rules and Usage.

Backend fully implemented: pipeline judging, hits contract, one-instance-per-person, scan/event legs, escalation chains, workbench REST, YAML round-trip, 8 practical seed rules (disabled by default), with unit tests. Front-end workbench not yet shipped: /exception/* APIs are ready; the UI exists as design prototypes (bea/page 09–11), and visual rule editing (V2) is in design.
How to define exception rules, write judging pipelines, and which REST APIs are available. Overview: Business Exception.

Rules live in platform_exception_rule (DDL db/exception-schema.sql, idempotent). Key columns: Column Description rule_code / rule_name / domain_code Code (EXC-{domain}-{seq}, UK), name, domain level P0~P3 rule_kind / escalation_of_rule_code ALERT / ESCALATE (points to the parent rule code) trigger_type / cron_expression CHANGE / SCAN / BOTH; SCAN cron listen_entities Event subscriptions: [{entity, operations, role, refField, fields}] pipeline_json Judging pipeline {steps:[{name, lang, content}]} threshold_json Threshold parameters, read as $params in scripts owner_selector {handlers:[…], cc:[…]} (six selector kinds, same as alert) storm_json {hitLimit, overflowPolicy, cooldownMinutes, inhibitedBy} storm control resolve_policy / mutual_exclusive_group / flow_template ANY/ALL/SELF, exclusive group, STANDARD/INTERCEPT/NOTICE biz_url_template "Go handle" jump template ({bizId} placeholder) engine_version / version Script contract snapshot / caliber version
POST /api/exception/rule/import-yaml, POST /import-yaml-batch, GET /{id}/export-yaml provide lossless YAML round-trip for version-controlling rules.

A pipeline is an ordered run of single scripts: steps[{name, lang, content}]; lang supports js (GraalVM, IIFE return) and python (assign __result__); each step's output feeds the next step's $input. Bindings: $ctx{trigger, bizId, rule{code, level, kind}}, thresholds $params, previous step $input. Data access: $gl.sql.query(sql, $params) supports :name parameters; $gl.dao for ORM writes; $gl.target.targetInstance(bizId) for escalation chains. Exit contract: the final step returns a hits array — {bizId required, bizType?, bizLabel?, title?, anchorTime?, snapshot?, …extras}; step output is snake→camelCase normalized with a size circuit breaker. Validation at three points: save-time static check (js must contain return, python __result__), enable-gate dry-run (real TRIAL execution), runtime fallback (non-array drops all HITS_NOT_ARRAY; missing bizId drops the entry with a log; missing title/snapshot/anchorTime logs only).

// threshold_json: {"daysAfer":7,"lookbackDays":90} const rows = $gl.sql.query(` SELECT 'ORDER' AS biz_type, b.order_id AS biz_id, e.eco_no AS biz_label, COALESCE(g.grant_time, b.update_at) AS grant_time, DATEDIFF(NOW(), COALESCE(g.grant_time, b.update_at)) AS days_since_grant FROM il_order_bol b JOIN il_eco e ON e.id = b.order_id AND e.del_status = 0 WHERE b.del_status = 0 AND b.bol_status IN ('2','3','4') AND DATEDIFF(NOW(), COALESCE(g.grant_time, b.update_at)) >= :daysAfer `, $params) return rows.map(r => ({ bizId: r.biz_id, bizType: r.biz_type, bizLabel: r.biz_label, title: `Order ${r.biz_label} released ${r.days_since_grant} days, receivable not written off`, anchorTime: r.grant_time, snapshot: { daysSinceGrant: r.days_since_grant } })) :::warning Performance SCAN condition queries run in full inside the database; ensure indexes exist for large-table rules (bea/rules-practical/_scan_rule_indexes.sql lists the scan-leg indexes). :::
documents.s: Example (seed rule EXC-BL-015, single-step js pipeline)

This page explains the current Geelato file download and preview capability, including runtime entry points and the difference between local files and OSS files. The description is based on: DownloadController FileHandler BaseHandler AttachController
The main runtime entry is: GET /api/resources/file Common parameters include: id isPdf isPreview isThumbnail

The runtime does not directly expose a disk path. The flow is: load attachment metadata by attachment ID optionally switch to a thumbnail record decide whether the attachment is local or OSS based open a stream or local file write the response in preview or download mode
documents.s: How the Runtime Resolves the File

documents.t: When: objectId is empty the runtime treats the attachment as a local file and reads: Attachment.path as a local filesystem path.

When: objectId is not empty the runtime treats the attachment as an OSS object. It then: uses Attachment.path as the object name calls FileHelper.getFile(...) reads the OSS input stream sends it through the same unified download output

The download entry supports: isPreview isPdf If isPdf=true, the runtime converts the original file to PDF first, then outputs the PDF file. The temporary converted PDF file is stored under: geelato.upload.convert-directory There is also: GET /api/attach/toPdf/{id} which converts an Excel attachment into a new PDF attachment record.
The runtime also provides: GET /api/resources/json to read .config files from: geelato.upload.config-directory

Related attachment APIs include: GET /api/attach/get/{id} POST /api/attach/image/{id} POST /api/attach/valid POST /api/attach/storage/{type} DELETE /api/attach/remove/{id} These support validation, storage migration, and deletion workflows around download.
File Upload OSS Module

This page explains the current Geelato file upload capability, including upload entry points, storage modes, attachment metadata tables, and OSS configuration. The description is based on: UploadController FileHandler UploadService Attachment

The main upload entry is: POST /api/upload/file The runtime flow is: UploadController receives the upload request it calculates the save path from tableType / tenantCode / appId / root / isRename it builds FileParam FileHandler chooses local storage or Aliyun OSS by serviceType the binary content is stored attachment metadata is persisted through AccessoryHandler an Attachment is returned So the framework clearly separates: binary storage attachment metadata persistence

API: POST /api/upload/file Important parameters include: file serviceType tableType root isRename objectId formIds genre batchNo invalidTime validDuration isThumbnail onlyThumb dimension thumbScale appId tenantCode The most important ones are: serviceType chooses local or OSS storage tableType marks the attachment source root overrides the local root directory isRename decides whether the original filename is replaced with a UID

The runtime also provides: POST /api/upload/object POST /api/upload/json POST /api/upload/model/{entityName}/{id} These are not normal attachment uploads. They write serialized content into: geelato.upload.config-directory
Local storage is controlled by: geelato.upload.root-directory geelato.upload.convert-directory geelato.upload.config-directory They are initialized in UploadService as static roots.

For standard uploads without a custom root, the runtime usually uses: UploadService.getRootSavePath(...) The path usually contains: the upload root the attachment source such as attach tenantCode/appId a date-based directory the final filename

If root is passed in the request, the runtime switches to: UploadService.getSaveRootPath(root, fileName, isRename) So the file goes directly under the requested directory instead of the default upload root layout.
FileHandler is the actual storage dispatcher. The rule is simple: serviceType = aliyun means OSS otherwise it falls back to local storage
In local mode: the file is written to disk Attachment.path stores the local absolute path Attachment.objectId is normally empty

In OSS mode: FileHelper.putFile(...) uploads to Aliyun OSS OSS returns objectId and objectName attachment metadata is then saved Attachment.path stores the OSS object name Attachment.objectId stores the OSS object ID So path is not always a local path. When objectId is present, the file is usually stored in OSS.

Image uploads can enable: isThumbnail The current behavior includes: only image files generate thumbnails multiple thumbnail resolutions are supported onlyThumb=true can keep only the thumbnail records parent-child relations are linked through pid
The framework stores file metadata through: Attachment Important fields include: id pid appId name type genre size path objectId formIds invalidTime batchNo resolution

Runtime attachment queries aggregate three tables: platform_attach platform_compress platform_resources They are unified as one Attachment view for the upper layer. The SQL also derives: storageType = aliyun storageType = local from the presence of object_id.

Aliyun OSS configuration comes from: properties/oss.properties Key properties are: geelato.oss.accessKeyId geelato.oss.accessKeySecret geelato.oss.endPoint geelato.oss.bucketName geelato.oss.region In quickstart they are normally injected through environment variables. If OSS is not configured and serviceType is set to aliyun, FileHandler throws a clear error.

After upload, attachment metadata can be managed through AttachController, including: POST /api/attach/copy/{id} POST /api/attach/quote/{id} GET /api/attach/get/{id} POST /api/attach/update/{id} POST /api/attach/list POST /api/attach/pageQuery DELETE /api/attach/remove/{id} POST /api/attach/storage/{type} GET /api/resources/file?id={id}&isPreview=true Notes: resources/file returns the file content by attachment id isPreview=true typically returns preview-friendly content type for images/PDFs
File Download OSS Module

The unified entry for third-party callbacks and its internal dispatch are handled by two cooperating modules: Third-party system │ POST /cxf/unified/callback/{token} ▼ geelato-dyn-unified-api (north-bound entry) │ ① token → bizTag resolution (whitelist match) │ ② raw request persisted to unified_callback_capture │ ③ processor dispatch via CallbackProcessorDispatcher ▼ UnifiedConsumerCallbackProcessor (enabled by default) │ Camel vm: in-process routing ▼ geelato-dyn-unified-consumer-main (consumer bus) │ resolve registry by bizCode → recipientList(${header.targetVm}) ▼ Each consumer module's dispatchVm route (business handling)

Base path /cxf/unified/callback: Endpoint Notes POST /callback Token-less generic entry; bizTag falls back to URL-based matching (default default) POST /callback/{callbackToken} Token-based precise routing: whitelist match first, then map to the actual bizTag GET /callback/{callbackToken} Token only; the body is persisted as an empty string while Query / Header / URL are still captured Constraints and response: GET /callback (without token) is not supported; An unmatched token returns 400; a duplicate token fails hard, silent overrides are never allowed; Uniform response: { "requestId": <persisted id>, "bizTag": <matched business tag> }. Call example: curl -X POST "http://localhost:8181/cxf/unified/callback/o4c8n1t6r?source=test" \ -H "Content-Type: application/json" \ -d '{"bizNo":"A2001","status":"UPDATED"}'

Table Contents unified_callback_capture Raw capture: URL / headers / body / params / biz_tag / tenant_code unified_callback_processed Processing result: capture_id, processor_name, process_status, error_message Conventions: snowflake primary keys, tenant_code defaults to geelato, DDL in the module's src/main/resources/sql/schema.sql. Joining the two tables shows the full chain (capture → processed); troubleshooting SQL is in the repo's geelato-dyn-unified-api/UNIFIED_CALLBACK_GUIDE.md.

AbstractCallbackProcessor (processorName() / supports(bizTag) / doHealthCheck() / doProcess()), tried in order by CallbackProcessorDispatcher. Built-in processors: Processor Default Behavior UnifiedConsumerCallbackProcessor enabled Hands over to the unified consumer bus (Camel vm: dispatch) DbCallbackProcessor disabled Direct database write RabbitMqCallbackProcessor disabled Publishes to a RabbitMQ exchange Switches are enabled properties in unified-api's spring-jdbc.xml.

A consumer module modifies nothing in unified-api or consumer-main — it publishes an OSGi service in its own module and is discovered dynamically: Field Notes module Module name bizCode Business code (dispatch routing key) callbackToken Callback token (lowercase alphanumeric, 9 characters recommended) dispatchVm This module's Camel vm: dispatch endpoint healthVm This module's health self-check endpoint enabled Whether active <bean id="xxxBinding" class="cn.geelato.dyn.xxx.binding.XxxUnifiedConsumerBinding"/> <service ref="xxxBinding" interface="cn.geelato.dyn.unified.api.service.UnifiedConsumerBinding"/> unified-api collects all bindings dynamically with <reference-list availability="optional">; consumer-main collects them the same way for routing and self-checks. Duplicate tokens fail at registration time.

Exposes the OSGi service UnifiedConsumerService.consume(bizCode, payload), which unified-api calls internally via <reference>; Camel main route vm:geelato-dyn-unified-consumer-main-dispatch: resolves the binding by bizCode from the registry and dispatches with recipientList(${header.targetVm}) to the target consumer's dispatchVm; bizCode=_health is reserved: it runs the healthVm self-check across all bindings (paired with a 30s scheduled health route); Built-in HTTP query endpoint: GET http://<host>:9080/geelato-dyn-unified-consumer-main/branch-logic, returning the currently collected module / bizCode / callbackToken / targetVm / healthVm — useful for verifying that registration took effect.

Generate a new lowercase alphanumeric token (9 characters recommended); Implement and publish a UnifiedConsumerBinding in the consumer module (declare bizCode / callbackToken / dispatchVm / healthVm); Implement a Camel routeBuilder in the module that consumes its own vm: endpoint; Publish the module and install the feature — the bus picks up routing and health self-checks automatically, with zero changes to unified-api / consumer-main.
