This document is intended for developers of business systems, explaining how to call the message enqueue API of geelato-message, and how to construct request data for four types of messages: SMS, Email, Bot, and WeCom (Weixin Work).
This is the most conventional and recommended integration method for business systems. Request URL: POST /message/enqueue Content-Type: application/json

Under normal circumstances, regardless of how many receivers are passed in, according to the external protocol agreement, one request only enqueues one message body and returns the generated ID of that message: { "ids": [ "1938475629384756293" ] }

Field Required Type Description type Yes string Message type. e.g., sms, email, bot, weixin_work_group. content Yes string Message content. Email/Bot supports enhanced JSON format. receiver Yes string Receiver JSON string. See format below. bizKey Recommended string Business unique key. Recommended to be constructed by the sender and kept unique (e.g., workflow-approve-order123-email). sender Recommended string Sender identifier. Must be recognizable in WeCom scenarios. buss Recommended string Business line identifier. sourceSystem Recommended string Source system identifier. Defaults to unknown if not passed. title No string Message title. Recommended for Email. planSendTime No datetime Planned send time. If later than the current time, it enters the delayed sending queue. Debug Mode Note: The message center internally supports a "debug mode", which can forcibly forward messages to testers. This logic is transparent to the caller. The caller should always construct the receiver according to the real receiver.
The receiver field must be a JSON string. Its basic internal structure is as follows: { "type": "mobilePhone", "list": ["13800138000"], "cc": ["copy@example.com"] }

Receiver type Applicable Message Type Description mobilePhone sms Pass mobile phone number list directly userId sms, email System parses mobile phone or email based on User ID during sending phase emailAddress email Pass email address list directly weixinWorkUserId weixin_work_group Pass WeCom User ID directly weixinWorkGroupId weixin_work_group Pass WeCom Group ID directly (Note: Bot scenarios do not use the above structure, see examples below)

curl -X POST "http://localhost:8080/message/enqueue" \ -H "Content-Type: application/json" \ -d '{ "title": "Verification Code SMS", "content": "Your verification code is 123456.", "sender": "user_1001", "buss": "login", "type": "sms", "bizKey": "login-1001-sms", "sourceSystem": "passport", "receiver": "{\"type\":\"mobilePhone\",\"list\":[\"13800138000\"]}" }'

The content of an email supports plain HTML, as well as enhanced JSON (used to carry attachments). curl -X POST "http://localhost:8080/message/enqueue" \ -H "Content-Type: application/json" \ -d '{ "title": "System Notification", "content": "{\"text\":\"

Please check today's report.

\",\"contentType\":\"html\",\"attachments\":[{\"name\":\"report.xlsx\",\"url\":\"https://example.com/report.xlsx\"}]}", "sender": "user_1001", "buss": "notice", "type": "email", "bizKey": "notice-20260702-email", "sourceSystem": "oa", "receiver": "{\"type\":\"emailAddress\",\"list\":[\"a@example.com\"],\"cc\":[\"copy@example.com\"]}" }'

Both receiver and content in Bot scenarios have special JSON structure requirements: curl -X POST "http://localhost:8080/message/enqueue" \ -H "Content-Type: application/json" \ -d '{ "title": "Bot Group Message", "content": "{\"content_type\":\"text\",\"text\":\"Hello, this is a test message\"}", "sender": "demo_sender_001", "buss": "bot-notice", "type": "bot", "bizKey": "bot-msg-20260702-001", "sourceSystem": "crm", "receiver": "{\"session_type\":\"group\",\"session\":\"CP20260000X-TestCustomer\"}" }'

The key to whether a WeCom message can be sent successfully is that the sender (sender) information must be complete and recognizable, because the underlying RouteHandler needs to use the sender to reverse-query the corresponding company WeCom configuration. curl -X POST "http://localhost:8080/message/enqueue" \ -H "Content-Type: application/json" \ -d '{ "title": "WeCom Notification", "content": "Please process the approval task promptly.", "sender": "demo_sender_001", "buss": "workflow", "type": "weixin_work_group", "bizKey": "workflow-approve-001", "sourceSystem": "workflow", "receiver": "{\"type\":\"weixinWorkUserId\",\"list\":[\"zhangsan\",\"lisi\"]}" }'

Integration Management is the capability provided by the message center to bridge external systems with the message center. It is divided into two categories by data flow direction: Push integration: An external system actively calls the message center to enqueue messages (see Message Enqueue Integration). Integration Management is responsible for registering the external system, and can optionally verify the caller's identity against the Auth Server. Pull integration: The message center periodically pulls data from an external data source (JDBC) according to configuration. Each pulled row is automatically turned into a message and enqueued, going through the same unified dispatch pipeline as push. Prerequisite: It is recommended to first understand the routing and message type concepts in Message Center Overview.

Dimension Push Integration Pull Integration Data flow External system → message center External data source → message center Trigger External business system actively calls Message center scheduled task Registered object External system (systemCode / clientId) JDBC pull source (connection string + SQL + templates) Credential source Reuses Auth Server oauth_client; no secret stored locally DB password stored locally (AES-GCM ciphertext + UI masking) How it lands Calls /message/enqueue into platform_msg Pulled rows rendered and inserted into platform_msg Authentication Optional, verifies token against Auth Server Not applicable (center calls out) Both are maintained under the Integration Management menu in the ops console.

The clientId / systemCode registered for push integration reuse the oauth_client already registered in the Auth Server (geelato-auth). The message center does not store the client secret again. systemCode: Unique code of the external system, corresponding to oauth_client.system_code in the Auth Server. clientId: Client ID issued by the Auth Server. In the create/edit dialog you can pick from the Auth Server's clients (requires geelato.message.integration.auth-base-url to be configured). When enqueue verification is enabled, the message center calls the Auth Server to verify the access_token carried by the caller. On success, the message's sourceSystem is back-filled with the registered system's systemCode.

Field Required Description systemCode Yes System code (unique), corresponds to Auth Server oauth_client.system_code. systemName Yes System name, for straightforward identification. clientId No Auth Server clientId (referenced, no secret stored). authType No Auth method: oauth_token / api_key / none, default none. authVerifyEnabled No Whether to verify token on enqueue: 1 verify / 0 skip, default 0. contact No Contact/owner. enableStatus No Enabled status: 1 enabled / 0 disabled. remark No Remark.

By default /message/enqueue does not verify the caller identity (backward compatible). To verify against the Auth Server: Configure the Auth Server URL: geelato.message.integration.auth-base-url=http://<auth-server> Enable verification: geelato.message.integration.auth-verify-enabled=true The caller must carry these headers on enqueue: X-Client-Id: <clientId> Authorization: Bearer <accessToken> On success, the message's sourceSystem is back-filled with the systemCode of the registered system matching that clientId; on failure, 401 is returned. curl -X POST "http://localhost:8086/message/enqueue" \ -H "Content-Type: application/json" \ -H "X-Client-Id: order-center" \ -H "Authorization: Bearer <accessToken>" \ -d '{ "type": "sms", "content": "Your order has been shipped.", "bizKey": "order-1001-sms", "receiver": "{\"type\":\"mobilePhone\",\"list\":[\"13800138000\"]}" }' When verification headers are absent or the master switch is off, enqueue proceeds as before, without affecting existing callers.

Unified scheduling: The message center scans all enabled pull sources at a single global interval (geelato.message.integration.pull.interval-seconds, default 30 seconds). Execute pull: For each source, a short-lived connection is opened using its JDBC connection string, and pullSql is executed (in incremental mode the last watermark :last_pull_at is bound). Template rendering: For each row in the result set, the target_* templates render the title, content, and receiver. Enqueue & dispatch: The rendered message goes through the same enqueue logic as push into platform_msg, reusing the idempotency key (pull:<sourceCode>:<primary key>) for deduplication, plus routing, retry, and archiving. Record watermark: The source's last_pull_at / last_pull_status / last_pull_count are updated for ops visibility and incremental use. The pull frequency is managed centrally by the message center. An individual pull source can only be enabled or disabled; it cannot define its own frequency.

Field Required Description sourceCode Yes Pull source code (unique). sourceName Yes Pull source name. jdbcUrl Yes JDBC connection string of the external data source. dbUsername No DB username. dbPassword No DB password (entered in the UI; stored as AES-GCM ciphertext; masked on display). dbDriver No JDBC driver class, default com.mysql.cj.jdbc.Driver. pullSql Yes Pull SQL, supports the :last_pull_at placeholder (incremental). incrementalFlag No Incremental flag: 1 incremental / 0 full, default 0. targetMsgType Yes Message type the row is turned into: sms / email / bot, etc. targetReceiver No Target receiver JSON, supports ${col} placeholders. targetBuss No Business identifier. targetTitleTemplate No Title template, supports ${col} placeholders. targetContentTemplate No Content template, supports ${col} placeholders; when blank the whole row JSON is used as content. enableStatus No Enabled status: 1 enabled / 0 disabled. lastPullStatus — Last pull status: idle / running / success / fail (system-maintained). lastPullAt — Last pull watermark (system-maintained, for incremental). lastPullCount — Row count of the last pull (system-maintained).

Row field placeholders: Use ${columnName} in targetTitleTemplate / targetContentTemplate / targetReceiver. It is replaced with the current row's column value at pull time. For example, if the SQL returns columns order_no and mobile, the template can be Order ${order_no} shipped, contact ${mobile}. Incremental watermark placeholder: Use :last_pull_at in pullSql. When incremental mode is on, the last pull time is bound automatically, e.g.: SELECT id, order_no, mobile FROM orders WHERE update_at > :last_pull_at Idempotent deduplication: Each row is enqueued with the business key pull:<sourceCode>:<primary-key-column-value>. The primary key column is identified in the order id / *_id / *_no / *_code / biz_key. In full mode, repeated pulls do not produce duplicate messages.

Scenario: Pull orders to be notified from the order database every 30 seconds and send an SMS to customers. Pull source configuration: Config Value sourceCode order-alert jdbcUrl jdbc:mysql://10.0.0.5:3306/orders?useSSL=false incrementalFlag 1 pullSql SELECT id, order_no, mobile FROM orders WHERE update_at > :last_pull_at AND notify_flag = 0 targetMsgType sms targetReceiver {"type":"mobilePhone","list":["${mobile}"]} targetTitleTemplate Order ${order_no} Notice targetContentTemplate Your order ${order_no} status has been updated. Please check it in time. targetBuss order After pulling a row {id: 8821, order_no: "SO2026080101", mobile: "13800138000"}, the rendered and enqueued message is equivalent to: { "type": "sms", "title": "Order SO2026080101 Notice", "content": "Your order SO2026080101 status has been updated. Please check it in time.", "bizKey": "pull:order-alert:8821", "sourceSystem": "pull:order-alert", "buss": "order", "receiver": "{\"type\":\"mobilePhone\",\"list\":[\"13800138000\"]}" } This message then follows the exact same routing and sending pipeline as a pushed message.

Configured in application.properties (all have defaults and work out of the box): Property Default Description geelato.message.integration.enabled true Master switch for integration management. When off, scheduling and verification are disabled (registration/query still work). geelato.message.integration.pull.enabled true Pull scheduling switch. geelato.message.integration.pull.interval-seconds 30 Global pull interval, in seconds. geelato.message.integration.pull.max-rows 1000 Maximum rows per pull (0 means unlimited). geelato.message.integration.auth-base-url (empty) Auth Server URL; once set, oauth client passthrough and enqueue token verification are enabled. geelato.message.integration.auth-verify-enabled false Whether to verify access_token on enqueue. geelato.message.integration.crypto-key built-in default Credential encryption key. In production, always override it via the environment variable GEELATO_MESSAGE_INTEGRATION_CRYPTO_KEY.
All integration management APIs share the prefix /message/ops/integration and return the unified envelope {code, msg, data, total, page, size}.

Method Path Description GET /systems Page query for push systems (params keyword / authType / enableStatus / page / size). GET /systems/{id} Push system detail. POST /systems Create a push system. PUT /systems/{id} Update a push system. POST /systems/{id}/enable Enable. POST /systems/{id}/disable Disable. DELETE /systems/{id} Delete (logical). GET /auth-clients Passthrough of Auth Server oauth client list, for selecting a clientId.

Method Path Description GET /pull-sources Page query for pull sources (params keyword / enableStatus / lastPullStatus / page / size). GET /pull-sources/{id} Pull source detail (password masked). POST /pull-sources Create a pull source. PUT /pull-sources/{id} Update a pull source (leave password blank to keep unchanged). POST /pull-sources/{id}/enable Enable. POST /pull-sources/{id}/disable Disable. DELETE /pull-sources/{id} Delete (logical). POST /pull-sources/{id}/test?sample=3 Pull once immediately (no persistence); returns row count and first 3 sample rows. POST /pull-sources/{id}/run Execute one pull immediately and persist messages.

Open the Integration Management menu in the ops console. The page is organized into two tabs: Push Systems: The list supports search by code/name/clientId; the create/edit dialog pulls the clientId dropdown from the Auth Server; you can enable/disable/delete. Toggling "Enqueue Verification" on means callers of that system must carry a token. Pull Sources: The list shows code, name, JDBC, last pull status/count/time; the create/edit dialog configures connection info, pull SQL, and target message templates; the password field is left blank to keep unchanged when editing. Row actions: Test: Pull once immediately; a dialog shows the row count and sample data for debugging SQL and templates, without producing messages. Run: Pull once immediately and persist messages, for ad-hoc triggers or verification. Before enabling, run the schema script platform_msg_integration.sql (located in the geelato-message module root).

Similar to the unified authentication service, geelato-message is essentially an independent message center service, rather than a mandatory framework underlying capability. It mainly provides the following core capabilities: Unified Message Sending Gateway: Consolidates sending requests from the entire platform and various business systems. Multi-channel Distribution: Built-in support for multiple sending channels such as SMS, Email, WeCom Bot, and WeCom Application Messages. Tenant & Route-based Configuration Isolation: The core framework of the message center only understands "Tenant Domain" and "Route". Complex distribution logic such as company and business lines is carried by the underlying RouteHandler. This document mainly explains: How external business systems or internal platform modules can integrate message push requests into this unified message center.

When the message center processes a message, there are two core fields: channel (Content Processing Pipeline): Responsible for message content preprocessing (e.g., template rendering, sensitive word filtering, etc.). Currently, it defaults to the default pipeline. route (Send Routing Processor): Responsible for deciding which configuration this message will ultimately use to be sent out. This is the core design of the message center.

The message center does not use a massive and complex general configuration domain (no concept of scope is introduced), but adopts a minimalist "Tenant Domain + Routing Processor" model: When upstream requests are enqueued, there is no need to pass the route parameter. The message center enqueue service (RouteAssignService) automatically fills in the route based on the message type (type) (e.g., sms -> tenantSmsRouteHandler). The corresponding RouteHandler takes over the message and reads the entire message content (including tenantCode, sender, etc.). The RouteHandler internally decides how to hit the final sending configuration from the database (or external interfaces). This design keeps the core framework very clean, while complex business distribution logic (e.g., parsing the corresponding WeCom configuration based on the sender) is completely submerged and isolated within specific RouteHandlers.

Currently, the message center natively supports the enqueue and sending of the following message types: Message Type (type) Receiver Type (receiver.type) Applicable Scenarios Corresponding Built-in Route sms mobilePhone, userId Mobile SMS tenantSmsRouteHandler email emailAddress, userId Email (Supports HTML and attachments) tenantEmailRouteHandler bot Dedicated session structure Group chat bot notifications (e.g., WeCom) tenantBotRouteHandler weixin_work_group weixinWorkUserId, weixinWorkGroupId WeCom Application/Group messages companyWeworkRouteHandler

Business systems call the /message/enqueue API to enqueue messages, sending a lightweight JSON. The message center automatically completes the remaining internal fields (such as Primary Key ID, Status, Route, etc.). For detailed integration message formats and sequence, please read the next section 《Business System Message Integration Guide》.

This page answers one question: with metadata in place, what does the platform extend from it? Every subsystem treats the MetaManager registry as the single source of truth; each section below lists the consumption entry (class#method), the metadata objects consumed, and the purpose. :::info How to Read This Sections run from "closest to metadata" to "furthest from it". Every entry path can be located in the corresponding module's source; class names are the last segment of the full path. :::

All SQL providers call MetaBaseSqlProvider#getEntityMeta first and only then start generating SQL — when metadata is absent they fail hard; there is no "degraded SQL without metadata". Entry What it reads What it does MetaInsertSqlProvider#buildOneSql tableName, getColumnName(field), ColumnMeta.dataType Builds INSERT structure/column lists, binds JDBC types per column type MetaUpdateSqlProvider#buildOneSql tableName, isIgnoreUpdateField() Builds the UPDATE SET clause, skipping creation fields and the primary key MetaDeleteSqlProvider#buildOneSql tableName, deleteMode (via DeleteCommands.resolve) Emits an update for logic delete, a delete for physical delete MetaQuerySqlProvider#buildOneSql/buildForeignJoins field column mapping, TableForeign, ViewMeta.viewConstruct, dbType Builds SELECT, auto left joins from foreign-key metadata with display columns, dialect quoting per dbType MetaBaseSqlProvider#requireFilterFieldMeta FieldMeta + dataType Filter-field validation (throws InvalidFilterFieldException when absent), parameter SQL type binding, comparison disabled for JSON columns EntitySaveParser#parse all fieldMetas, primary key, newDefaultEntityMap Entity object → SaveCommand: insert/update decided by the primary key, key generation, field-fill SPI trigger Dao#convert / CommonRowMapper getJsonFieldKeys, field column mapping Row data → entity/Map mapping + JSON column deserialization + encrypted column decryption EncryptedColumns#resolve getEncryptedColumnNames Query-column decryption (including the column union of joined entities) PageTotalStrategy#uniqueKeyBounded getId() primary key Skips the count SQL when a primary-key equality condition hits SaveCommandAdapter / DeleteCommandAdapter (Fluent API) primary key, defaults, deleteMode Adapts MetaInsert/MetaUpdate/MetaDelete → SaveCommand/DeleteCommand

This page explains where metadata comes from, when it is registered, how same-name conflicts are adjudicated, and what role caching plays. The model classes are documented in Metadata Model; runtime query and refresh APIs in Runtime Operations.

Path: cn.geelato.core.meta.MetaManager (geelato-core). A global singleton (singleInstance() with a ReentrantLock); its constructor first registers the two definition classes themselves — parseOne(ColumnMeta.class) and parseOne(TableMeta.class) — so that "the definition of metadata" also has metadata.

Field Default Meaning metaStore null Injected MetaStore SPI (the data source of the online definition source) metaResourceProvider DefaultMetaResourceProvider Static-resource SPI (default columns / column select types / structure upgrade columns) conflictStrategy CLASS Same-name conflict strategy; config key geelato.meta.conflict-strategy conflictDetectEnabled false Conflict detection switch; config key geelato.meta.conflict-detect.enabled catalogConnectIdMapping empty map catalog → connectId mapping from geelato.datasource.dynamic.catalog-mapping

OrmAutoConfiguration#ormEntityMetadataInitializer in geelato-orm is a SmartInitializingSingleton bean — it runs after all singleton beans are ready: AutoConfigurationPackages.get(applicationContext) gets the Spring Boot main class package; metaManager.isPackageAlreadyScanned(pkg) filters already-scanned packages; ClassPathScanningCandidateComponentProvider with AnnotationTypeFilter(Entity.class) finds @Entity classes; Each class is loaded via ClassUtils.forName and registered through MetaManager#parseOne(Class).

documents.t: The framework does not mandate where metadata definitions live. Definitions can be designer-maintained structure lists, Excel files, MongoDB collections, config-center entries, or external metadata services — the framework only knows the interface: SPI Method / responsibility Notes MetaStore load(Map) / loadByEntityName(String) / loadByViewName(String) The definition-source interface: full load, load by entity name, load by view name MetaDefinitionBundle five final Lists The contract bundle of load results: table definitions / column definitions / view definitions / CHECK constraint definitions / foreign-key definitions — the storage medium is decided by the implementation MetaStoreProvider getMetaStore() Provider extension point MetaBootstrap bootstrap(MetaManager, Dao) Host-specific initialization hook after loading MetaResourceProvider default columns / column select types / structure upgrade columns Static-resource source SPI; the default implementation reads classpath JSON resources The platform ships the default implementation DefaultMetaStore, which reads from the platform's design-time storage; the full guide to a custom source (field conventions and wiring) is MetaStore Extension.

Two sources coexisting means a same-name entity may yield two definitions. Adjudication rules: Scenario Behavior Conflict detection off (default) First-come-first-served: when the entityName is already in the main map, the online source only supplies its TableMeta to the existing EntityMeta without a full override Entities with catalog=platform Always the Java class definition, under any strategy Detection on + conflictStrategy=CLASS Ignore online-definition overrides, keep the ORM annotation source Detection on + conflictStrategy=DATABASE removeOne(entityName) then a full override by the online definition Detection on compareEntitySourcesAll emits field-level diffs for same-name entities, queryable by conflict-query consumers Related configuration: geelato: meta: conflict-strategy: CLASS # CLASS | DATABASE conflict-detect: enabled: false # when on, dual-source diffs are emitted and conflict lists become queryable

Three layers of "cache" are involved in the metadata system, with entirely different responsibilities: Layer Carrier What is cached Characteristics Metadata registry HashMaps inside MetaManager EntityMeta itself Purely in-process, no distributed cache; cross-instance consistency relies on explicit synchronization (refreshDBMeta) or a restart reload Meta-driven query-result cache MetaCacheProvider (j2cache metaquery region; falls back to a static LocalBoundedCache, ttl 60s / capacity 2000 when j2cache is unavailable) Results of metadata-driven queries, not the registry Eviction handled by the PlatformQueryCacheEvictOnDelete/OnSave listeners and removeCacheByPattern (supports *x/x*/*x*) Entity-level query cache gate EntityMeta.isBackEndCacheEnabled() — Decided by the design-time configured cache type (EntityMeta.cacheType, values None/BackEnd/FrontEnd/BackEndAndFrontEnd) Beyond these, several places use LocalBoundedCache for short-lived caches of metadata derivatives (e.g. the $gl.sql table locator at 60s/4096); these are downstream snapshots of the registry and expire naturally after registry changes. :::warning Sharing and Eviction The MetaManager registry is mutable singleton state; a runtime refresh (refreshDBMeta) only affects the current process. In multi-instance deployments, refreshes triggered by design-time changes must reach every instance (the platform achieves this via sync interfaces or restarts); writing to the storage directly leaves other instances unaware. :::

@ComponentScan scans Spring beans; metadata scanning scans @Entity classes — the two are independent. An @Entity class does not need to be a Spring bean to get registered; a bean without @Entity never enters the registry. The historical auto-scan/base-packages configurations have been removed; the scan scope is now fixed to "main class package + geelato.meta.scan-package-names".

This page documents every model class in the metadata system, attribute by attribute. Code locations: the cn.geelato.core.meta.model package in geelato-core; annotations in the cn.geelato.lang.meta package in geelato-lang. These models describe structured data itself, independent of the storage medium: the same attribute contracts can sit behind a MySQL table, an Excel worksheet, a MongoDB collection, or any other structured carrier. MetaManager#refreshDBMeta(String entityName) reloads a named entity's online-definition source, replacing the stale in-memory definition:

Trigger When Design-time entries (table/column/view designers, materialized-view management) After a design-time definition is saved or changed Explicit synchronization Manual triggers or cross-instance synchronization, reloading a named entity getByEntityName(name, cache=false) Ad-hoc lookups needing the freshest definition The design-time change loop is closed end to end: the definition storage changes → refreshDBMeta fires → the registry immediately reflects the new definition, no restart required.

The dual-source model's cost is drift between class definitions and design-time definitions. The framework provides: Means Entry Conflict detection With geelato.meta.conflict-detect.enabled=true, parseDBMeta emits diffs Per-entity comparison compareEntitySources(entityName) Three-way consistency check ConsistencyChecker in geelato-maintenance: field-by-field diff and repair across ORM annotation source / online definition source / physical DB source Reverse generation EntityJavaSourceGenerator regenerates annotated Java source from metadata to eliminate ORM annotation-source drift Packaging check Before packaging, "physical structure columns ⊆ entity FieldMeta columns" is enforced; inconsistency blocks packaging (see Packaging)

Metadata is the foundation of the Geelato framework. It is a mapping description of structured data: for every entity (business object), the framework collects the complete definition — its name, its fields, the primary-key and foreign-key relations between fields, the datasource it belongs to, and its delete mode — into one unified runtime object: EntityMeta. Every upper-layer capability is derived from this definition; no capability carries a second copy of the mapping. Metadata describes structured data itself and is bound to no fixed storage: the same metadata model can sit behind a MySQL table, an Excel worksheet, a MongoDB collection, or any other structured carrier. Likewise, where the metadata definitions themselves live is abstracted behind an SPI — the framework does not mandate a medium.

The complete facts about an entity are held by the EntityMeta aggregate root: Identity: entityName, entityTitle (Chinese title), entityType (Table / View / Class source forms), catalog (logical database grouping) Structure definition: tableMeta (structure name, schema, connect id connectId, data dialect dbType, cache type cacheType, etc.) Fields and columns: fieldMetas (each FieldMeta embeds a ColumnMeta carrying field name, data type, length, precision, nullability, default value, encryption flag, etc.) Primary key: id (the primary key FieldMeta) Relations: foreign keys tableForeigns, CHECK constraints tableChecks, associated views viewMetas Behavior switches: delete mode deleteMode, ignore-update field map ignoreUpdateFieldMap, encrypted column set encryptedColumnNames, JSON column set jsonFieldKeys

Without metadata, none of the framework's upper-layer capabilities can exist. Every subsystem treats the MetaManager registry as the single source of truth: Upper-layer capability What it reads from metadata ORM SQL generation Structure name, field→column mapping, primary key, dialect quoting, foreign-key JOINs, encrypted/JSON column handling MQL query language Entity and field validation, logic-delete field filling, default value fallback Datasource routing resolveConnectId turns "entity→datasource" ownership into a routing key and resolves the SQL dialect per entity Row-level permission / tenant filter Permission rules are attached by entity name; bare column names in rules are qualified as alias.column Generic data APIs One entity name is enough to expose full CRUD and publish slim field metadata to the low-code frontend Audit field filling EntityMeta.containsField decides writability: create-time fields on insert, update-time fields on update Delete mode Entity-level deleteMode is the middle layer of the call-site > entity > global configuration chain Archive, packaging, Excel import, code generation, designer Structure consistency checks, value conversion and locating, reverse Java source generation, DDL upgrades The complete consumer map is in Where Metadata Extends.

Metadata has two sources. Each is registered into its own source cache, then merged into the main registry: Source How it is produced Where it lives Characteristics ORM annotation source Startup scan of ORM @Entity classes — the declaration form of entity mapping — reflection over annotations entityMetadataMapFromClass Has classType; field types derived from Java types; lengths come from annotation defaults Online definition source Startup and runtime reads via the MetaStore SPI of design-time maintained definitions entityMetadataMapFromDatabase No classType; fields come from the maintained structure definitions (type/length/precision/encryption); entityType is Table or View Merged main map Merged per the conflict strategy at registration entityMetadataMap The only map ORM/MQL read at runtime; same-name entities are first-come-first-served by default; entities with catalog=platform always take the class definition You can compare the two sources at any time: MetaManager provides getClassSourceEntity / getDatabaseSourceEntity / compareEntitySources, and the designer also performs conflict checks through this mechanism. See Metadata Loading and Runtime Operations. Read the ORM annotation source together with the ORM chapter: the @Entity/@Col/@Title annotations on entity classes are at once ORM's entity-mapping declarations and the declaration form of metadata — ORM's SQL generation consumes exactly the metadata parsed from these annotations; declaring is mapping. See ORM Annotations for annotation usage and ORM for how ORM is metadata-driven.

The framework abstracts "where metadata definitions come from" into the MetaStore SPI: the framework layer only knows the interface and does not mandate a storage medium — MySQL, Excel, MongoDB, config centers, and external metadata services can all be sources; implement the interface and the whole source chain is replaceable. The loading flow and the SPI contract are in Metadata Loading; the full guide to a custom source is MetaStore Extension. The platform ships a default implementation (DefaultMetaStore) whose design-time storage lives in the platform database — its table structures and the platform entity catalog are outside the scope of framework documentation; see Platform Entities.

This page targets developers and explains the full pipeline that turns an MQL JSON payload into the final SQL statement and executes it. Syntax and keyword usage are covered in MQL Usage Guide; this page answers what happens to the payload on the server side and what each step produces.

Processing a query MQL involves six stages: Entry: the HTTP request body is the MQL text itself; the query endpoints of MetaController read the raw body. @pf extraction and parameter merge: before parsing, @pf view template parameters are extracted from the JSON and merged with externally supplied template parameters (external wins). Parsing and validation: JsonTextQueryParser turns the JSON into a QueryCommand, validating the entity and fields against metadata whitelist, and injecting tenant and data-permission conditions via SPI. Command post-processing: view template parameters are attached (VIRTUAL views only), $fn.now* variables are expanded, and fuzzymatch routing is decided. SQL generation: SqlManager dispatches to MetaQuerySqlProvider, which assembles the SQL text in a fixed order and produces a BoundPageSql (main SQL + count SQL + params + types). Binding and execution: Dao hands the BoundSql to Spring JdbcTemplate, which binds positional parameters and executes.

Entry Request form Notes /api/meta/list body is a single-entity JSON single-entity list query, POST / GET /api/meta/multiList body is a JSON array each element is a single-key entity object; queries several entities at once Script $gl.mql.list(...) MQL JSON passed in the script kit same MqlQueryProcessor as the REST path MQL playground /mql-playground.html explain / validate / execute, all going through MqlQueryProcessor ORM Fluent DSL Java fluent API no JSON involved; QueryCommandAdapter adapts it into QueryCommand and joins the same SQL pipeline

The raw body is processed as MQL directly; GET requests read the body as well. The only URL query parameter is withMeta (whether field metadata is returned with the response); URL parameters never merge into the MQL. /api/meta/multiList takes a top-level array; each element still satisfies "exactly one root key = entity name".
documents.s: The request body is the MQL text

documents.t: { "platform_user": { "@fs": "id,name,ref(platform_org->orgName) orgName", "@order": "createAt|-", "@p": "1,10", "loginName|eq": "admin", "@b": [ { "or": [ { "status|eq": "1" }, { "status|eq": "2" } ] } ] } } Where each part goes: JSON fragment Handled at Output Root key platform_user parsing command.entityName, validated against metadata @fs parsing field list + aliases + foreign-key fields @order parsing order-by fragment already translated to column names with asc/desc @p parsing pageNum / pageSize @b parsing nested condition groups (the FilterGroup tree) "loginName|eq": "admin" parsing flat filter (missing operator defaults to eq) @pf extracted before parsing view template parameters, VIRTUAL views only

MqlQueryProcessor.extractPfAndSerialize runs before parsing: It walks every entity node of the root object, moves @pf into paramsByEntity[entityName] and removes it from the JSON, so it never reaches keyword validation. Callers (Controller pre-processing, script kits) may pass template parameters through the external channel; when merged with @pf inside the JSON, external parameters win (same-key override).
JsonTextQueryParser.parse converts the cleaned JSON into a QueryCommand.

Single root element: an entity query JSON has exactly one root key, and that key is the entity name. Entity validation: the entity must be registered in MetaManager. Field whitelist: filter, order and projection fields must exist in the entity metadata; ref(...) must reference a registered foreign key; the reserved values * and forceId are exempt. Failures accumulate into one error message and throw. Materialized view pre-processing: a materialized view entity only contains the columns of the user-defined SELECT; references to non-existent fields (such as audit fields carried in by the query builder) are stripped before parsing, while validation itself stays strict.

Keys inside the root object fall into three groups: @ keywords → handled by QueryKeyword (@fs / @order / @group / @p / @b); unknown keywords fail immediately. ~ prefix keys → parsed recursively into sub-commands (nested sub-entity queries). Everything else → filter conditions in the form "field" or "field|operator": "value"; a missing operator defaults to eq. Function expressions such as fuzzymatch($platform_user.name,'张三') are reconstructed into canonical function form first.

Keyword Parsing behavior @fs comma split (commas inside function parentheses are kept); supports ref(fkField->remoteField) alias, the two-segment field alias rename, and function expressions kept verbatim; ref items are recorded as foreign-key fields @order `field @group stored verbatim into groupBy; table alias is added during SQL generation @p "page,size"; non-numeric or ≤ 0 values fail with a format error @b JSON array; each element is one bracket group whose conditions are joined by the group key and / or (defaults to or when both keys are absent); groups may nest further

At the end of parsing, platform-level default filters are injected through the MqlQueryFilterInjector SPI (the runtime resolver follows "0 implementations skip, 1 obeys isEnabled, multiple fail"): Tenant filter: a regular filter tenantCode = current tenant is appended (parameter-bound). Data permission: command.originalWhere is set to a server-generated SQL fragment (by default creator = current user, or resolved from permission rules), which is appended to the where clause later.

Field Source SQL destination entityName root key from fields / alias / foreignFields @fs select + left join orderBy @order (already column names) order by groupBy @group group by pageNum / pageSize @p limit ... offset ... where (FilterGroup) filter keys + @b where originalWhere SPI data-permission injection and ( ... ) viewTemplateParams @pf FROM derived-table template rendering commands ~ sub-entity keys each sub-command generates its own SQL

Complex conditions are not assembled into SQL directly; they are first expressed as a tree: logic: how conditions of the current level are joined (top level defaults to and). filters: flat conditions of the current level; each Filter carries field / operator / value / rawValue / arrayValue. childFilterGroup: bracketed sub-groups (from @b). Joining rules during assembly: Flat conditions of the top level are joined by the top-level logic (and). Each element of @b produces one sub-group; sub-groups, and sub-groups versus flat conditions, are always joined by and. Inside a sub-group, its conditions are joined by the group's and / or key. A further nested bracket inside a group is joined by the enclosing group's logic. Therefore the @b example in usage.md renders as (loginName = ? or phone = ?) and (status = ?). Filters on the same field (for example two in conditions on one field) are auto-renamed in the parameter map to avoid key collisions.
documents.s: Stage 3: FilterGroup, the Intermediate Condition Model

documents.t: SqlManager dispatches by commandType; SELECT goes to MetaQuerySqlProvider.generatePageQuerySql (producing the main SQL and the count SQL together). The assembly order is fixed: select → from → join → where → and (originalWhere) → group by → having → order by → limit offset having is not an MQL JSON keyword; it is set only via the ORM Fluent DSL and the segment is generated only when present.

Query target FROM generation Regular entity physical table name Physical DB view (no platform view metadata) query the view name directly DEFAULT view query the view name directly (DDL already created in the database) MATERIALIZED view query the view name directly (the engine guarantees the object exists) CUSTOM view viewConstruct inlined verbatim as a derived table ( ... ) VIRTUAL view viewConstruct rendered with @pf and inlined as a derived table ( ... ) Derived-table alias: when ref/JOIN exists the main table gets t0 (foreign tables get t1, t2, …), otherwise the view derived table gets a fixed vt. An empty viewConstruct on a CUSTOM / VIRTUAL view is a metadata defect and fails immediately instead of falling back silently. Materialized views are read-only, enforced by the write gate.

Template fragments inside viewConstruct are rendered when the FROM clause is assembled: #...# marks a template segment; {param} inside a segment is a placeholder. A parameter that is missing or blank removes the whole segment; segments without placeholders stay verbatim. Parameter values: numbers / booleans are inserted as-is; strings are wrapped in single quotes with internal ' escaped to ''. Template example: select o.id, o.order_no, o.status from mql_test_order o # {statusFilter} and o.status = {statusFilter} # # {minAmount} and o.amount >= {minAmount} # Rendering result when only @pf: {"statusFilter": "pending"} is passed: select o.id, o.order_no, o.status from mql_test_order o and o.status = 'pending' Gate: @pf is accepted for VIRTUAL views only. Non-view entities, physical DB views, and DEFAULT / CUSTOM / MATERIALIZED views receiving a non-empty @pf throw ViewTemplateParamException instead of silently dropping it.

MQL JSON does not express JOIN directly; ref(...) is the only implicit source: ref(fkField->remoteField) in @fs produces left join foreign_table t1 on t0.fk_col=t1.remote_col based on the entity's foreign-key metadata. Aliases are allocated per foreign-key source column: two different foreign keys pointing at the same target table each get their own JOIN and alias. Multiple ref references to the same foreign key produce a single JOIN. Explicit custom JOINs (inner/left/right join with custom on conditions) are provided only by the ORM Fluent DSL.

Identifier quotes: mysql uses backticks `, sqlserver uses brackets [], postgresql / oracle and other dialects use double quotes. Dialect aliases are normalized through the Dialects registry (for example RisingWave maps to the postgresql family). dbType resolution order: TableMeta.dbType → the datasource of the current connectId → TableMeta.connectId → the default datasource → primary. A view without its own connectId inherits the main entity's dbType. Pagination is always limit {pageSize} offset {(pageNum-1)*pageSize} regardless of dialect. Reserved words (index / inner / enable / key) are quoted automatically when used as column names.

The count SQL wraps the main query: select count(*) from ( ... ) t, without order by or limit, sharing the same parameters as the main SQL. When the total is derivable (full query, primary-key equality, first page not full), the count is skipped and the total is derived from existing rows.
MetaBaseSqlProvider produces the BoundSql (sql / params[] / types[]) in three steps:

MQL operator SQL fragment (col is the column name) Bound params JDBC type eq col = ? 1 per column type neq col != ? 1 per column type gt / gte / lt / lte col > ?, >= ?, < ?, <= ? 1 per column type startwith col like CONCAT('',?,'%') 1 VARCHAR endwith col like CONCAT('%',?,'') 1 VARCHAR contains col like CONCAT('%',?,'%') 1 VARCHAR in col in(?,?,…) N (value split into an array) per column type nin (alias of notin) col not in(?,?,…) N per column type nil col is NULL when the value is 1/true, otherwise col is NOT NULL 0 — bt col between 'start' and 'end' 0, values written into the SQL text — fis or-chain of FIND_IN_SET('v', col) > 0 0, values written into the SQL text — JSON column + comparison JSON_CONTAINS(col->'$',"v") > 0 0, value written into the SQL text — Function condition function expression + comparison sign + ?; fuzzymatch under the experiment gate rewrites to (col <> '' AND col REGEXP ?) 1 VARCHAR Type mapping: int → INTEGER, bigint → BIGINT, decimal → DECIMAL, datetime → TIMESTAMP, blob → BLOB, everything else defaults to VARCHAR; the three like-family operators are always VARCHAR.

The order in which ? appears in the SQL, the order of params[] and the order of types[] are strictly identical. in expands to N placeholders and contributes N parameters; nil / bt / fis produce no bound parameters. Filter.rawValue keeps the original Java-typed value (filled by the ORM DSL adapter and the external parameter path) and takes precedence over the string value when assembling parameters, so numbers, booleans and dates are not bound as strings on strict-typing databases such as PostgreSQL.

Most condition values go through ? binding. The following are written into the SQL text directly: @pf template parameter values (strings escaped, VIRTUAL views only) values of bt / fis / JSON column conditions the originalWhere data-permission SQL (server-generated, never user input) Protections: field names pass the entity metadata whitelist first and unregistered fields fail immediately; @pf string parameters escape single quotes and strip SQL comments.
documents.s: Which values end up in the SQL text

documents.t: Dao.queryForMapList(BoundPageSql) → JdbcTemplate.query(sql, params, types, RowMapper); when types is non-empty, values are bound with setObject(i, value, types[i]). Row mapping handles JSON column post-processing and decryption of encrypted columns. A page query fetches the records first, then the total; the count is skipped when the total is derivable. Observation points: p6spy is enabled by default (slf4j + multiline) and shows the final SQL with parameters; a final-sql debug log prints each generated statement.

Input (POST /api/meta/list body): { "mql_test_order": { "@fs": "orderNo,amount,ref(userId->name) userName", "@order": "amount|-", "@p": "1,10", "orderNo|contains": "PO", "@b": [ { "or": [ { "amount|gte": "100" }, { "status|eq": "pending" } ] } ] } } Step-by-step trace (mysql dialect): Stage What happens 1. @pf extraction no @pf, JSON unchanged 2. Parsing fields=[orderNo, amount], foreignFields=[userId->name], alias={userId->name: userName}; orderBy="amount desc"; pageNum=1, pageSize=10; flat condition orderNo contains "PO"; @b yields an or-group 3. Post-processing no $fn variables; at platform runtime SPI also appends the tenant condition and data permission (omitted below to keep the main path clear) 4. SQL assembly ref present → main table alias t0, foreign table t1; field names translated to column names (orderNo → order_no) 5. Parameter assembly ? in order binds PO, 100, pending 6. Execution main SQL and count SQL are sent in turn Final SQL: select t0.order_no, t0.amount, t1.name `userName` from mql_test_order t0 left join mql_test_user t1 on t0.user_id=t1.id where t0.order_no like CONCAT('%',?,'%') and ( t0.amount >= ? or t0.status = ? ) order by t0.`amount` desc limit 10 offset 0 Parameters and types: params: ["PO", "100", "pending"] types: [VARCHAR, DECIMAL, VARCHAR] -- types come from column metadata count SQL (same parameters): select count(*) from ( select t0.order_no, t0.amount, t1.name `userName` from mql_test_order t0 left join mql_test_user t1 on t0.user_id=t1.id where t0.order_no like CONCAT('%',?,'%') and ( t0.amount >= ? or t0.status = ? ) ) t Key points: Field names are translated to column names; @fs aliases and order-by columns are quoted per dialect. At platform runtime, the SQL in p6spy logs additionally contains the SPI-injected tenant_code = ? and and ( data-permission fragment ). With a JOIN present the order-by column carries the table alias (t0.amount``), and the quote wraps only the column name.

documents.t: Save and delete reuse the same parse → SQL generation → BoundSql → Dao pipeline; only the SQL provider differs: Operation Provider Result Insert / Update MetaInsertSqlProvider / MetaUpdateSqlProvider insert into table(cols…) values(?,…) / update table set col=? … where … Conditional delete MetaDeleteSqlProvider logical-delete mode produces update table set del_status=? …; physical mode produces delete from table /api/meta/save/{biz} decides insert versus update by "contains id without forceId → update". Update values support function expressions such as increment($platform_user.loginCount,1), which go into the set clause verbatim. Default fields (creator / createAt / tenantCode / updateAt, …) are injected by the MqlSaveFieldValueFiller SPI; $ctx.* and $parent.* variables are expanded in the save pipeline. See the MQL Usage Guide.

MQL, short for Meta Query Language, is the JSON-based metadata query and mutation protocol provided by the Geelato platform. Its purpose is not to replace backend Java ORM Fluent DSL usage, but to provide a unified data access language for frontend pages, low-code screens, and generic platform data endpoints.

MQL is mainly used when: frontend pages need to query, save, or delete data by entity the platform wants generic data endpoints instead of one controller per entity query conditions need to travel between page configuration and runtime as JSON the runtime should reuse metadata, default field filling, nested save, and related core capabilities

The typical MQL entry is a group of generic endpoints exposed by MetaController. It is best understood as: an internal platform data protocol a frontend-to-runtime metadata access language a JSON description of entity CRUD behavior It is not the same as: the official external OpenAPI contract the backend Java Fluent DSL in MetaFactory a strongly typed MyBatis mapper layer

These two layers solve different problems: MQL: primarily for frontend and platform protocol flow, expressed in JSON Fluent DSL: primarily for backend Java services, expressed through chained MetaFactory calls Recommended boundary: use MQL first for pages, generic platform controllers, and low-code configuration use Fluent DSL first for backend service CRUD, light joins, and procedure calls keep native SQL or MyBatis for very complex SQL and mapping-heavy scenarios

The main MQL handler is MetaController, with endpoints such as: /api/meta/list /api/meta/multiList /api/meta/save/{biz} /api/meta/batchSave /api/meta/multiSave /api/meta/delete/{biz}/{id} /api/meta/delete2/{biz}

MQL requests are JSON payloads built around entity names, protocol keywords, and condition expressions. Typical features include: @fs for field selection @p for pagination @order for sorting @group for grouping @b for nested boolean logic @pf for view template parameter passthrough ref(...) for referenced fields functions such as increment(...), findinset(...), and fuzzymatch(...) built-in variables such as $ctx.*, $fn.*, and $parent.*
documents.s: What You Will See in MQL

documents.t: When the queried entity is a view entity, MQL can also carry: @pf This is not used as a normal field filter. It is a parameter container for SQL template fragments inside the view definition. A typical template fragment looks like: #and order_type={orderType}# The client can send: { "order_view": { "@pf": { "orderType": 123 } } } Rules: if @pf.orderType has a value, the fragment body is kept and rendered from the parameter value: numbers and booleans are inserted as-is, strings are wrapped in single quotes and escaped if @pf.orderType is missing, null, or an empty string, the whole #...# fragment is removed @pf applies to virtual (VIRTUAL) views only; non-view entities or other view types receiving a non-empty @pf fail with an error So @pf should be understood as a view-query template parameter container rather than a generic MQL filter keyword.

Start with MQL Usage Guide To understand how an MQL payload becomes the final SQL, continue with MQL Details Then read API Reference for the OpenAPI and SrvExplain dual-track model If you need backend Java-side data access, continue with Fluent DSL Guide
This page explains how MQL is used on the platform side for query, save, delete, and expression-based data access.

The main MQL handler is MetaController, which exposes the following endpoints: Action Path HTTP Method Description List query /api/meta/list POST / GET Query one entity with filtering, pagination, and sorting Multi-list query /api/meta/multiList POST Query multiple entity lists in one request Single save /api/meta/save/{biz} POST Save one entity payload Batch save /api/meta/batchSave POST Save multiple rows of the same entity Multi-entity save /api/meta/multiSave POST Save multiple entities in one request Delete by ID /api/meta/delete/{biz}/{id} POST Delete by one or more IDs Conditional delete /api/meta/delete2/{biz} POST Delete by MQL filter conditions
A typical query payload looks like this: { "platform_user": { "loginName": "admin" } } This means querying platform_user with loginName = admin.

MQL uses keywords prefixed with @ to control query behavior. Keyword Meaning Example @fs field selection "@fs": "id,name,loginName" @p pagination (page,size) "@p": "1,10" @order sorting `"@order": "createAt @group grouping "@group": "type" @b nested boolean logic see example below @pf view SQL template parameters see example below

MQL supports "field|operator": "value" syntax. If the operator is omitted, it defaults to eq. Operator Meaning Example eq equals "name": "Tom" neq not equals "status|neq": "0" lt less than "age|lt": "18" lte less than or equal "age|lte": "18" gt greater than "age|gt": "18" gte greater than or equal "age|gte": "18" startwith starts with "name|startwith": "Tom" endwith ends with "name|endwith": "son" contains contains "name|contains": "om" in in set "type|in": "1,2,3" nin not in set "type|nin": "4,5" bt between "age|bt": "10,20" nil null check "memo|nil": "1"

Use @b for nested AND / OR conditions: { "platform_user": { "@b": [ { "or": [ { "loginName|eq": "admin" }, { "phone|eq": "13800000000" } ] }, { "and": [ { "status|eq": "1" } ] } ] } } This means: (loginName = 'admin' OR phone = '13800000000') AND status = '1'

You can use ref(...) in @fs to fetch fields from a related entity: { "platform_user": { "@fs": "id,name,ref(platform_org->orgName)", "orgId|eq": "some_org_id" } } This means reading orgName from the related platform_org entity.

When the queried entity itself is a view entity, you can pass: @pf inside the entity node. It is used for view SQL template rendering rather than normal field filtering. For example, if the view SQL contains a fragment like: #and order_type={orderType}# the request can be written as: { "order_view": { "@fs": "id,orderNo,orderType", "@pf": { "orderType": 123 } } } Rules: @pf is extracted before standard MQL parsing, so it does not participate in normal keyword validation template rendering is applied only for virtual (VIRTUAL) views; non-view entities or other view types receiving a non-empty @pf fail with an error instead of silently dropping it if {orderType} has a value, the fragment becomes and order_type=123 if {orderType} is missing, null, or an empty string, the whole #...# fragment is removed parameter values: numbers and booleans are inserted as-is; strings are wrapped in single quotes with internal ' escaped to ''

The /api/meta/save/{biz} endpoint automatically decides between insert and update. Rules: if the payload contains id and does not set forceId, it is treated as an update if the payload has no id, or has id together with forceId, it is treated as an insert Insert example: { "platform_user": { "name": "NewUser", "loginName": "new_user", "password": "123", "type": 1 } } Update example: { "platform_user": { "id": "1234567890", "name": "UpdatedName" } } Default behavior: updates automatically fill updateAt, updater, and updaterName inserts automatically fill fields such as createAt, creator, and tenantCode

MQL supports cascading save of a parent entity together with child entities. Child keys start with #. { "platform_user": { "name": "UserWithRoles", "loginName": "u_roles", "#platform_user_role": [ { "roleId": "role_admin_id" }, { "roleId": "role_guest_id" } ] } }
Endpoint: /api/meta/batchSave { "platform_user": [ { "name": "UserA", "loginName": "a" }, { "name": "UserB", "loginName": "b" } ] }

Delete by ID: single: /api/meta/delete/1/12345 multiple: /api/meta/delete/1/12345,67890 Conditional delete endpoint: /api/meta/delete2/{biz} { "platform_user": { "loginName|eq": "temp_user", "status|eq": "0" } } Use this carefully and ensure the filter is accurate.

MQL supports function expressions in both query and save payloads. Basic rules: function format: functionName(param1, param2, ...) entity fields can be referenced by $entity.field numbers can be written directly, while string literals use single quotes

Used for increment logic or computed fields: { "platform_user": { "@fs": "id,name,increment($platform_user.loginCount,1) loginCountNext" } } Increment during update: { "platform_user": { "id": "123", "loginCount": "increment($platform_user.loginCount,1)" } }

Used to check whether a value exists inside a set-like field. The fis operator is usually more convenient. Recommended form: { "platform_user": { "roleCodes|fis": "admin,manager" } } Function form: { "platform_user": { "findinset($platform_user.roleCodes,'admin')|gt": "0" } }
Used for fuzzy string matching and can also be combined with sorting: { "platform_user": { "fuzzymatch($platform_user.name,'Tom')|gt": "0", "@order": "fuzzymatch($platform_user.name,'Tom')|-" } }

MQL provides several built-in variable families: $ctx.*: session context values such as $ctx.userId $fn.nowDate and $fn.nowDateTime: current date and time $parent.*: values generated from the parent command during nested save Example: { "platform_user": { "lastLoginAt": "$fn.nowDateTime", "updater": "$ctx.userId" } }

List queries usually return ApiPagedResult: { "code": "200", "msg": "Success", "data": [ { "id": "...", "name": "...", "createAt": "..." } ], "page": 1, "size": 10, "total": 100, "dataSize": 10, "meta": [] } Save or delete requests usually return ApiResult: { "code": "200", "msg": "Success", "data": "123456789" }

This page explains the recommended containerization boundary for Geelato Framework. The repository already separates runtime and design-time responsibilities into independent deliverables: geelato-web-runtime geelato-web-platform geelato-web-designer geelato-app-scaffold Docker packaging should keep the same boundaries instead of merging every responsibility into one opaque image.

Use this shape when you only need business execution capabilities. Package one of: geelato-web-runtime or an application built from geelato-app-scaffold This container should expose runtime-facing APIs only and should not carry design-time management capabilities by default.

Use this shape when you need metadata design, script management, and platform governance capabilities. Package: geelato-web-designer It carries design-time capabilities, so it should remain distinct from pure runtime deployment.

inject database URL, username, and password through environment variables provide upload and conversion directories through mounted volumes For example: spring.datasource.primary.jdbc-url=${GEELATO_PRIMARY_JDBCURL} spring.datasource.primary.username=${GEELATO_PRIMARY_JDBCUSER} spring.datasource.primary.password=${GEELATO_PRIMARY_JDBCPASSWORD} geelato.upload.root-directory=/data/upload geelato.upload.convert-directory=/data/upload/convert geelato.upload.config-directory=/data/upload/config

At the current stage of the official repository, it is better to finish these checks first: verify standard local deployment verify database initialization confirm the runtime/design-time boundary Then externalize the same configuration into Docker images and orchestration.

The web platform is delivered as one shared base module plus two runnable boot modules: geelato-web-platform (shared base: controllers/services/boot) geelato-web-runtime (runtime boot) geelato-web-designer (designer boot) This page explains their relationship, deployment pattern, and minimal configuration differences.

The current relationship is: geelato-web-runtime depends on geelato-web-platform geelato-web-designer depends on geelato-web-platform no dependency between runtime and designer Both boot modules currently expose the full endpoint set from the shared base. The endpoint surface is not yet split at the shared-base level.

The two current application entries are: PlatformWebRuntime PlatformDesginer Both reuse the current BootApplication startup base class. The official business-facing scaffold is: geelato-app-scaffold It depends on runtime capabilities. Endpoint boundary will be reflected after the module-level endpoint split.
Runtime currently defaults to: spring.application.name=geelato-web-runtime Designer currently defaults to: spring.application.name=geelato-web-designer
Design-time / runtime exposure is not controlled via a switch. It is controlled by module dependency. In the current phase, both boot modules expose the same endpoints.
Use this for: business execution environments end-user facing host systems environments that must not expose metadata design, script management, or package publishing APIs
Use this for: low-code designer environments metadata, model, script, and publishing governance platform management environments

This page explains the ORM annotations currently recommended by Geelato Framework for backend entity declaration and metadata mapping.

ORM annotations define how a Java class is recognized as a framework entity and how its fields relate to database columns, titles, and non-persistent properties. They answer the question of how entity metadata is declared. Data access itself is covered by the Fluent DSL Guide.

@Entity marks a class as a persistent entity and maps it to a database table. Typical use cases: creating a new framework entity making the class discoverable by the metadata scanner explicitly binding the entity to a table name Common property: name: the table name; when omitted, the framework usually derives it from the class name with camel-to-snake conversion Example: @Entity(name = "platform_org") public class Demo { private String name; private String code; private String pid; private String type; private String category; private int status; private String description; } Notes: classes marked with @Entity are treated as framework entities regular fields participate in mapping by default field names are usually converted from camel case to snake case for column names

@Col defines an explicit column mapping or column constraint for a field. Typical use cases: the database column name does not match the Java field name the field needs explicit length, precision, or scale constraints Common properties: name: database column name charMaxlength: max string length precision: numeric precision scale: numeric scale Example: @Entity(name = "platform_file") @Title(title = "File") public class FileInfo extends BaseEntity { private String name; @Col(name = "saved_name") @Title(title = "Saved Name", description = "The file name stored on disk") private String savedName; @Col(name = "path") @Title(title = "Relative Path", description = "Usually relative to the file storage root") private String relativePath; private int size; @Col(name = "type") @Title(title = "File Type", description = "File extension") private String fileType; } Constraint example: @Entity(name = "platform_permission") public class Permission extends BaseEntity { @Title(title = "App Id") @Col(name = "app_id") private String appId; private String name; private String code; private String type; private String object; @Title(title = "Rule") @Col(name = "rule", charMaxlength = 1024) private String rule; private String description; @Transient private boolean isDefault; }

@Title adds a business-facing title and optional description to an entity or field. Typical use cases: giving an entity a readable display name documenting important fields with domain meaning Common properties: title: display title description: supplemental description Example: @Entity(name = "platform_file") @Title(title = "File") public class FileInfo extends BaseEntity { @Title(title = "File Name") private String name; @Col(name = "saved_name") @Title(title = "Saved Name", description = "The file name stored on disk") private String savedName; }

@Transient marks a property that should not be mapped to a database column. These properties can still be used in Java-side logic, but they are not persisted as part of the entity metadata model. Typical use cases: runtime-only calculated fields temporary display fields aggregation or external service payload fields Example: @Entity(name = "platform_user") public class User extends BaseEntity { private String name; private String loginName; private String password; @Transient private boolean isOnline; @Transient private String temporaryData; }

Backend entities are typically expected to extend BaseEntity so they can reuse the standard common fields. Typical fields: public class BaseEntity { protected String id; protected String tenantCode; protected String creator; protected String creatorName; protected String updater; protected String updaterName; protected Date createAt; protected Date updateAt; } These fields also fit naturally with the default field filling behavior in the Fluent DSL write path.

use lowercase snake case for table names, such as platform_user use lowercase snake case for column names, such as login_name use camel case for Java properties, such as loginName use PascalCase for entity classes, such as UserInfo

add @Entity to every persistent entity use @Col only when the mapping or constraints differ from the default convention add @Title to entities and important business fields use @Transient only for fields that truly should not be stored
annotations define entity metadata Fluent DSL executes queries and writes against that metadata if the metadata is inaccurate, query, join, and write behavior can also become inaccurate

@Entity(name = "platform_user") @Title(title = "User") public class User extends BaseEntity { @Title(title = "User Name") private String name; @Title(title = "Login Name") private String loginName; @Title(title = "Password") private String password; @Col(name = "phone_number") @Title(title = "Phone Number") private String phoneNumber; @Col(name = "email") @Title(title = "Email") private String email; @Title(title = "Status") private int status; @Transient private List<Role> roles; }
