This page covers the ORM's datasource binding, runtime datasource switching, and the SPI extension entries for query filtering and field filling — three common tasks: Getting the ORM bound to the right Dao. Switching datasources at runtime. Extending query filtering and field-filling rules through SPIs. To understand how the dynamic datasource capability itself works first, read Dynamic Datasource.

Before changing any configuration, identify the scenario so you don't reach for the wrong entry point: Route a single Fluent DSL query to a specific datasource: use .useDataSource(...). Switch a block of code or an entire request to a dynamic datasource: use DynamicDataSourceScope.withDataSource(...) / switchTo(...). Switch a whole service or method to a dynamic datasource: use @UseDynamicDataSource. Replace the dynamic datasource definition source: implement DynamicDataSourceDefinitionLoader. Automatically add tenant/permission conditions to queries, or fill default fields on save: implement the corresponding SPI. These capabilities are related but not interchangeable; picking the wrong entry point leads to configuration confusion.

The current ORM auto-configuration entry is OrmAutoConfiguration, with two core concerns: creating MetaCommandExecutor creating SaveDefaultValueFiller MetaCommandExecutor requires a Dao bean in the host application.
When integrating a new host application, work in this order.

Minimal example: @Configuration public class OrmDaoConfiguration { @Bean public Dao primaryDao(JdbcTemplate jdbcTemplate) { return new Dao(jdbcTemplate); } } Without a Dao, the ORM's main execution chain has no stable landing point.
documents.s: Step 1: Make Sure a Dao Exists

documents.t: The ORM auto-resolution binds dynamicDao preferentially (the only Dao that supports .useDataSource(...) switching); it falls back to primaryDao, then to the single Dao bean — no explicit configuration needed in multi-Dao scenarios. Only configure a property when you need to bind some other custom Dao: geelato.orm.dao-bean-name=myDao
documents.s: Step 2: Confirm Which Dao the ORM Binds

documents.t: Not every project needs it. Continue only when you have one of these requirements: one set of service code needs to access multiple databases certain queries/stored procedures must switch to other databases by key the host application needs to manage the dynamic database list itself
documents.s: Step 3: Decide Whether You Need the Dynamic Datasource

documents.t: Without explicit configuration, the ORM's auto-resolution order is: dynamicDao (built on the routing datasource, the only Dao that supports .useDataSource(...) / entity connectId switching) primaryDao the single Dao bean That is: as long as dynamicDao exists in the container, the ORM binds it — no explicit configuration needed in multi-Dao scenarios. If the host application sets geelato.orm.dao-bean-name, the explicit configuration wins and is used to bind some other custom Dao bean.
documents.s: Which Dao Does the ORM Bind

documents.t: When spring.datasource.primary.jdbc-url exists, the starter creates: primaryDataSource primaryJdbcTemplate primaryDao dbGenerateDao If spring.datasource.secondary.jdbc-url is also configured, it additionally creates: secondaryDataSource secondaryJdbcTemplate secondaryDao
The explicit configuration prefix for the dynamic datasource is: geelato.datasource.dynamic.*

The dynamic datasource beans follow these naming conventions (useful for troubleshooting and overriding): prerequisite: primaryJdbcTemplate auto-configured dynamic datasource beans: dynamicDataSource dynamicJdbcTemplate dynamicDao In a typical project the Starter provides primaryJdbcTemplate; without the Starter, the business application can provide a primaryJdbcTemplate itself (e.g. a JdbcTemplate built on Spring Boot's primary datasource) to trigger the dynamic datasource auto-configuration. Key defaults include: delay-load-data-source=true enable-jta-transaction=false enable-seata-proxy=false default pool settings and connection-test-query=SELECT 1
This is the most common part. Start with the lightest usage.

This fits "route just one ORM query or procedure call to a specific datasource". Query example: List<Map<String, Object>> rows = MetaFactory.query("DevDbConnect") .useDataSource("portal") .page(1, 10) .list(); Stored procedure example: List<Map<String, Object>> rows = MetaFactory.procedure("proc_query_user_orders") .in("userId", "U1001") .useDataSource("portal") .list(); Passthrough SQL example: List<Map<String, Object>> rows = MetaFactory.sql("select id, name from platform_user where del_status = ?") .param(0) .useDataSource("portal") .list(); If your need is only "switch this one chain", prefer this style — the most direct.
documents.s: Style 1: Explicit Switching in the Fluent DSL

documents.t: @UseDynamicDataSource fits more component-level scenarios. It can be placed on: a class a method a field The simplest class-level example: @Service @UseDynamicDataSource("portal") public class PortalUserService { } Method-level example: @Service public class PortalUserService { @UseDynamicDataSource("portal") public void syncUsers() { } } It also supports entity-to-datasource mappings: @UseDynamicDataSource( value = "primary", mappings = { @UseDynamicDataSource.EntitySourceMapping(entityName = "Order", dataSource = "portal"), @UseDynamicDataSource.EntitySourceMapping(entityName = "Customer", dataSource = "crm") } ) public class SyncService { } If a group of methods should share one datasource, or you need to wire the dynamicDao stack, @UseDynamicDataSource is more concise than writing .useDataSource(...) on every query.
documents.s: Style 2: @UseDynamicDataSource on Classes, Methods or Fields

documents.t: When you need "this block of code / this entire request on another database", use the single switching entry point cn.geelato.datasource.DynamicDataSourceScope (business code should not read or write the underlying DynamicDataSourceHolder directly): // block scope: effective inside the block, restored on normal or exceptional exit List<Map<String, Object>> rows = DynamicDataSourceScope.withDataSource("portal", () -> dao.querys(SomeEntity.class)); // request-scoped default: stays in effect until the next switch or the end of the request, // reclaimed by the cleanup safety net DynamicDataSourceScope.switchTo("portal"); The switchDbByConnectId(...) retained on the platform BaseController / BaseService is a thin delegate of switchTo — call it directly in Controller scenarios. For nested semantics, the cleanup safety net and the in-transaction limits, see Switching.

If most ORM operations in the application should land on the dynamic-source chain, no configuration is needed: as long as dynamicDao exists in the container the ORM binds it automatically, and the Fluent DSL gets the dynamic-source capability by default (useDataSource switching works) without per-call designation.
documents.s: Style 4: Let the ORM Bind the Dynamic-Source Dao by Default

documents.t: The previous styles decide the datasource "at call time", "inside a code block", or "at component level". To make an entity's datasource ownership fixed and written into the entity declaration, declare it with the @Entity annotation. This fits: an entity that inherently belongs to another database (e.g. orders fixed in the order database) a batch of entities grouped by module onto different databases (e.g. an email group on the mail database) avoiding repeated datasource designation on every service or query This style sits at a different level from the previous ones and can be combined: the annotation declares the entity's "default ownership", while .useDataSource(...) can still override it on a single call. Path A: Explicit connectId​ Declare the datasource directly on the entity — the highest priority: @Entity(name = "demo_order", table = "t_demo_order", connectId = "order_db") public class DemoOrder { // ... } From then on, every ORM operation on this entity routes to order_db automatically; no per-call switching needed. Path B: catalog Grouping + Configuration Mapping​ If a batch of entities belongs to the same database, tagging each with connectId is tedious. Tag them with the same catalog instead, then map the catalog to a datasource via configuration: // a group of entities all tagged with the same catalog @Entity(name = "demo_order", catalog = "business") public class DemoOrder { } @Entity(name = "demo_order_item", catalog = "business") public class DemoOrderItem { } Then map the catalog to a datasource in configuration: geelato.datasource.dynamic.catalog-mapping.platform=primary geelato.datasource.dynamic.catalog-mapping.business=order_db Equivalent YAML: geelato: datasource: dynamic: catalog-mapping: platform: primary business: order_db The benefit: switching databases means changing configuration only, not code. All entities in the business group move to the new datasource together. Resolution Priority​ Which datasource an entity finally uses is determined in this order (high → low): TableMeta.connectId is non-blank — an explicit @Entity(connectId) and a runtime-registered value (the registration entry is provided by the platform) write into the same slot (runtime registration merges later and can overwrite the annotation value for non-platform entities); they are not two priority levels the mapping of @Entity(catalog) in catalog-mapping neither → handed over to the Dao-call-time fallback chain (annotation default > outer explicit key > request-level override > platform default > primary) Resolution happens on demand at runtime via MetaManager.resolveConnectId, so it does not matter when the configuration is injected. See Binding & Priority for the full priority chain and decision flow. Notes​ The datasource key a mapping points to must be a registered dynamic datasource (the key has been provided by the definition source, or supplied through a custom loader or another registration channel); when unregistered, the first resolution fails hard (an IllegalStateException is thrown, refusing silent fallback to primary). System entities with catalog = "platform" keep their existing protection (Java class definition always wins, refresh and hand-over forbidden); mapping platform to primary in catalog-mapping is recommended to stay consistent with the system database. Resolution completes on demand at query time, independent of entity scan order — no need to worry about framework startup sequencing.
documents.s: Style 5: Declare Entity Ownership with the @Entity Annotation

documents.t: Just like the metadata source (MetaStore), the dynamic datasource definition source is abstracted as an SPI. Understanding the motivation helps you decide whether to replace it.
documents.s: Why the Definition Source Is Abstracted

documents.t: In earlier versions, the connection details of dynamic datasources were hard-bound to a single connection table on the platform side — the default loader simply read the whole table and turned each row into a datasource definition. This coupled the framework layer (geelato-orm) to a specific table structure, with three real pain points: Pain point Scenario Hard to manage across environments Datasource configurations for dev / test / prod are scattered across their own databases; changing one connection means editing SQL in a database — no audit, no versioning. Configuration centers unusable Wanting Nacos / Apollo to centrally manage and push datasource lists meant bypassing the framework and building your own. Lightweight projects forced onto platform tables A small service that only wants multi-datasource support had to adopt the whole platform table set — too costly.
documents.s: Before: Definitions Hard-Bound to the Platform Table

documents.t: The framework abstracted the loading logic into the DynamicDataSourceDefinitionLoader SPI (in the cn.geelato.datasource.spi package of geelato-orm), and "read from the platform table" was demoted to a default implementation, PlatformDynamicDataSourceDefinitionLoader (moved to the business layer geelato-web-platform). Key design: DynamicDataSourceRegistry injects the loader with @Nullable — when no loader is provided at all, the framework only uses primary / secondary and still runs standalone. This matches the MetaStore philosophy of "runs without a database".
documents.s: Design Decision: Abstract "Where Datasources Come From" into an SPI

documents.t: Centralized management in a configuration center: Nacos / Apollo manages multi-environment datasources; changing configuration takes effect immediately (with the hot refresh below) — no SQL editing in a database. Zero framework changes: implement the interface + @Primary, without touching a single line of framework code. No platform tables required: start from files / in-memory definitions, upgrade when needed. Operations friendly: change or expand databases without code changes or restarts (host mapping + two-step hot refresh). Everything is inherited: lazy pool creation, pool tuning, Seata / JTA, entity→datasource auto-routing — after switching the source, all of it is reused automatically.

The current default dynamic datasource definition loader is PlatformDynamicDataSourceDefinitionLoader (business layer geelato-web-platform), which loads from the connection definitions maintained platform-side. Because the loader is optional-injected, it is used when you provide no custom implementation; providing one replaces it.
The host application only needs to provide its own DynamicDataSourceDefinitionLoader to replace the default loading logic.

This is exactly isomorphic to the override mechanism in MetaStore Extension, and it is the most frequent misuse: the default PlatformDynamicDataSourceDefinitionLoader is a @Component and has no @Primary; the injection point on DynamicDataSourceRegistry is a constructor parameter @Nullable DynamicDataSourceDefinitionLoader definitionLoader, without @Qualifier; writing @Component implements DynamicDataSourceDefinitionLoader directly → two candidates in the container → startup fails with NoUniqueBeanDefinitionException. The correct way is to add @Primary on your implementation: @Component @Primary public class MyDataSourceDefinitionLoader implements DynamicDataSourceDefinitionLoader { // ... } warning Do not rely on same-name bean overriding (spring.main.allow-bean-definition-overriding is false by default). Enabling global overriding has side effects and is not recommended.
documents.s: Making Your Implementation Take Effect: @Primary Is Required

documents.t: public interface DynamicDataSourceDefinitionLoader { List<Map<String, Object>> loadAll(); // all datasource definitions; each Map's "id" is the routing key Map<String, Object> loadOne(String key); // load a single one by routing key (for hot refresh) } Every Map<String, Object> returned by loadAll() must contain the following fields (the field convention is snake_case; the platform default implementation provides rows in this shape): Field Required Description id required datasource routing key (what .useDataSource(id) and @Entity(connectId) use) db_type required database type, see the table below db_hostname_ip required host address (can be redirected by host mapping) db_port required port db_user_name required username db_name required database / schema name db_password optional password, see the encryption convention below Supported db_type values: db_type Driver Notes mysql com.mysql.cj.jdbc.Driver case-insensitive postgresql / postgres org.postgresql.Driver both spellings are equivalent others — throws UnsupportedOperationException: unsupported database type Password encryption convention: plain text works as-is; to encrypt, the format must be algorithm:ciphertext where the algorithm is aes / rsa / sm2 / sm4 (the framework picks the decryption algorithm by prefix). Values without an algorithm: prefix are passed through as plain text.
documents.s: Contract: Interface and Map Field Conventions

documents.t: Use case: quickly verify that "a custom source gets wired", or build a minimal runnable demo. package com.acme.platform.ds; import cn.geelato.datasource.spi.DynamicDataSourceDefinitionLoader; import org.springframework.context.annotation.Primary; import org.springframework.stereotype.Component; import java.util.HashMap; import java.util.List; import java.util.Map; @Component @Primary public class InMemoryDataSourceLoader implements DynamicDataSourceDefinitionLoader { @Override public List<Map<String, Object>> loadAll() { Map<String, Object> ds = new HashMap<>(); ds.put("id", "biz-mysql"); // routing key (required) ds.put("db_type", "mysql"); // required ds.put("db_hostname_ip", "10.0.0.10");// required ds.put("db_port", 3306); // required ds.put("db_user_name", "biz_user"); // required ds.put("db_name", "biz_db"); // required ds.put("db_password", "biz@psd"); // optional; plain text here return List.of(ds); } @Override public Map<String, Object> loadOne(String key) { return loadAll().stream() .filter(m -> key.equals(String.valueOf(m.get("id")))) .findFirst().orElse(null); } } Expected result: after startup, .useDataSource("biz-mysql") routes to a HikariCP pool; the log shows HikariPool-... poolName=biz-mysql.

Use case: manage the datasource list with files shipped with the application; use different files per environment profile. First prepare src/main/resources/datasource/biz-mysql.json: { "id": "biz-mysql", "dbType": "mysql", "host": "10.0.0.10", "port": 3306, "userName": "biz_user", "dbName": "biz_db", "password": "sm4:Y3yK9+...ciphertext..." } Then implement a loader that reads all of classpath:datasource/*.json at startup: package com.acme.platform.ds; import cn.geelato.datasource.spi.DynamicDataSourceDefinitionLoader; import com.alibaba.fastjson2.JSON; import com.alibaba.fastjson2.JSONObject; import org.springframework.context.annotation.Primary; import org.springframework.core.io.Resource; import org.springframework.core.io.support.PathMatchingResourcePatternResolver; import org.springframework.stereotype.Component; import java.io.InputStream; import java.nio.charset.StandardCharsets; import java.util.*; @Component @Primary public class JsonFileDataSourceLoader implements DynamicDataSourceDefinitionLoader { private final List<Map<String, Object>> definitions = new ArrayList<>(); public JsonFileDataSourceLoader() throws Exception { var resolver = new PathMatchingResourcePatternResolver(); for (Resource res : resolver.getResources("classpath:datasource/*.json")) { try (InputStream in = res.getInputStream()) { String text = new String(in.readAllBytes(), StandardCharsets.UTF_8); JSONObject json = JSON.parseObject(text); // note: the Map keys must follow the framework's snake_case convention Map<String, Object> ds = new HashMap<>(); ds.put("id", json.getString("id")); ds.put("db_type", json.getString("dbType")); ds.put("db_hostname_ip", json.getString("host")); ds.put("db_port", json.getIntValue("port")); ds.put("db_user_name", json.getString("userName")); ds.put("db_name", json.getString("dbName")); ds.put("db_password", json.getString("password")); // supports encrypted forms like sm4:xxx definitions.add(ds); } } } @Override public List<Map<String, Object>> loadAll() { return definitions; } @Override public Map<String, Object> loadOne(String key) { return definitions.stream() .filter(m -> key.equals(String.valueOf(m.get("id")))) .findFirst().orElse(null); } } Expected result: dropping a new *.json into the datasource/ directory makes it an available datasource automatically.
documents.s: Example B: Loading from JSON / YAML Files (Most Common)

documents.t: Use case: the enterprise runs a central "database connection registry"; the application pulls the list at startup and keeps a single source of truth. package com.acme.platform.ds; import cn.geelato.datasource.spi.DynamicDataSourceDefinitionLoader; import org.springframework.context.annotation.Primary; import org.springframework.core.ParameterizedTypeReference; import org.springframework.stereotype.Component; import org.springframework.web.client.RestClient; import java.util.List; import java.util.Map; /** * The agreed endpoint returns an array conforming to the field conventions: * [{ "id": "biz-mysql", "db_type": "mysql", "db_hostname_ip": "...", ... }] */ @Component @Primary public class HttpApiDataSourceLoader implements DynamicDataSourceDefinitionLoader { private final RestClient client = RestClient.builder() .baseUrl("http://ds-registry.internal.svc") .build(); @Override public List<Map<String, Object>> loadAll() { return client.get() .uri("/api/datasources") .retrieve() .body(new ParameterizedTypeReference<List<Map<String, Object>>>() {}); } @Override public Map<String, Object> loadOne(String key) { return loadAll().stream() .filter(m -> key.equals(String.valueOf(m.get("id")))) .findFirst().orElse(null); } } Expected result: after a new datasource is added and published in the registry, it becomes usable after an application restart or a hot refresh.
documents.s: Example C: Loading from an External HTTP API

documents.t: After implementing a loader, don't stop at a successful Spring startup — run a real query right away: List<Map<String, Object>> rows = MetaFactory.query("DevDbConnect") .useDataSource("biz-mysql") .page(1, 1) .list(); If this executes successfully, "definition loading + datasource switching + the ORM execution chain" is working end to end.

After datasource definitions change, no restart is needed. The framework provides two refresh entries, and both steps are required: @Autowired(required = false) private cn.geelato.datasource.DynamicDataSourceRegistry dynamicDataSourceRegistry; @Autowired(required = false) @org.springframework.beans.factory.annotation.Qualifier("dynamicDataSource") private cn.geelato.datasource.DynamicRoutingDataSource dynamicRoutingDataSource; public void refresh(String key) { // step 1: rebuild the config and the connection pool for that key boolean ok = dynamicDataSourceRegistry.refreshDataSource(key); // step 2: refresh the routing table so DynamicRoutingDataSource notices the change if (ok) { dynamicRoutingDataSource.refreshDataSource(key); } } DynamicDataSourceRegistry.refreshDataSource(key) / refreshAllDataSources(): rebuild the configuration (and the pool when necessary). DynamicRoutingDataSource.refreshDataSource(key) / refreshAllDataSources(): reassemble the routing table and make Spring recompute it. warning Calling only the first step and not the second is the most common cause of "the source changed but switching doesn't take effect" — the configuration changed while the routing table still points at the old pool.

If you only need to register a datasource temporarily in code (e.g. built from application.properties, or obtained from a pool factory), you can bypass the loader and register directly: dynamicDataSourceRegistry.registerDataSource("my-key", alreadyBuiltDataSource); dynamicRoutingDataSource.refreshAllDataSources(); This approach depends on no loader implementation and suits "a few, static, known-at-startup" datasources.
documents.s: Don't Want to Replace the Loader? Register an Already-Built DataSource Directly

documents.t: Datasource extensions often appear together with platform rule extensions. For example: after switching to a tenant datasource, tenant filters should be appended automatically certain save chains should fill tenant code, creator, update time, etc. Don't hard-code these into business services — implement the SPIs instead.

Choose by entry point: to affect Fluent DSL queries: implement FluentQueryFilterInjector to affect Fluent DSL saves: implement FluentSaveFieldValueFiller to affect MQL queries: implement MqlQueryFilterInjector to affect MQL saves: implement MqlSaveFieldValueFiller
documents.s: First Decide Which SPI to Implement

documents.t: @Component public class DemoFluentQueryFilterInjector implements FluentQueryFilterInjector { @Override public boolean isEnabled() { return true; } @Override public void inject(QueryCommand command, MetaQuery query) { // inject platform-level filter conditions into the Fluent DSL query command here } }
documents.s: Example 1: Fluent DSL Query Filter SPI

documents.t: @Component public class DemoFluentSaveFieldValueFiller implements FluentSaveFieldValueFiller { @Override public boolean isEnabled() { return true; } @Override public void fill(FluentSaveFieldValueFillContext context) { // fill default save fields here } }
documents.s: Example 2: Fluent DSL Save Field Fill SPI

documents.t: Every SPI class follows the same key rules: 0 implementations: skipped 1 implementation: executed per isEnabled() multiple implementations: exception thrown immediately This means: do not enable two FluentQueryFilterInjectors at the same time do not enable two FluentSaveFieldValueFillers at the same time with multiple candidates in the project, converge them into a single enabled implementation upstream For a more complete SPI description, see Query Filter and Field Fill SPI.
documents.s: The SPI Runtime Rules You Must Remember

documents.t: Neither JTA nor Seata is enabled by default. They only enter their capability chains after explicit configuration, for example: geelato.datasource.dynamic.enable-jta-transaction=true So the minimal skeleton and ordinary business applications stay free of heavy-transaction dependencies by default.

When a new project needs ORM, dynamic datasources and platform rules at once, the recommended order is: first verify primaryDao or another basic Dao works then confirm the ORM auto-bound dynamicDao (bound whenever present; switching does not work when primaryDao is bound) then enable dynamic datasources and verify .useDataSource(...) then add @UseDynamicDataSource as needed finally implement the query filter and field fill SPIs The benefit: when something breaks, you can quickly locate whether it is the Dao not wired correctly the dynamic source not taking effect the datasource definition not loaded an SPI extension written incorrectly

When "switching doesn't take effect" or "the SPI doesn't fire", check in this order: whether primaryDao / dynamicDao really exist in the container whether the ORM bound dynamicDao (it should be auto-bound when geelato.orm.dao-bean-name is not configured) whether the dynamic source definition really loads the target key whether the code really calls .useDataSource("...") or hits @UseDynamicDataSource whether more than one implementation of the same SPI is registered whether the SPI's isEnabled() returns true a custom loader fails at startup with NoUniqueBeanDefinitionException → the implementation is missing @Primary UnsupportedOperationException: unsupported database type → the Map's db_type is neither the built-in mysql / postgresql nor a dialect family registered via Dialects.registerAlias the source changed but switching doesn't take effect → only DynamicDataSourceRegistry was refreshed, not DynamicRoutingDataSource (both steps are required)

prefer the ORM for regular backend CRUD override the definition source through the extension point instead of hard-modifying the default implementation no configuration needed in multi-Dao scenarios — the ORM auto-binds dynamicDao; configure geelato.orm.dao-bean-name only to bind some other custom Dao do not enable JTA / Seata by default unless clearly needed prefer .useDataSource(...) for single-chain source switching consider @UseDynamicDataSource for component-level switching use DynamicDataSourceScope.withDataSource(...) / switchTo(...) for block / request-scoped switching; do not read or write DynamicDataSourceHolder directly when an entity's datasource ownership is fixed, declare it with @Entity(connectId/catalog) instead of switching per call prefer SPIs for platform-level query and field rules rather than scattering them across business code

This page explains the built-in ORM event mechanism in Geelato Framework and how developers can use it to add their own custom logic around save and delete flows. The current event capability lives in: cn.geelato.core.orm.event It is not a standalone message bus and not just a thin wrapper over Spring ApplicationEvent. It is a lightweight hook mechanism inside the ORM execution chain itself.

The purpose of the ORM event mechanism is to decouple generic CRUD execution from business-specific side effects. It is suitable for scenarios such as: adding extra validation or values before save blocking or guarding delete before execution synchronizing a mirror table after save writing audit logs, sending notifications, or refreshing cache after save cleaning downstream state, maintaining side indexes, or doing async compensation after delete With this model, developers do not need to modify Dao directly or duplicate the CRUD flow. They only need to attach listeners.

The current ORM event system has two major groups: save events delete events Each group has two timing points: Before After So the current extension points are: BeforeSaveEventListener AfterSaveEventListener BeforeDeleteEventListener AfterDeleteEventListener

Events are triggered inside the actual Dao save, batch save, multi save, delete, and multi delete flows. That means whether the write operation starts from: Dao.save(...) Dao.batchSave(...) Dao.multiSave(...) Dao.delete(...) Dao.multiDelete(...) or from a higher-level Fluent DSL path that eventually lands in these ORM write paths, the event mechanism is still part of the execution chain.

Before events run synchronously. That means they run: before the real SQL execution with the ability to modify BoundSql with the ability to validate with the ability to throw exceptions and stop the main flow If a before-listener throws an exception, the current save or delete operation fails immediately. So Before events are best for: normalization SQL adjustment permission or state validation hard pre-check interception

After events run asynchronously. The current implementation uses a fixed thread pool: save event thread name prefix: save-event-* delete event thread name prefix: delete-event-* The default pool size is: 4 So After events mean: the main SQL has already finished the listener is scheduled asynchronously listener exceptions are logged, but they do not break the main flow This makes them suitable for: audit logging mirror-table synchronization cache refresh non-critical notifications async side processing

The save-event context currently contains: Dao dao SessionCtx sessionCtx IdEntity entity BoundSql boundSql SaveCommand command Map<String, Object> resultValueMap String eventId long startTime Meaning: dao: lets the listener reuse ORM execution capability sessionCtx: shared session-level context of the save flow entity: direct entity object when the entry path is entity save boundSql: the final SQL and parameters for this write command: ORM save command information such as entity name and values resultValueMap: the result values after the main save finishes eventId: unique ID for log correlation startTime: event start timestamp for timing and diagnostics

The delete-event context currently contains: Dao dao SessionCtx sessionCtx BoundSql boundSql DeleteCommand command int affectedRows String eventId long startTime It is mainly used for: viewing or adjusting delete SQL reading delete-command metadata checking affected row count after delete tracing this delete event in logs or compensation flows

The base save-listener interface defines: beforeSave(SaveEventContext context) afterSave(SaveEventContext context) supports(...) enabled(...) Important detail: supports(...) returns false by default enabled(...) returns false by default So if a developer does not override these methods explicitly, the listener may be registered but still never execute.

The base delete-listener interface defines: beforeDelete(DeleteEventContext context) afterDelete(DeleteEventContext context) supports(...) enabled(...) Again: listeners are not enabled automatically by default they must explicitly declare both support and enabled behavior

The current model does not rely on Spring auto-discovery. It uses static event managers. Save events use: SaveEventManager.registerBefore(...) SaveEventManager.registerAfter(...) SaveEventManager.registerBeforeIfAbsent(...) SaveEventManager.registerAfterIfAbsent(...) Delete events use: DeleteEventManager.registerBefore(...) DeleteEventManager.registerAfter(...) DeleteEventManager.registerBeforeIfAbsent(...) DeleteEventManager.registerAfterIfAbsent(...) The managers also support: unregistering listeners clearing listeners replacing the executor with setExecutor(...) This means the current event model is: globally registered process-local bounded by the current JVM

The current save-event manager registers one built-in example listener: ReadonlyShadowTableListener Its purpose is to mirror save SQL into a corresponding: *_readonly shadow table. For example: insert into xxx (...) update xxx set ... can be rewritten as: insert into xxx_readonly (...) update xxx_readonly set ... However, the internal switch is currently disabled by default: READONLY_EVENT_ENABLED = false So it works more as a reference implementation that shows how the event mechanism can support: readonly mirror synchronization side-write behavior data shadow maintenance
documents.s: Built-In Example: Readonly Shadow Table Listener

documents.t: If you want to validate domain rules before the write happens, implement: BeforeSaveEventListener Typical uses: blocking updates in certain states validating cross-field constraints enriching values before persistence Example: public class CustomerBeforeSaveListener implements BeforeSaveEventListener { @Override public void beforeSave(SaveEventContext context) { if ("crm_customer".equalsIgnoreCase(context.getCommand().getEntityName())) { Object code = context.getCommand().getValueMap().get("code"); if (code == null || String.valueOf(code).isBlank()) { throw new IllegalArgumentException("customer code must not be empty"); } } } @Override public void afterSave(SaveEventContext context) { } @Override public boolean supports(SaveEventContext context) { return context.getCommand() != null; } @Override public boolean enabled(SaveEventContext context) { return true; } }

If you want non-blocking side effects after the main save succeeds, implement: AfterSaveEventListener Typical uses: writing audit logs refreshing cache pushing change notifications synchronizing search indexes Example: public class CustomerAfterSaveListener implements AfterSaveEventListener { @Override public void beforeSave(SaveEventContext context) { } @Override public void afterSave(SaveEventContext context) { if ("crm_customer".equalsIgnoreCase(context.getCommand().getEntityName())) { System.out.println("customer changed, eventId=" + context.getEventId()); } } @Override public boolean supports(SaveEventContext context) { return context.getCommand() != null; } @Override public boolean enabled(SaveEventContext context) { return true; } }
documents.s: Scenario 2: Async Side Processing After Save

documents.t: If you want to protect delete operations before execution, implement: BeforeDeleteEventListener Typical uses: blocking deletion of built-in system data checking downstream references rewriting physical delete into a guarded strategy
If you want to do cleanup after delete, implement: AfterDeleteEventListener Typical uses: cache cleanup index cleanup side-table cleanup delete audit logging

It is better to centralize listener registration in one explicit startup location instead of registering listeners in many scattered places. Examples: application startup initialization one dedicated ORM configuration class one shared base module initialization entry This helps keep: registration order predictable duplicate registration under control enable/disable behavior easier across environments
If a before-listener fails, the main save or delete fails too. So Before should be used for: hard constraints mandatory validation must-succeed preconditions
documents.s: 1. Before Can Break the Main Flow

documents.t: After listeners run asynchronously, so they should not be the only place for logic that must stay strongly consistent with the main transaction. If the logic must remain fully aligned with the main write transaction, it is better to: handle it before execution or orchestrate it explicitly in the service layer transaction flow
documents.s: 2. After Is Not for Strong Transaction Semantics

documents.t: Because After listeners run in a thread pool, developers should not assume they can freely rely on: thread-local state web request context security context that was never explicitly propagated If the listener needs such information, it should read it from the event context or make it explicit before the event is dispatched.

Although register*IfAbsent(...) exists, duplicate behavior can still happen if different modules create different listener instances and register them repeatedly. A better approach is: centralize listener instances centralize registration

The current ORM event mechanism in Geelato Framework is a built-in extension point around Dao save and delete flows: before-events run synchronously and fit validation or interception after-events run asynchronously and fit notifications or side processing context objects expose SQL, command, result, and session information to listeners developers can use the listener abstraction to implement custom audit, mirror, cache, index, and validation logic So it works especially well as: a unified ORM extension mechanism a reusable domain hook shared across business modules a customization entry that avoids direct intrusion into core CRUD implementation

This page explains how backend Java services use the Geelato Framework Fluent DSL through MetaFactory. Sample projects: Repository: geelato-hello-example ORM integration sample: geelato-sample-orm
provide a Java-style metadata CRUD entry for backend developers avoid direct MQL JSON construction while still reusing the existing MetaQLManager + SqlManager + Dao execution kernel

In the current ORM system, the Fluent DSL is the backend Java API. Its boundary relative to other parts is: ORM annotations declare entity metadata MQL serves frontend and platform-side JSON protocol access the Fluent DSL serves backend Java CRUD and lightweight advanced querying events, dynamic datasource, and query/filter fill SPI inject platform rules into the execution path So the Fluent DSL is not a string wrapper around MQL. It is the Java-facing ORM entry for service code.

when backend services need metadata query, insert, update, or delete by entity name or entity class when the service wants to reuse built-in capabilities such as dynamic datasource switching, view parameters, and $ctx/$fn/$parent value references

when frontend pages already go through the platform data API based on MetaController + MQL when an existing service already works well with BaseService + entity class and does not need metadata-driven unification when the query has clearly become SQL-first and is better maintained as final SQL or MyBatis mapping

By entity name: List<Map<String, Object>> users = MetaFactory.query("User") .select(new String[]{"id", "name", "mobilePhone"}) .where(Filter.eq("delStatus", 0)) .order(Order.desc("updateAt")) .list(); By entity class: List<Map<String, Object>> users = MetaFactory.query(User.class) .select(new String[]{"id", "name"}) .page(1, 20) .list();

Single row: Map<String, Object> user = MetaFactory.query("User") .where(Filter.eq("id", "1912345678901234567")) .one(); Paged query: PageResult<Map<String, Object>> page = MetaFactory.query("User") .select(new String[]{"id", "name", "updateAt"}) .where(Filter.like("name", "zhang")) .order(Order.desc("updateAt")) .page(1, 10) .page(); Single-column query: List<String> ids = MetaFactory.query("User") .select(new String[]{"id"}) .where(Filter.eq("delStatus", 0)) .oneColumn(String.class); Result types — auto unwrap and typed overloads: When wrapperResult(...) is not set and each result row has exactly one column, list()/one()/page() return the bare column value instead of wrapping it in a Map: List<String> names = MetaFactory.query("User") .select(new String[]{"name"}) .where(Filter.eq("delStatus", 0)) .list(); Multi-column results are unchanged (still Map<String, Object>), and bare values are not type-converted. Java type erasure prevents a no-arg list() from knowing the declared element type, so the inference is based on the result-set shape; use the typed overloads list(Class)/one(Class) when you need conversion or object mapping: Target type Behavior Simple types (String, numbers, Boolean, Date, java.time, ...) requires a single column and converts the value (for example Long to Integer/String) Map.class returns row maps as-is Custom classes (DTO/entity) maps each row to an object instance, including snake_case columns to camelCase fields (email_address to emailAddress) List<Integer> ages = MetaFactory.sql("select age from platform_user where del_status = ?") .param(0) .list(Integer.class); List<UserOrgDto> orgs = MetaFactory.sql("select o.id, o.name, oru.default_org as defaultOrg from platform_org_r_user oru ...") .param("U1001") .list(UserOrgDto.class); These rules apply to list()/one() of MetaFactory.sql(...), MetaFactory.query(...), and MetaFactory.procedure(...), as well as to page() records; oneColumn(Class) remains available for executor-level single-column queries. When wrapperResult(...) is set it takes precedence; to keep row maps for a single-column query, use .wrapperResult(row -> row). Complex wrapping still uses wrapperResult(...): List<UserSimpleDto> users = MetaFactory.query("User") .where(Filter.eq("delStatus", 0)) .wrapperResult(row -> new UserSimpleDto( String.valueOf(row.get("id")), maskMobilePhone(String.valueOf(row.get("mobilePhone"))) )) .list();

Insert: String userId = MetaFactory.insert("User") .value("name", "test user") .value("mobilePhone", "13800000000") .save(); Default fields are filled before save: inserts align with the current MQL rules and fill fields such as createAt, creator, creatorName, tenantCode, buId, deptId, updateAt, updater, updaterName, and deleteAt updates fill updateAt, updater, and updaterName the behavior comes from the built-in default filler and can be customized by overriding SaveDefaultValueFiller Update: String userId = MetaFactory.update("User") .value("id", "1912345678901234567") .value("name", "new name") .save(); Delete: int affected = MetaFactory.delete("User") .where(Filter.eq("id", "1912345678901234567")) .execute(); By default delete(...) performs a logical delete (update ... set del_status = 1, delete_at = ...). The effective mode resolves as call-level MetaFactory.physicalDelete(...) (or MQL "@physicalDelete": true) > entity-level @Entity(deleteMode = LOGIC | PHYSICAL) > global default (the GEELATO_DELETE_MODE env variable, read once at class load by GlobalContext and then fixed; default logic). A physical delete generates delete from ...: int affected = MetaFactory.physicalDelete("User") .where(Filter.eq("id", "1912345678901234567")) .execute();

Besides building field by field with .value(field, value), MetaFactory also offers overloads that accept an entity instance directly: they pre-fill SQL from the entity's non-null properties, so you do not have to assemble field values by hand. To switch the data source, chain .useDataSource(...) on the returned builder as usual. Convention: only non-null mapped properties of the entity instance are collected; null fields are skipped (inserts fall back to defaults, updates never overwrite existing columns). The entity must be a JavaBean with getters/setters (e.g. extend IdEntity and add accessors). Save directly (one-liner, auto insert-or-update): User user = new User(); user.setName("demo user"); user.setMobilePhone("13800000000"); // blank id -> insert, PK generated by the framework String id = MetaFactory.save(user); user.setId(id); user.setName("new name"); // non-blank id -> update by PK MetaFactory.save(user); Build from an entity instance (returns a builder, chainable): // insert builder MetaFactory.insert(user).useDataSource("portal").save(); // update builder (when id is present, where(PK) is appended automatically) MetaFactory.update(user).useDataSource("portal").save(); // query by example: non-null fields become conditions List<Map<String, Object>> rows = MetaFactory.query(user) .order(Order.desc("createAt")) .list(); Notes: save(entity) is the only one-liner that executes immediately and returns the PK; the other overloads return builders, consistent with insert(Class) / update(Class) / query(Class) PK detection: blank id (null or empty string) -> insert; non-blank id -> update by PK The object overloads are fully equivalent to the field-name versions under the hood, reusing the same default-field fill, UID generation, and dynamic data source support

Referenced field join: List<Map<String, Object>> orders = MetaFactory.query("Order") .select(new String[]{"id", "code"}) .selectRef("userId->name", "userName") .list(); Custom join: List<Map<String, Object>> rows = MetaFactory.query("Order") .as("o") .select(new String[]{"id", "code"}) .selectExpr("u.name", "userName") .leftJoin("User", "u", on -> on.eqField("userId", "u.id")) .groupBy("id", "code", "u.name") .havingSql("count(*) > 0") .page(1, 20) .page(); Dynamic datasource: List<Map<String, Object>> rows = MetaFactory.query("DevDbConnect") .useDataSource("portal") .page(1, 10) .list(); Skip injected filters: // Skip injected filters for this query (tenant isolation, data permission, etc. are not appended). // Only for trusted scenarios such as system back office or scheduled tasks; // it risks cross-tenant / unauthorized reads. List<Map<String, Object>> rows = MetaFactory.query("platform_user") .disableInjectFilter() .list(); disableInjectFilter() skips all injectors for this query. If an injector (such as tenant isolation) must never be bypassed by a single query, override FluentQueryFilterInjector.isForceInject() to return true in its implementation; then disableInjectFilter() no longer affects that injector. See Query Filter and Save Field Fill SPI. View parameters: List<Map<String, Object>> rows = MetaFactory.query("SomeViewEntity") .viewParams(Map.of("customerId", "C001")) .page(1, 10) .list(); Context and function value references: String id = MetaFactory.insert("Notice") .value("creator", ValueRefs.ctx("userId")) .value("createAt", ValueRefs.fnNowDateTime()) .save(); MySQL procedure: List<Map<String, Object>> rows = MetaFactory.procedure("proc_query_user_orders") .in("userId", "U1001") .in("status", 1) .useDataSource("portal") .list(); Native SQL passthrough: List<Map<String, Object>> rows = MetaFactory.sql("select id, name from platform_user where del_status = ?") .param(0) .useDataSource("portal") .list(); Parent-child nested save: String parentId = MetaFactory.insert("App") .value("name", "demo-app") .child("AppVersion", child -> child .value("appId", ValueRefs.parent("id")) .value("code", "v1")) .save();

selectRef(...) fits the case where the main entity already has foreign-key metadata the framework can derive the left join automatically, so the service code does not need to write the join condition if you omit an explicit alias in selectRef(...), the result column uses the remote field name by default List<Map<String, Object>> orders = MetaFactory.query("Order") .select(new String[]{"id", "code", "amount"}) .selectRef("userId->name", "userName") .selectRef("userId->mobilePhone", "userMobile") .where(Filter.eq("delStatus", 0)) .order(Order.desc("updateAt")) .list(); custom join fits cases without foreign-key metadata or cases that need explicit join control use a stable alias convention, such as .as("o") for the main table and short aliases such as u or d for joined tables keep aliases consistent across selectExpr(...), groupBy(...), and havingSql(...) List<Map<String, Object>> rows = MetaFactory.query("Order") .as("o") .select(new String[]{"id", "code"}) .selectExpr("u.name", "userName") .selectExpr("d.name", "deptName") .leftJoin("User", "u", on -> on.eqField("o.userId", "u.id")) .leftJoin("Dept", "d", on -> on.eqField("u.deptId", "d.id")) .groupBy("id", "code", "u.name", "d.name") .havingSql("count(*) > 0") .page(1, 20) .page();

current procedure support is intentionally lightweight and mainly targets MySQL-style IN parameters plus one result set parameters are added in call order through .in(name, value) the name is mainly for readability; runtime binding is positional Map<String, Object> row = MetaFactory.procedure("proc_query_user_orders") .in("userId", "U1001") .in("status", 1) .one(); Object mapping works through the typed overloads, and complex wrapping still uses wrapperResult(...): List<OrderSimpleDto> rows = MetaFactory.procedure("proc_query_user_orders") .in("userId", "U1001") .in("status", 1) .list(OrderSimpleDto.class); List<OrderSimpleDto> masked = MetaFactory.procedure("proc_query_user_orders") .in("userId", "U1001") .in("status", 1) .wrapperResult(row -> { OrderSimpleDto dto = new OrderSimpleDto(); dto.setId(String.valueOf(row.get("id"))); dto.setCode(String.valueOf(row.get("code"))); return dto; }) .list();

use MetaFactory.sql(...) when the service already owns the final SQL and only wants to reuse the execution chain this path provides datasource switching, parameter binding, and terminal execution methods it does not add metadata-aware joins, default audit fields, or expression conversion single-column results are auto-unwrapped to bare values, and list(Class)/one(Class) support typed conversion and DTO mapping (see Query Examples) Map<String, Object> row = MetaFactory.sql("select id, name from platform_user where id = ?") .param("U1001") .one(); List<String> emails = MetaFactory.sql("select email_address from platform_user_email_account where user_id = ?") .param("U1001") .list(); Long total = MetaFactory.sql("select count(1) from platform_user where del_status = ?") .param(0) .queryForObject(Long.class); int affected = MetaFactory.sql("update platform_notice set status = ? where id = ?") .params("read", "N1001") .execute();

use toSql() to inspect the generated SQL or procedure call use toCountSql() when checking pagination count issues for join issues, verify aliases and foreign-key metadata first for procedure issues, verify parameter order, datasource choice, and result-set shape first for native SQL, verify the SQL itself, placeholder count, and terminal method choice first

use Fluent DSL first for standard single-table CRUD, light references, and lightweight aggregation use selectRef(...) first when foreign-key metadata already exists use explicit join only when the metadata path is not enough use MetaFactory.sql(...) when the team intentionally owns the SQL text keep MQL, SQL Key, or MyBatis for very complex filtering, recursive SQL, window functions, or multi-result-set procedures

ORM stands for Object-Relational Mapping. In Geelato Framework, it is the operational layer between programming-language objects and relational databases such as MySQL and PostgreSQL. In practice, Geelato does not expose ORM as a single monolithic API. It is a capability system built around metadata, JSON protocol access, Java DSL access, and extension hooks: annotation layer: declares how Java objects map to entities, tables, and columns protocol layer: uses MetaController + MQL for frontend and platform-side data access Java API layer: uses MetaFactory + Fluent DSL for backend service code extension layer: uses events, dynamic datasource, and SPI-based rule injection for platform-specific behavior

The current Geelato ORM state can be summarized as: it is not a heavyweight JPA/Hibernate-style stateful ORM it is not only a thin table-mapping helper either it is a metadata-centered data access system different entry points serve different runtime layers The recommended mental model is: @Entity / @Col / @Title / @Transient answer how objects map to relational structures MQL answers how platform-side JSON requests describe query and save behavior Fluent DSL answers how backend Java code performs CRUD and light advanced querying events, dynamic datasource, and SPI extensions answer how platform rules are injected into the execution path

This ORM system is designed to: keep Java objects, relational tables, columns, and metadata titles declared in one place let frontend protocol flow and backend Java flow reuse the same metadata model reduce repeated DAO boilerplate, scattered SQL assembly, and direct MQL JSON construction in services centralize dynamic datasource, view parameters, value references, default field filling, and query-rule injection move platform rules out of low-level CRUD and expose them through events or SPI extensions

Annotations answer: what is the entity? They define: which entity name and table a Java class maps to which column a field maps to which properties stay transient which titles and descriptions are attached to entities and fields See ORM Annotations.

MQL answers: how does the platform-side JSON protocol access data? It mainly targets: frontend pages platform-wide generic data APIs low-code or JSON-driven scenarios It typically includes capabilities such as: @fs field selection @p pagination @order sorting @group grouping @b nested boolean logic @pf view template parameters ref(...) referenced fields $ctx.* / $fn.* / $parent.* built-in variables MQL is closely related to ORM, but it is a platform protocol rather than the backend Java DSL. See MQL Overview and MQL Usage.

The Fluent DSL answers: how does backend Java service code access data? It mainly targets: server-side service code standard CRUD in Java light join, pagination, aggregation, and procedure use cases scenarios that want to reuse datasource switching, view parameters, and value references See Fluent DSL Guide.

Advanced features answer: how are platform rules injected beyond standard CRUD? Current extension areas include: ORM events around save and delete dynamic datasource switching query-filter SPI for tenant, permission, or organization rules field-filling SPI for audit and default values See: ORM Event Features ORM / Datasource Extension Query Filter and Field Fill SPI

Use the Geelato ORM system first when: backend services need standard CRUD by entity name or entity class platform APIs or frontend requests need JSON-based metadata access queries need pagination, sorting, light joins, lightweight aggregation, or lightweight procedure support the service wants to reuse datasource switching, view parameters, default filling, or value references Do not force it when: the query is SQL-first and depends on recursive CTEs, window functions, or very complex filtering the scenario depends on multi-result-set procedures or mapping-heavy MyBatis behavior the team already intentionally owns the final SQL text

MetaFactory + Fluent DSL: preferred for backend Java metadata CRUD MetaController + MQL: preferred for platform data APIs and frontend-facing protocol flow MetaFactory.sql(...): preferred when the team already owns the final SQL and only wants the execution chain MyBatis / native SQL: still the better fit for highly complex SQL and mapping-heavy cases

This page describes what an application package carries and the role each kind of content plays at runtime. The packing scope is determined jointly by the platform-table whitelist and each entity's data-pack strategy: the 19 platform tables are packed in full per app, and business tables are carried only when configured so at modeling time.

Packing runs select * per table with the following row scope: Table Scope Description platform_app by id The single app row; written into the package header appCode/appName, not into appMetaList platform_tree_node by tree_id The menu tree rooted at the app id Other platform tables (17) by app_id Whitelist detailed per layer below Business data tables by app_id Only entity tables with pack_bus_data > 0 and enabled Packable platform tables are restricted by the whitelist PlatformTableConstant; an application package can never carry tables outside it (tenants, users, platform-level configuration, etc.).

Table Entity Carried contents platform_app App Name/code/icon/theme/home link/watermark, designer file tree tree (jsTree JSON), dependency declaration depend_app_code, app secret app_key and token, version info version_info Runtime role: the basis of app registration and entry — the user-visible app list is computed from the role-app relation (platform_role_r_app); depend_app_code declares dependent app module codes (e.g. dev,sys) for the front end to load at startup; the header basePlatformVersion comes from the platform app geelato_admin's version_info and is quoted in the deployment validation upgrade message.

Table Entity Carried contents Runtime role platform_app_page AppPage Page source source_content and released release_content (component tree JSON), checkout status The runtime front end renders pages by fetching release_content via GET /api/page/getPageAndCustom/{pageId}; event logic embedded in pages travels inside the page JSON platform_tree_node TreeNode Menu tree (tree_id = app id), leaf extend_id pointing to pages The front end builds the navigation menu from the tree; clicking a menu leaf renders the page located by extend_id

Table Entity Carried contents Runtime role platform_dev_db_connect ConnectMeta Database connection definitions (dbType/host/db name/credentials…) Registered as dynamic data sources after startup; an entity's connect_id routes it to its database platform_dev_table TableMeta Entity definitions: entity name/table name/datasource/pack_bus_data strategy/cross-app flag Together with the three tables below, parsed at startup by MetaManager into in-memory EntityMeta, driving ORM reads/writes, the generic GQL endpoints (`/api/meta/list platform_dev_column ColumnMeta Field definitions: column/type/label/validation Same as above; API output shapes and page form fields derive from field metadata platform_dev_table_foreign TableForeign Foreign keys / constraints Basis of relation validation and cascades platform_dev_view TableView View definitions (incl. materialized views) View queries and materialized acceleration The data layer is the core of an application package: after persistence the metadata cache is refreshed entity by entity, so model changes take effect hot.

Whether business data travels with the package is decided by the data-pack strategy configured per entity at modeling time (platform_dev_table.pack_bus_data): Value Meaning Packing Deployment 0 Do not pack Not in the package — 1 Incremental All rows of this app in that table Target data is not cleared; rows with an existing id are skipped (idempotent merge) 2 Full All rows of this app in that table Target rows of this app are cleared, then package rows inserted Typical usage: incremental for dictionary-like seed data and base parameters; full for data that should migrate and be replaced with the app as a whole. The strategy is configured in the model designer's entity form.

Table Entity Carried contents Runtime role platform_role Role Roles (type distinguishes app/platform level) The principal of the authorization system platform_permission Permission Permission points and data rules rule (MQL fragments) rule is spliced into queries during reads/writes, implementing row-level data filtering platform_role_r_permission RolePermissionMap Role-permission relations Which permission points a role owns platform_role_r_tree_node RoleTreeNodeMap Role-menu relations Which menus a role sees platform_role_r_app RoleAppMap Role-app relations Which apps a user can enter platform_dict / platform_dict_item Dict / DictItem Dictionaries and items Front-end dropdown/tag rendering and value translation (GET /api/system/dictionary/{code}) platform_sys_config SysConfig App config key-values Merged with platform and tenant levels and served via GET /api/config platform_export_template ExportTemplate Export templates Format definitions for list/report exports platform_encoding Encoding Encoding rules Template-based generation of business numbers/codes platform_resources Resources Resource metadata rows (path/name/type…) Resource index; not the file binary contents (see below)

:::warning Handle separately when migrating The following are NOT carried by an application package: Contents Tables Description Service interfaces platform_api Standalone service-interface scripts (GraalJS) are not whitelisted; logic embedded in pages is unaffected, but pages depending on standalone interfaces will miss them after deployment SQL orchestrations platform_sql Custom SQL orchestrations (/api/sk/{key}) Scheduled tasks platform_schedule cron task definitions File binaries platform_file etc. platform_resources carries only metadata rows; attachments/images must be migrated separately through file storage Referenced contents of other apps — Entities/pages referenced across apps do not travel with this package (next section) :::

Inter-app dependencies are declared via platform_app.depend_app_code (comma-separated app codes); packing does no dependency analysis — the contents of depended-on apps are not pulled into the package automatically, so the target environment must already contain them before deployment. Cross-app authorization mounts for models/views/SQL orchestrations (platform_app_r_table/view/sql) are not in the manifest; re-grant them in the target environment. Entity metadata registers globally by entity name (no app filtering), so cross-app entity references are directly accessible with access control left to permission rules; platform_dev_table.across_app is only a model-level flag.

This page describes what happens when an application package reaches its target environment: the entry point and environment gate, pre-deploy validation, backup & rollback, the persistence strategy, activation, and failure behavior. The UI entry is the "Deploy" action in the version management page, endpoint GET /package/deploy/{versionId} (branching by geelato.package.engine).

Validation runs in the following order; any failure aborts with no data change: Environment gate: deployment is forbidden in environments whose geelato.package.env is init_source (60010), protecting the initialization source environment from being overwritten. Version & package readable: the version record exists with a valid packagePath; .zgdp files are read as archives (attachment ids resolved through the file service); a package without metadata raises 60003. Meta-model compatibility: every metaName in the package must have a matching entity definition in the target platform's MetaManager, and every column of every row must resolve to field metadata. Any miss raises 60004 with "please update the platform app geelato_admin to version X" (X being the package's basePlatformVersion). :::note What 60004 really means The baseline of this check is the target platform's current meta model, not a version-string comparison. 60004 means the package carries a table or column absent from the target platform's entity definitions — usually a too-old target platform or an unsynced source table structure. Upgrade the platform app geelato_admin as prompted and retry. :::

Automatic backup (v2 only): before deploying a non-backup version, the target app's current data is packed into a backup version (version suffix _backup, status backup). The backup commits independently and survives a failed deployment. Rollback: GET /package/rollback/{appId} re-deploys the latest backup version (deploying a backup version does not create another backup). The v1 engine produces no real backups, so rollback reports that no backup version was found.

Deployment writes each table of the package into the target database under one of two strategies. Incremental tables = the 5 platform incremental tables (platform_dict, platform_dict_item, platform_sys_config, platform_encoding, platform_resources) ∪ business tables with pack_bus_data=1; everything else is overwrite-type. Strategy Tables Delete phase Insert phase Semantics Overwrite Pages, menus, models, datasources, roles/permissions, export templates… Clear this app's old rows by app_id (platform_app by id, platform_tree_node by tree_id) Insert all package rows, primary keys preserved Package contents replace this app's data in the target environment Incremental The 5 platform incremental tables + pack_bus_data=1 business tables No deletion Insert package rows; rows whose id already exists are skipped Idempotent merge, safe to re-deploy All inserts preserve the package's original primary keys (forceId semantics) so cross-table references such as page–menu–model remain valid after deployment. Persistence runs in batches of 500 rows (the MQL SaveCommand pipeline, with the LargeObject serialization feature for large tables) and never round-trips a whole table through serialization, avoiding out-of-memory on large packages.

v1: delete and insert run inside one programmatic transaction; any metadata failure (unknown entity/column fails hard with 60005) rolls everything back, leaving the target database as before the deployment. v2: persistence runs batch-wise; unknown entities/columns are skipped with a warning; on a mid-way failure the already-written batches remain — there is no whole-package rollback. Incremental tables can be re-deployed safely (existing ids are skipped); overwrite tables simply replace their scope again on re-deploy. :::warning Handling a failed deployment Do not patch data manually after a v2 deployment failure: check ${LOG_DIR}/pack/ for the failing table and cause, fix it, and re-deploy the same version — overwrite tables replace wholesale and incremental tables skip existing ids, so repeated deployments converge to a consistent state. :::

After persistence succeeds, the runtime metadata of the deployed app is refreshed (refreshDBMeta entity by entity) and related query caches are invalidated — hot reload, no platform restart needed. Pages, dictionaries and config data are read on demand through caches, so the new data is served right after deployment. If the metadata cache refresh fails, error 60009 is raised ("deployment succeeded but refreshing the app metadata cache failed"): data is persisted, the deployment is not rolled back — handle per the log and reload.

Error codes are defined in PackException (60xxx segment): Code Phase Meaning 60001 Pack App not found 60002 Pack Pre-pack column-consistency check failed, packing blocked 60003 Deploy Version/package data missing or corrupted 60004 Deploy Meta-model validation failed; upgrade the platform app geelato_admin first 60005 Deploy Metadata or field missing on the target platform (hard failure in v1) 60006 Deploy Package data write failed 60007 General Illegal table name (injection guard) 60008 General Package file read/write failure 60009 Deploy Deployed successfully but metadata cache refresh failed 60010 General Operation not allowed in this environment / no backup to roll back

All pack and deploy logs are routed by logger name cn.geelato.web.platform.srv.pack into ${LOG_DIR}/pack/ (date-rolled, not leaked into the main log), covering start/end and timings of each pack/deploy, per-table row counts, every delete SQL, and every persisted or skipped entity. When investigating deployment differences, compare the logged per-table row counts against the package expectations first.

This chapter covers the packaged delivery of low-code applications only: an application package is the designer-produced app data bundle (.gdp / .zgdp), carrying metadata and business data between environments through pack → transfer → deploy → rollback; module cn.geelato:geelato-package + the /package service in web-platform. :::note Not in this chapter Plugin jars and host/launcher artifacts are different deliverables and are not part of application packaging: see Plugin Mechanism for plugins, and the Deployment Guide for host builds. :::

An application package is a complete data snapshot of an application at a point in time: it carries, as JSON, all configuration data the app produced in the designer, and can be transferred between environments and deployed into effect. Package data AppPackData: sourceAppId / targetAppId / version / appCode / appName + appMetaList (metadata entries, each {metaName, metaData} where metaName is the table/entity name and metaData is the row array) + appResourceList (resource entries) + basePlatformVersion (platform baseline at pack time, taken from the platform app geelato_admin's version_info). Two-level artifact: .gdp (full UTF-8 JSON package, default name geelatoApp) compressed into .zgdp (zip containing <appCode>/<appCode>.gdp). Package files are archived per tenant and app, and registered in the app version table platform_app_version (source packet/upload/sync, status draft/release/unused/deployed/backup). Module: cn.geelato:geelato-package; config prefix geelato.package.

Packaged contents fall into four layers by runtime responsibility; per-item details in Packaged Contents & Runtime Roles: Layer Contents Tables App body App definition, designer file tree, dependency declaration platform_app UI layer Pages, menu tree platform_app_page, platform_tree_node Data layer Database connections, models/fields/constraints/views platform_dev_db_connect, platform_dev_table/column/table_foreign/view Business data Carried per entity's data-pack strategy Business tables with pack_bus_data > 0 Governance layer Roles/permissions/authorizations, dictionaries, app config, export templates, encoding rules, resource metadata platform_role*, platform_dict(_item), platform_sys_config, platform_export_template, platform_encoding, platform_resources Service interfaces, SQL orchestrations and scheduled tasks are NOT in the package manifest and need separate handling for cross-environment migration; the full list and each item's runtime role are in Packaged Contents & Runtime Roles.

documents.t: Pack: export the app's rows from 19 whitelisted platform tables plus business tables selected by data-pack strategy, produce a .zgdp and register a version (status draft); see Packaging Flow. Transfer: download the .zgdp to the target environment and upload it there, or deploy directly in the same environment. Deploy: environment gate → package validation (every entity and column must exist in the target platform's meta model) → backup (v2) → persistence (overwrite tables are delete-then-insert, incremental tables merge by id) → metadata cache refresh; hot-reload takes effect without restart. See Deploying Application Packages. Rollback (v2 only): roll back to the latest backup version when a deployment fails or behaves unexpectedly.

Key (geelato.package.*) Default Description env — Environment tag; init_source environments reject deployment path — Root directory for package files uploadFolder — Upload sub-directory engine v1 Pack/deploy engine version: v1 (original) or v2 (evolved, below); backup and rollback are v2-only :::note Default engine is v1 engine defaults to v1. Backup, rollback and table-name guarding only take effect with v2; production environments should set geelato.package.engine=v2 explicitly. The three base keys are also described in System Configuration: Package Module. :::

geelato.package.engine selects the engine (strangler pattern: v1 is frozen, new capabilities land in v2 only): Dimension v1 v2 Entry points /package/packet, /deploy (same endpoints branch by engine) same State management singleton mutable state method-local context, no singleton state Deployment persistence programmatic transaction — delete+insert in one transaction, rolled back on failure batched persistence (500 rows/batch); on mid-way failure already-written batches remain and a re-deploy converges the state Backup/rollback no real backup auto backup before deploy + GET /package/rollback/{appId} Partial-pack semantics appointMetas is a whitelist: unlisted tables are excluded entirely appointMetas selects rows: unlisted tables are still packed in full Data cleansing — platform-table whitelist + table-name guard + batch 500
Commercial delivery across tenants/apps adds placeholder reset and id regeneration on top of application packages — see the app market docs (System Configuration: Market Module).
